The front end accepts the module. Not a match-lowering defect as far as the error goes; the match arm is only what routes emission through the site. Repro: `async def run(s: Step, n: int)` matching an enum subject, one arm doing `v = await tick(n)` and another returning directly. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, loud) An `@overload` group whose stubs are a plain param and an `Optional` of the same type emits two C++ signatures that an untyped literal cannot choose between.** A `describe(v: int32)` / `describe(v: int32 | None)` pair emits an ambiguous overload set: the call `describe(1)` fails with "call of overloaded 'describe(int)' is ambiguous". Sema resolves the overload happily, so the ambiguity is introduced by the emitted signatures rather than present in the source -- the Optional stub's parameter renders to something an `int` converts to just as well as the plain one. Fix shape: either mangle the specializations apart the way the Literal-stub path does, or emit the call already resolved to the selected stub instead of leaving the choice to C++. Repro: `@overload def describe(x: int) -> str: ...` plus `@overload def describe(x: int | None) -> str: ...` over an `x: int | None` implementation, called as `describe(5)`. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (silent CPython divergence, because the warning that exists for it MISSES the inherited case) The parent-`__del__` warning only inspects the DIRECT parent, so a `__del__` inherited from further up the chain fires no diagnostic while still running.** Base destructor chaining itself is deliberate, documented (`docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md`, the `__del__` entry: "Parent destructors are called automatically after child body") and warned: with `Base.__del__` and `Leaf(Base).__del__`, compiling emits "Parent class has `__del__()` which will be called automatically by C++ after this destructor runs. Unlike Python, you do not need `super().__del__()` -- but it also means the parent destructor always runs even without an explicit call." Insert a middle class that defines no `__del__` -- `Base.__del__`, `Middle(Base)`, `Leaf(Middle).__del__` -- and the behaviour is identical (both destructors run, CPython runs only `Leaf`'s) but **no warning is emitted at all**. So the divergence the warning exists to announce becomes silent exactly when the inheritance chain is deep enough for a reader to miss it unaided. Fix shape: walk the base chain for an inherited `__del__` rather than testing the immediate parent. Repro: `Base` with a printing `__del__`, `Middle(Base)` with none, `Leaf(Middle)` with its own printing `__del__`; construct a `Leaf` and let it drop -- TPy prints both, CPython prints one, and neither `tpyc` run warns. **An earlier draft of this entry filed the chaining itself as an undocumented silent divergence; both halves of that were wrong** (it is documented and it is warned), and the real defect is one level in -- recorded because the wrong version would have sent someone to write documentation that already exists. Surfaced measuring cpy-parity over the sweep's routing probes; corrected by /tpy-review (docs-sync).

- **[MED small] (latent, inconsistent spelling) Whether an integer literal takes an explicit `BigInt(...)` construction is decided per render site, not by a policy.** Two witnesses, pulling opposite ways. (1) An int literal at an inherited `@overload` stub through a subclass receiver: AST emits `d.greet(::tpy::BigInt(3))`, THIR emits `d.greet(3)` (`class Dog(Animal): pass` over `greet(x: int)` / `greet(x: str)`). (2) A list-literal for-loop source compiled at `--default-int BigInt`: AST emits `auto __obj_0 = {10, 0, 1};`, THIR emits `auto __obj_0 = {::tpy::BigInt(10), ...}`. Both witnesses compile, link, and print byte-identical output on both paths, so each instance is benign -- filed because the CLASS is not: an overload set with an ambiguous implicit conversion or a narrower integral overload would resolve differently between the two spellings, and the AST's bare `{10, 0, 1}` deduces `std::initializer_list<int>` at a width where the elements are meant to be `BigInt`, which is only harmless while the conversion happens to be reachable. Fix is to decide which spelling is intended and hold one policy across the sites, not to pick per site. The AST body emitter this was measured against was deleted 2026-09-03, so the witnesses below record what the two spellings were rather than a live disagreement -- what survives is that lowering has no single rule. **Note the second witness is invisible at `--default-int int32`** -- it is the first option-gated AST/THIR divergence anyone has caught, and the reason the sweep runner now sweeps all three widths. The second witness needs `--default-int BigInt`; at int32 it is byte-identical. **Re-swept 2026-09-02 at the cutover flip's parent tree (`1be2cf003`): breadth only, no new mechanism.** The same class reproduces at eight further sinks -- `ListPrinter` / `TuplePrinter` print arguments, a tuple literal at an `Optional[tuple]` parameter (three variants), a generic-record constructor argument, a tuple-compare RHS, a nested list-inside-tuple literal and a resumable-frame tuple assign -- plus one at a `list[list[int32]]` call argument, all at `--default-int BigInt` and all in the THIR-wraps direction, and at one further reverse-direction sink (`y = (t := 5)`: AST `::tpy::BigInt(5)`, THIR bare `5`). The fix is still to decide one spelling, not to patch a sink. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. **Current faces (2026-09-28, THIR only, identical at all three widths):** the same literal at three `int` slots is spelled three ways -- a method argument bare (`c.bump(1073741824);`), a free-function argument wrapped (`f(::tpy::BigInt(1073741824))`), an async return bare into the `::tpy::BigInt __tpy_async_ret` slot; a literal past the int32 range gains `static_cast<int64_t>(...)` at all three and keeps the wrap only at the free function (`f(::tpy::BigInt(static_cast<int64_t>(1099511627776LL)))`, `c.bump(static_cast<int64_t>(1099511627776))`, `::tpy::BigInt __tpy_async_ret = static_cast<int64_t>(1099511627776);`). Probes `/tmp/agents/ge/file/q_bigint_wrap2.py`, `q_bigint_wrap3.py`.

- **[LOW small] (codegen quality) A `for` loop over ANOTHER module's pointer-slot global takes the generic `__iter__`/`__next__` path instead of the native begin/end peephole.** [`thir-module-global-foreach-no-peephole`] `import sys` then `for a in sys.argv:` emits `auto& __obj_0 = (*::tpystd::sys::argv); auto __beg_0 = __obj_0.begin(); auto __end_0 = __obj_0.end(); for (; __beg_0 != __end_0; ++__beg_0)` on the AST path, against `auto&& __itr_0 = ::tpy::__iter__(__src_0);` plus a per-step `__itr_0.__next__()` and an `unwrap_ref` through THIR. All three widths, zero fallback in the diverging body. The trigger is the module-QUALIFIED read of another module's pointer-slot global: a global of the ENTRY module (`xs = [1, 2, 3]` then `for a in xs:`) is byte-identical on both paths. The AST render is the better one (a raw iterator pair over the container against an optional-returning protocol call per step), so this is a **codegen-quality regression relative to the AST for that one shape, not a correctness one** -- and since THIR now authors every body, the generic form is what actually ships. Text-level only: the sweep that found it ran the FRONT END only, so no C++ build stands behind either render. No corpus witness -- no case in `tests/cases` for-loops over `sys.argv` (the four that mention it use `len()`, `__len__()` or a slice), and `os.environ` is a record with its own `__iter__`, which never takes the peephole either. Distinct from the TODO.md peephole entry about a narrowed-Optional receiver, which is a single-path perf item on the AST side. Repro: `import sys` / `def f() -> None: for a in sys.argv: print(a)` / `f()`. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (latent, `--default-int int64` only) A folded integer constant outside the int32 range is emitted without its `static_cast<int64_t>`.** [`thir-folded-wide-literal-drops-int64-cast`] `print(2**40 + 1)` emits `std::cout << static_cast<int64_t>(1099511627777)` on the AST path against a bare `std::cout << 1099511627777` through THIR, and `def use(n: int) -> None: print(n < 2**40 - 1)` diverges the same way at the compare operand (`(n < static_cast<int64_t>(1099511627775))` vs `(n < 1099511627775)`). Both fold to the same value; the cast is what pins the operand's TYPE, and without it C++ gives the literal the first of `int` / `long` / `long long` that fits it, which is not necessarily the width the surrounding overload set or template deduction wanted, and is not the same choice on every target. **The cast is believed right** (the deleted AST body emitter spelled it), and the bare literal is what users get today. Byte-identical at int32 and BigInt, so this is option-gated like the BigInt-wrapping class above. **Build-verified 2026-09-02:** the bare literal that ships today builds and runs at `--default-int int64` and prints what CPython prints (`1099511627777`, then `True` / `False` for the compare probe at 5 and 2**40), so on this target the dropped cast costs nothing observable -- what remains at risk is the width C++ picks for the literal on a target where `int` / `long` / `long long` differ, which one host cannot settle. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`. A fix was attempted in the 0.6 gate batch E and dropped: every consumer that picks its C++ from the literal's type needs one integer-literal spelling rule first (f-string `.to_string()`, `~` / `-` operands, `pow` / `abs` overload choice, index / slice bounds; TODO.md "One spelling rule for integer literals").

- **[HIGH small] (silent run-time panic at the DEFAULT width on code master ran; REGRESSION since v0.5.0) A variable-free constant at an `int` METHOD ARGUMENT is not folded by THIR, so an intermediate wider than int32 traps at run time where the AST folded it.** [`thir-int-methodarg-shift-not-folded`] `class C` with `def bump(self, k: int) -> int`, called as `c.bump((2**30 * 4) // 4)`: CPython prints 1073741824, master's AST emit was `c.bump(1073741824)`, THIR (now the author) emits `c.bump(div_check<int32_t>(mul_check<int32_t>(pow_check<int32_t>(2, 30), 4), 4))` and aborts with `int32 overflow in multiplication`. No warning. The free-function and constructor argument positions were already unfolded on BOTH paths (a pre-existing panic there); the method-argument position is what the THIR switch regressed. A fix -- uniform constant folding in both authors, plus sema range checks at the slots that silently wrapped -- exists on the parked branch `thir-fold-wip` and grew into a redesign of the emitter's per-site target threading; the narrow fix is to mirror the AST's target-less fold at this one position, or to promote the literal chain to BigInt when an intermediate leaves the default width. The original sweep text follows for the int64 face.  `class Counter` with `def bump(self, k: int) -> int`, called as `c.bump((1 << 33) + 1)`, emits `c.bump(static_cast<int64_t>(8589934593))` on the AST path against `c.bump((::tpy::add_check<int64_t>(::tpy::lshift_check<int64_t>(1, 33), 1)))` through THIR -- THIR does not fold the argument at all, so the value is computed at run time through two overflow-checked ops the folded literal skips. Same value either way at this width; the difference is one constant against two guarded runtime ops, and at a width where the shift DID overflow the two paths would disagree about whether the program raises at compile time or at run time. **The AST spelling is believed right.** Byte-identical at int32 and BigInt. Sibling of the folded-literal entry above -- both are the constant fold not reaching a THIR sink -- but the proximate causes differ: there the fold happens and the cast is dropped, here the fold does not happen. Text-level only: no C++ build stands behind either render (front-end sweep). With THIR the author, the checked chain is what ships. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`. A fix was attempted in the 0.6 gate batch E and dropped: every consumer that picks its C++ from the literal's type needs one integer-literal spelling rule first (f-string `.to_string()`, `~` / `-` operands, `pow` / `abs` overload choice, index / slice bounds; TODO.md "One spelling rule for integer literals").

- **[MED small] (rejects valid, loud) A field common to EVERY member of a union is not accessible after `isinstance` narrows to a proper sub-union.** `def classify(x: A | B | C)` with `if isinstance(x, (A, B)): return x.tag` is rejected "Cannot access field 'tag' on type A | B", although all three classes declare `tag: str`. The tuple form of `isinstance` narrows correctly -- the reported type IS `A | B` -- but field access requires a single concrete member, so a narrowing that lands on two members leaves the value unusable even for a field they share. CPython runs the program. The single-member forms work, so the gap is specifically a union with more than one remaining member. Fix shape: allow field access when every member declares the name at a compatible type, emitting a visit over the variant. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. Needs `/tpy-add-feature` (a capability gap, not a violated invariant).

- **[MED small] (rejects valid, loud -- two equivalent spellings disagree) A class pattern against `Optional[A | B]` is rejected, while the identical type spelled `A | B | None` is accepted.** `match v: case Card(): ...` where `v: Optional[Card | Cash]` fails with "class pattern not valid for Optional inner type 'Card | Cash'"; rewriting the annotation as `Card | Cash | None` compiles and runs. The Optional analysis path special-cases a single-record inner type only, while the plain union path handles multi-member class dispatch, so the two spellings of one type take different code paths and only one of them works. The same asymmetry rejects a class pattern against an Optional VALUE type (`case int32():` on an `int32 | None`), which the union path also accepts in its own spelling. Fix shape: normalize `Optional[Union[...]]` to the union form before pattern analysis so one path serves both. The value-type sibling is `match b.val: case int32() as v if v > 10:` where `b.val: int32 | None`. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (rejects valid, loud) A structural protocol declaring BOTH `__len__` and `__contains__` makes the conforming class's own `__len__` body fail to analyze.** A `Protocol` with both dunders, used as a parameter type, makes `Basket.__len__`'s ordinary body (`return int32(len(self.items))`) fail with "No matching overload for len(readonly[list[int32]])" -- `self` is apparently re-analyzed as `readonly[Basket]`, and `len` has no overload for a readonly container. Isolated: `__len__` alone conforms fine; `__len__` + `__eq__` conforms fine; the concrete class called directly conforms fine; only the `__len__` + `__contains__` pair triggers it. The same `int32(len(self.items))` body appears unmodified in committed protocol cases, so this is a conformance-checking side effect rather than a body defect. Two candidate fixes and they are not the same: give `len` a readonly-container overload (widest, also fixes any other readonly-receiver call), or stop the implicitly-readonly `__contains__` from forcing a readonly re-analysis of its sibling methods. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (rejects valid, loud) Slice assignment on a `bytearray` is entirely unimplemented, including the non-stepped form.** `ba[1:4] = b"AB"` fails with "Slice assignment not supported for type 'Own[bytearray]'". `list` supports basic and stepped slice assignment and `str` slicing works, so `bytearray` -- the mutable byte container, whose whole point is in-place edits -- is the one container with none of it. Distinct from the tracked stepped-slice READ entry, which is about the returned type. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. Needs `/tpy-add-feature`.

- **[MED small] (rejects valid, loud) A tuple-unpack target list may hold only bare names, so the idiomatic in-place swap `xs[i], xs[j] = xs[j], xs[i]` is rejected at parse time.** "Tuple unpacking targets must be simple variable names" -- subscript and attribute targets are refused, although the same targets are accepted in a chained multi-assignment. `docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md` documents the restriction only for multiple assignment, so a reader looking for this one does not find it. Rejected in the parser, so both codegen paths agree and there is no divergence risk -- it is purely a missing capability, and a common one: element swap is the canonical form in sorting and shuffling code. Surfaced by the pre-deletion adversarial dual-path sweep. Needs `/tpy-add-feature`.

- **[HIGH small] (ill-formed C++ twice over) `@overload` on a GENERATOR emits one union-typed frame whose signature and whose body disagree about constness -- and the call site was resolved against the narrow stub.** Two `@overload` stubs (`walk(v: A)` / `walk(v: B)`) over a `def walk(v: A | B) -> Iterator[int32]` implementation emit a single factory `__gen_walk walk(std::variant<const A*, const B*> v)` and no per-stub specialization at all, so the call site emits a bare `walk(a)` with `a: A` and fails to convert (`could not convert 'a' from 'A' to 'std::variant<const A*, const B*>'`). Inside the frame the isinstance narrowing renders the TEST const-correctly (`std::holds_alternative<const A*>(v)`) but the EXTRACTION bare (`auto& __v = *std::get<A*>(v);`), a second, independent failure (`static assertion failed: T must occur exactly once in alternatives`) -- one render pair built from two different const sources. The signature's `const` comes from the overload group's param analysis in `codegen_cpp/functions.py`; the extraction alias comes from `_make_narrow_alias` under `_lower_narrowed_branch` (`tpyc/thir/lower/statements.py:5287`), which does not carry the group's constness. Distinct from the `async def` sibling above: async emits one frame PER overload entry (a redefinition), the generator emits ONE frame with a wrong signature -- a `...` stub body is not a generator, so only the impl reaches the frame emitter. The non-overloaded generator over the same union param is CONSISTENT and compiles (`std::variant<A*, B*>` in the signature, the tests, the extractions, and a wrapped `walk(std::variant<A*, B*>{&(a)})` call site) -- verified, which is what isolates the overload router as the source of both halves. Loud, toolchain-caught; no corpus case holds the shape. Fix shape: give the generator router the per-stub specialization the sync overload path already emits, and derive the frame body's extraction spelling from the same param types the signature uses. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[HIGH small, deferred: MIR] (rejects valid code) A nested `match` whose subject is a name the enclosing arm narrowed is rejected when an arm binds a `T | None` field inside a generator/`async`, but the program is correct.** `tests/cases/iterators/error_gen_match_nested_narrowed_ptr_bind` is that program, committed as an `error_` case (re-verified 2026-09-03: it still errors at line 31). Its own header comment claims the narrowed subject "renders to a dispatch-local extraction alias (`__case_N`), not a frame field -- so a pointer-repr `Optional` field binding from it would dangle across the suspension". That is wrong: every writer of the narrowing alias map emits a C++ REFERENCE (`auto& __case_0 = *std::get<0>(...)`, `T& l = *cast`, `(*init_local)`), never a copy, so the alias's address is the referent's; and in a resumable body every user local is already a frame field, so the referent is frame-rooted. With the guard neutralized the committed source compiles, links, runs and prints `1 / 5 / 2` -- byte-identical to CPython under `lib/cpy`. The guard is the `narrowed` conjunct of `resumable_match_subject_is_stable` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/emit_prims.py:1078`), consulted by `_select_match_route` (`tpyc/thir/lower/match.py:1110`) before it lets a capture land in an `opt_ptr_frame_locals` field; that conjunct is the wrong half. The `match_subject_is_lvalue` half is CORRECT and load-bearing -- with it removed, an rvalue subject stores the address of a by-value dispatch local into a frame field and prints garbage after the suspension (verified with a running binary). So the fix drops one conjunct, it does not drop the guard. **The counter-argument, recorded because it is not obviously wrong:** "it compiles, links, runs and matches CPython" is exactly what a use-after-free reading not-yet-reused stack memory does, so a passing run cannot on its own retire a dangling-pointer claim. What makes the evidence above stronger than that objection is the MECHANISM -- references rather than copies -- and the CONTROL, since removing the other conjunct does produce garbage, which shows the harness can detect the failure it is claimed not to be hiding. **The settlement, if anyone wants certainty:** neutralize the conjunct and run the case under ASan; a frame-rooted referent passes clean, a stack alias reports. Nobody has run that yet.
**Two claims in the paragraph above went stale on 2026-09-01 and are corrected here**, since a reader acting on them would be misled: THIR now DOES raise this diagnostic (both paths read one shared `resumable_match_subject_is_stable` predicate), and the error-path gate that tracked it (`tests/conftest.py::AST_ONLY_DIAGNOSTICS`) reached empty and was deleted with the AST emitters on 2026-09-03. The instruction this entry carried -- do not write the THIR mirror until the guard is fixed -- WAS overridden, deliberately and with reasoning recorded in the teardown inventory in `docs/THIR_COMPLETION_LEDGER.md`: the mirror is behaviourally inert (same message, same committed diagnostic, no snapshot moved), nothing about it is permanent, and consolidating the disputed condition into one shared predicate makes this very fix a single-line edit instead of two spellings that can drift. **So the fix is now: drop `not subject_is_narrowed` from `resumable_match_subject_is_stable` in `tpyc/codegen_cpp/emit_prims.py`, and both paths follow.**
**While in there:** that predicate consults the narrowed set only for a bare name subject. A nested field or subscript rooted at a narrowed name falls through to the plain lvalue test, whose name base case answers True regardless of narrowing -- so `match narrowed_x.field:` is admitted while `match narrowed_x:` is condemned, which is incoherent whichever way the conjunct question resolves. Pre-existing (the AST spelling had the identical non-recursive shape); it is called out here rather than filed separately because a third entry about one predicate is the duplication this reconciliation exists to remove. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[HIGH small] (rejects-valid at both scopes, the frame face at `res.local_storage`; was silent object slicing at frame scope) The polymorphic-rvalue-into-`Optional`-local diagnostics went with their emitter, and only one of the two shapes is still caught.** Re-measured 2026-09-03. SYNC scope: `d = Dog(); p: Optional[Pet] = d; p = Cat()` now fails at the DECL with `error: in function 'f': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.var_decl:decl.slot_type)`, and `p: Optional[Pet] = Dog(); p = Cat()` with `(stmt.var_decl:decl.opt_slot_source)` -- no wrong code escapes there, but the message no longer names the cause. FRAME scope is the live defect: inside a generator or `async` body, `p: Optional[Pet] = Dog(1)` with NO rebind anywhere COMPILES and emits `std::optional<Pet> __ptr_slot_f0;` plus `p = &*(__ptr_slot_f0 = Dog(::tpy::BigInt(1)));` -- the frame slot is typed from the DECLARED type, so the `Dog` rvalue slices into a `Pet`, silently. That is exactly the shape the deleted AST raise covered, and no corpus case carries it, which is why nothing caught it. Both wants a case. Note also that the deleted message named "with rvalue rebind" on a program containing no rebind, so whichever fix lands should word the init-only form for itself rather than reuse that sentence. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A pointer-repr `Optional[record]` local takes a plain NAME source at its first declaration and little else -- five ordinary source shapes still reject, same-type and upcast alike.** [`opt-ptr-local-non-name-sources`] With `class Dog(Pet)` and `d = Dog(1)`, each of these is a valid aliasing bind (a `Pet*` re-pointed at live storage, no copy) that the lowering has no arm for: (1) a FIELD-access source, `p: Pet | None = self.d` -> `decl.slot_type`; (2) a name-source decl that is later rebound, `p: Pet | None = d; p = c` -> `decl.slot_type` (the reseat pre-scan sends the decl down a rung the address-of lift is not on); (3) a None-init local re-pointed at a record LOCAL, `p: Pet | None = None; p = d` -> `decl.opt_reseat_source`, and at a record PARAM -> `decl.reseat_param_source` (a fence in the sync reseat arm whose own comment says its rationale no longer holds; the frame flavor of the same shape lowers); (4) a frame LOCAL record source, `d = Dog(1); p: Pet | None = d` inside a generator or `async` body -> `decl.opt_reseat_source` (a frame PARAM source lowers); (5) a record name at an Optional ELEMENT of a container literal, `lst: list[Pet | None] = [d]` -> `expr.container_literal`, deferred by the design comment in `_container_literal_elem_ok` (the storage slot is `std::optional<Pet>`, so this one is a COPY into the element rather than an alias, and wants the copy warning the field store gives). Not upcast-specific: the same-type sources reject with the same tags, so the fix is one address-of arm per position, keyed on the source's lvalue-ness, not on its type. Reproducers under `/tmp/agents/bug_upcast_opt_local/` (`c_selfd_same.py`, `c_rebind_opt_same_named.py`, `c_rebind_same.py`, `c_param_src_rebind_none.py`, `c_gen_same.py`, `c_list_same.py`; the `s_*.py` twins are the upcast forms). Found 2026-09-12 while closing the upcast-into-`Optional`-local reject.

- **[MED small] (uncompilable C++) A `@nocopy`-element container literal renders as a brace-init instead of `make_vector`, at more than one sink.** `Bag[T]` with `def __init__(self, xs: Own[list[T]])`, instantiated `Bag([Tok(1), Tok(2)])` for a `@nocopy` `Tok`: the AST emits `Bag<Tok>(::tpy::make_vector<std::array<Tok, 2>>(Tok(1), Tok(2)))`, THIR emits `Bag<Tok>({Tok(1), Tok(2)})`. A `std::vector<Tok>` brace-init goes through `initializer_list`, which COPIES, so the THIR spelling does not compile for a non-copyable element. The trigger is the `@nocopy` ELEMENT, not genericity, and not the ctor-arg position -- a first draft of this entry claimed it needed both a generic record and an open type param, because only ctor-param sinks had been probed. A second witness has no generic record and no ctor param at all: a nested container literal at a plain local decl, `pp = [[Box(Pet(3))]]`, emits `make_vector<vector<Box<Pet>>>(make_vector<std::array<Box<Pet>, 1>>(Box(Pet(3))))` on the AST path against `make_vector<vector<Box<Pet>>>({Box(Pet(3))})` through THIR. Copyable elements are byte-identical at both sinks, which is what isolates `@nocopy` as the trigger. So the shape is a container literal losing the `make_vector` materialization at more than one sink; treat the sink list as open rather than as the two probed so far. No corpus witness (neither the case corpus nor the stdlib oracle carries the pair), which is why the byte-diff has not caught it. **Confirmed pre-existing**: the identical divergence reproduces on master, so it is not a migration artifact -- which also means no gate will re-find it, because no corpus case pairs a generic record with a `@nocopy` element, the ratchet sees a routed body, and the move-join has nothing to join. Repro (compile the same source twice through `tpyc.thir.testutil._compile` with `thir_codegen` False then True and diff the emitted strings): `@nocopy class Tok: v: int32`; `class Bag[T]: xs: list[T]` with `def __init__(self, xs: Own[list[T]])`; then `b = Bag([Tok(1), Tok(2)])`. AST emits `make_vector`, THIR emits `Bag<Tok>({Tok(1), Tok(2)})`. Surfaced by the blast sweep of the generic hoisted-slot return rows. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (uncompilable C++) A nested `def` inside a RESUMABLE-FRAME generator that rebinds an enclosing record local via `nonlocal` writes the frame slot with `operator=`, which is deleted.** [`nested-def-nonlocal-frame-slot-assign`] The TUPLE local twin fails the same way: `t = mk(0); def reb(): nonlocal t; t = mk(10)` in a generator emits `t = ...` over `::tpy::frame_slot<std::tuple<A, A>>` (verified 2026-09-22 on `a6a22715c3`, probe `/tmp/agents/rv4r2/p08_nested_def_write.py`); with an element alias of `t` taken before, it now rejects at `res.alias_bind` first. The enclosing local lives in the coroutine frame as a `::tpy::frame_slot<Point>` member; the AST emits the rebind as `p.emplace(Point(7));`, THIR emits `p = Point(7);`. Both `frame_slot` specializations delete copy AND move assignment and deliberately provide no converting assign from a `T` value (`runtime/cpp/include/tpy/frame_slot.hpp` states this at the primary template: codegen is expected to spell the write explicitly), so the TU fails: `no match for 'operator=' (operand types are 'tpy::frame_slot<Point>' and 'Point')`, with both deleted candidates named. The AST build compiles, runs and prints the right answer, so this is purely the THIR render. **Confirmed pre-existing**: ablating BOTH cross-scope-rebind predicates (`cross_scope_rebind_site` and `_rejects_lambda_hoist`) leaves the emitted THIR byte-for-byte unchanged, and neither predicate's call site is on the resumable path at all -- so the recent sgen rebind-slot fix neither caused nor could have caught it. **Live on the DEFAULT path since the flip: THIR authors every body, so a plain `tpy` on the repro fails the C++ build** with `no match for 'operator='` and the deleted `frame_slot` candidates (re-verified 2026-09-02). Stays MED rather than HIGH: it is a loud build failure on an advanced shape (a nested `def` rebinding an enclosing record local through `nonlocal` inside a generator), which is how the file rates the sibling `resumable-comp-walrus-scope`. No gate sees it: no corpus case carries the shape, the ratchet only sees a routed body, and even if one did fall back the fallback would emit byte-identical AST. It is the same "which frame owns this slot" question the sgen lambda rebind-slot fix answered (`0312fbd19`), one scope further out -- there the slot was reserved in the enclosing function and consumed inside a lambda; here it is a frame MEMBER written from a nested def -- so whichever fix lands should settle the frame-slot write form for both, not just this render. Repro: `class Point:` with `x: int32` and an `__init__`; `def before_while(n: int32) -> Iterator[int32]:` whose body is `p = Point(11)`, then a nested `def bump() -> int32:` doing `nonlocal p` / `p = Point(7)` / `return p.x`, then `k = bump()` and a `while i < n:` loop yielding `p.x + k`. Run it once with `tpy`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.


- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A genuine `else:` after an isinstance chain over a 3+-member NULLABLE union is rejected.** For `h: A | B | C | None` (a pointer variant, `std::variant<std::monostate, A*, B*, C*>`), the chain `if isinstance(h, A): ... elif isinstance(h, B): ... else: ...` gives `error: in function 'probe': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.if:if.narrow_shape)` at the `if` line. The ill-formed `auto& __h = *std::get<std::optional<C>*>(h);` this entry recorded is GONE -- lowering declines instead of emitting it. The gate is `_narrow_facts_ok` on the else fact (`tpyc/thir/lower/statements.py:12955-12983`): sema hands the else branch `Optional[C]` rather than a concrete member, and only the no-else and elif-continuation shapes are excused. Two-member unions do not reproduce (the remainder is a plain member), and neither does an elif-only chain -- both compile clean. Everyday shape (an isinstance ladder with a fallback `else`), so worth queueing. Fix shape: normalise the remainder fact to the concrete member `C` before the narrow gate sees it, and skip the extraction when the alias is dead in the else body. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED] The CPython `Span` stub COPIES where TPy aliases, so every slice test is structurally parity-blind.** `lib/cpy/tpy/__init__.py`'s `Span.__getitem__` does `Span(self._data[index])` -- an independent Python list slice -- while TPy's documented contract is zero-copy (`docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md`: "Container slicing: `items[1:3]` -> `Span[T]` (zero-copy)"), and the builtin `list[T]` has the same view contract. Probed both directions: after `sp = a[1:4]`, mutating `a[1] = 999` is visible through the span under TPy and NOT under the stub; mutating `sp[0] = 999` propagates back to `a` under TPy and not under the stub. The consequence is not a wrong answer today -- it is that the cpy phase cannot ever catch a slice-aliasing regression, because the two sides are specified differently, so any test that WOULD detect one fails for the stub's reason instead. `tests/cases/list/tplib_array_list_slice` is read-only and therefore passes while proving nothing about the boundary it exists for, which is exactly what CLAUDE.md's "reference-type happy tests must force the value-vs-reference distinction" rule forbids. Fix shape is a decision, not a patch: either make the stub alias (a `memoryview`-like or index-offset view, so mutation coverage becomes meaningful under both) and then add the mutation assertions, or declare the divergence and mark the slice cases `no_cpython.txt` so the blindness is explicit rather than accidental. Blast radius is every case that slices a container, so it is not a drive-by. Surfaced by /tpy-review (cpython-parity) of the stdlib THIR grind, while threading `array_list::__getitem__`'s slice arm through THIR.

- **[MED small] (uncompilable C++) A lowered body emits a hoisted argument temp AFTER the storage-optional decl slot that consumes it, producing ill-formed C++ (`'__tmp_1' was not declared in this scope`).** THIR emits `std::optional<Node> __slot_1 = relay(__tmp_1); ... Node __tmp_1 = Node(1);` where the AST emits the temp FIRST. Three conditions are all required: the callee param is a bare reference-type annotation (a BORROW -- `x: Node`, rendering `const Node&`), the argument is an rvalue (a constructor call, not a name), and the call initializes a decl whose slot is the `Own[T | None]` storage optional (`__slot_N` + `optional_to_ptr`). Note the hoist keys on the DECLARED param form, not the rendered const-ness: `x: Node` and `x: readonly[Node]` emit the identical `const Node& x` signature and disagree about hoisting -- the explicit `readonly` spelling suppresses it, and `x: Own[Node]` passes inline so never hoists. Hoisting is not the bug: with a `-> int` return the same call hoists and both paths stay byte-identical. The bug is that the storage-optional decl-slot row emits its slot line before flushing pending argument temps. Loud (a hard g++ error, not a miscompile) but uncovered: no corpus case has the shape. Reproduced independently twice, and the emitted THIR `.cpp` was compiled to confirm the diagnostic while the AST `.cpp` compiles clean under the same command. Repro: `def relay(x: Node) -> Own[Node | None]: return None` called as `r = relay(Node(1))`. Fix shape: flush pending argument temps before the storage-optional slot line, not after. Surfaced by adversarial probing during the stdlib THIR grind. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED] (compiler crash, two triggers) Sema recurses to death (`Internal error: maximum recursion depth exceeded`) on a call returning one recursive type alias at a slot typed by a DIFFERENT but structurally identical recursive alias.** `type J = None | int | list[J]` and `type K = None | int | list[K]`, then `def mk() -> Own[K]` returned from `def load() -> Own[J]`. The program should get a type error (`K` is not `J`); instead the front end crashes before codegen, so THIR is not involved. The 1000-frame cycle is `compatibility.py deep_convertible_to_union -> _elem_convertible_to_union -> _check_compat -> _check_compat`, bottoming out through `_resolve_recursive_refs` -> `typesys.needs_wrapper` -> `wrapper_info` -> `__hash__`. Two DISTINCT but structurally identical aliases are required: a single alias, or two aliases without the cross-alias return, both compile fine. Fix shape: memoise or depth-bound the recursive-alias compatibility walk so structural identity terminates instead of unrolling. Surfaced during the stdlib THIR grind. **A second trigger, same cycle, confirmed separately:** a plain ASSIGN reaches it too -- with `type J = None | bool | int | str | list[J]` and `type K = None | int | str | list[K]`, binding a `K`-typed value at an `Own[J]` slot (`value = readk(n)` then `return value`) exits with `RecursionError` rather than a diagnostic, via `_check_compat`'s deep-union-leaf arm: checking `list[K]` against `J` re-enters on `list[J]` against `K`. So the defect is the missing visited-pair guard in the deep-union recursion, not anything specific to the return position, and a fix must be verified against both triggers. Whether either program should be ACCEPTED is a separate question (`K`'s members are not a subset of `J`'s once the list arms are compared) -- but a crash is never the right answer, and a seen-pair set threaded through the recursion lets the existing mismatch diagnostic fire. Second repro: `type J = None | bool | int | str | list[J]` and `type K = None | int | str | list[K]`, an `@error_return` `def readk(n: int32) -> Own[K]`, then `v = readk(1)` bound at an `Own[J]` slot, surfaced building a boundary fixture for the THIR wrapper-union return rows. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (a DIAGNOSTIC that misattributes -- claims something it did not measure) The `tpy| exec: stdlib output changed since last run` banner fires for ANY edit under `tpyc/`, even when the emitted stdlib C++ is byte-identical.** `_hash_files` keys each file on its path relative to `PROJECT_ROOT` and falls back to the ABSOLUTE path for anything outside it. The stdlib cache's generated `.cpp`/`.hpp` live under `~/.cache/tpyc/stdlib-objs/<key>/build/`, so their contribution to `output_hash` is salted by the cache key -- and `_stdlib_cache_key()` folds `_tpyc_hash()`. So any compiler edit re-keys the cache, changes the salt, and yields a different `output_hash` for unchanged output. Confirmed symmetric (a modified tree announces once then goes quiet; reverting to HEAD announces again), and an independent A/B over the 88-module sweep showed the emitted stdlib C++ byte-identical across the same edit. **Harmless for correctness** -- a `tpyc/` change legitimately re-keys every exec marker anyway, so the rebuild it announces is real -- but the banner names the wrong cause, and its whole purpose is to explain to a developer WHY a whole-suite re-verify just happened. Fix shape: hash the stdlib generated sources on a path key that excludes the cache directory, or word the banner for what it actually detects (the cache re-keyed) rather than what it asserts (the output changed). Surfaced during the arg-ladder fold's teardown step.


- **[LOW small] (latent render question -- no corpus case reaches the shape) A container literal target-typed to a BigInt-element span renders its elements wrapped on the THIR path and bare on the AST path.** `nums = [1, 2, 3]` feeding a `Span[readonly[int]]` slot emits `std::array<...>{1, 2, 3}` on the AST path against `{::tpy::BigInt(1), ::tpy::BigInt(2), ::tpy::BigInt(3)}` through THIR. This is a DECL-sink divergence, not an argument-gate one -- confirmed by removing the line, after which the same program is `IDENTICAL` with zero fallback. Pre-existing: reproduces identically on the PRE-FOLD tree of the branch that found it (the three folded source files stashed), which is what was actually measured -- it was not run against a named master commit. Since those three files are the only fold changes, that establishes the fold did not cause it; it does not establish when it started. No corpus case holds the shape, so the byte-diff and the ratchet are both blind to it. The AST render it was measured against is gone (the body emitters were deleted 2026-09-03), so what ships is the THIR spelling and the fix starts by deciding what the render should be, not by matching a second author. Shape of the fix if the wrap is wrong: carry the element target type through the span-slot decl sink. Surfaced by adversarial dualgen during the fold's step E.

- **[MED small] (THIR validator blind spot -- no repro produced) `THIRFrameSlotWrite` is exempt from the "BORROW value at a pointer-lifted storage sink" check, and resumable frames route exactly the guarded type family through it.** `_check_stmt` (`tpyc/thir/validate.py:270-281`) applies the rule only to a `THIRAssign` whose target is a `THIRFieldAccess`; every node reaches `_check_stmt`, but it carries no arm for `THIRFrameSlotWrite`, which gets a `_walk` arm granting the value a flush right and nothing else. Meanwhile `tpyc/thir/lower/resumable.py:1443-1446` admits pointer-repr `UnionType` frame locals as frame slots -- the same `is_ptr_variant_union` family `_pointer_lifted_storage` exists to guard -- and their writes lower to `THIRFrameSlotWrite`, not `THIRAssign`. So a borrow value emplaced into such a slot without its borrow->storage convert passes validation silently, where the field-write equivalent fails loudly. UNCERTAIN whether it is reachable: no repro was produced, and a real mismatch may well fail at the C++ build (`emplace` of a `T*` into a `variant<A, B>`) rather than miscompile -- what is certain is that the highest-value structural check does not cover the node kind the frames actually write through. Fix is NOT a one-line extension: adding a node kind to `_check_stmt` is the same move that surfaced 13 failures when the validator was first wired into the resumable seams, so the shapes admitted through frame slots have to be enumerated first. Needs `/tpy-add-feature` (design, not patch). Surfaced by the review of the resumable/simple-gen validator wiring.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A NESTED enum's `from_value` ctor rejects a runtime-BigInt argument, where the flat-enum arm narrows it.** `class Outer: class Kind(Enum): ...` then `Outer.Kind(n)` with `n: int` dies with `error: in function 'f': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (expr.method_call)`; the flat sibling `Flat(n)` in the SAME function compiles to `::tpy::EnumUtil<Flat>::from_value((n).to_fixed_check<int32_t>())`, and the nested form with an `int32` argument compiles too (all three verified with `uv run tpyc` on 2026-09-03). The nested arm -- `_lower_method_call`'s `is_nested_enum_constructor` at `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py:8805` -- bails on `_runtime_bigint(arg_type, ...)` instead of emitting the checked `.to_fixed_check<U>()` wrap its twin at `:7559` emits, so this is one arm out of sync with its twin, not a policy. The earlier symptom was ill-formed C++ (`cannot convert 'const tpy::BigInt' to 'int32_t'`); it is a loud reject now. It needs no widened local -- a plain `int` param breaks it. Everyday shape -- worth queueing.

- **[MED small] (AST rejects-valid, loud -- reference-type instantiation only) An RVALUE argument at a generic `T` parameter cannot bind its `param_val_or_ref_t<T>` slot.** `c[Key("a")] = 3` on a `Counter[Key]` (`Key` a record) emits `::tpy::__setitem__(c, Key("a"), ::tpy::BigInt(3))` against `void __setitem__(::tpy::param_val_or_ref_t<T> key, const ::tpy::BigInt& count)`; the trait is `T&` for a non-value `T`, which a prvalue cannot bind -- g++-14: `no matching function for call to '__setitem__(Counter<Key>&, Key, BigInt)'`. Binding the key to a local first (`k = Key("a")` then `c[k] = 3`) compiles and runs, so it is purely the argument's value category. For a VALUE `T` the trait is `const T&` and the rvalue binds, which is why no instantiation has tripped it. CPython accepts the rvalue form, so this is rejects-valid rather than a semantic gap. A `T()` parameter default hits it the same way: `def pick[T](x: T = T())` called `pick[Heir]()` with a reference `Heir` renders the default `x = T{}` against the `Heir&` slot, and the call `pick<Heir>()` fails the same way (identical on master `c854c7b482`; `/tmp/agents/docs_vt/md_ref.py`). The trait hands out the MUTABLE reference for every non-value `T` regardless of whether the callee mutates through it, and a callee that only reads -- or that copies into storage, as `__setitem__` does -- wants `const T&`. Surfaced while fixing the tuple-literal storing-sink defect. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (AST rejects-valid, latent -- ill-formed only at a reference-type instantiation) A borrow-returning call's `val_or_ref_t<T>` result is passed bare into an `own_param_t<T>` (`T&&`) slot.** [`own-slot-borrow-call-result`] A method declared `def peek(self) -> T` emits `::tpy::val_or_ref_t<T> peek()`; passing its result straight into a parameter spelled `::tpy::own_param_t<T> value` (which is `T&&`) is what the AST does today. For a VALUE `T` the two spellings coincide and the call compiles, which is why no instantiation has ever tripped it. For a REFERENCE `T` the result is `Payload&` and the slot is `Payload&&`, and g++-14 rejects the reduction: `cannot bind rvalue reference of type 'P&&' to lvalue of type 'P'`. Nothing in the corpus instantiates such a `T`, so the defect is latent rather than live. Same borrow-form-at-an-owning-sink family as the tuple-literal storing-sink defect (fixed: the `Own[tuple[...]]` slot now selects value-form element slots), but a distinct face -- a call RESULT at a move-consuming param, not a literal at a storing container sink -- and a distinct fix site. **Consequence for THIR admission, and this is the load-bearing half:** any arm admitting a call result at an `Own[T]` slot must exclude this shape via the callee's declared `fi.return_type` (`OwnType` vs `RefType`). `is_rvalue_source` is BLIND to the distinction -- it returns True for both the owning and the borrowing callee -- so a predicate keyed on it would route the ill-formed shape. Measured, not assumed. Surfaced while scouting the marker-qualified `Own[T]` argument row for `tpy.channel`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.


- **[LOW small] (latent mirror looseness, no witness) THIR's `_param_is_const` reads `const_borrow_params` without the `is_ref_param()` filter its AST counterpart applies.** The AST's body set (`_build_param_const_sets`) adds a name only when `inner.is_ref_param() or is_ptr_variant_union(inner)`; THIR's mirror has no such filter, so for a VALUE-typed param THIR can report const where the AST's body set does not. No corpus case and no probe produces a render difference today, and tightening it would change verdicts for bodies that currently route green -- so it is recorded rather than patched. Fix shape: give the THIR mirror the same `is_ref_param()` filter, and re-verify the bodies whose verdicts move. Surfaced by the tpy.atomic stdlib-routing cell while fixing the adjacent forced-const mirror.

- **[LOW small] (latent render question -- no corpus case reaches the shape) A `readonly[int]` parameter given a literal call argument keeps the BigInt wrapper on the THIR path.** A call `ro_aug(2)` against a `readonly[int]` param emits `ro_aug(2)` on the AST path and `ro_aug(::tpy::BigInt(2))` on the THIR path. Confirmed PRE-EXISTING by re-probing a stashed tree, and unwitnessed by the corpus, so the byte-diff and the ratchet are both blind. The AST render it was measured against is gone (the body emitters were deleted 2026-09-03), so what ships is the THIR spelling and the fix starts by deciding what the render should be, not by matching a second author. Shape of the fix if the wrapper is wrong: carry the literal's target slot through the readonly unwrap at the arg position. Found by the blast sweep of the widened-local narrow lane, outside that lane's rows. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (internal error, compiler invariant violation) An unannotated tuple local carrying a pending-str element inside a GENERATOR body fails the resumable-frame pending assertion.** `def gen() -> Iterator[int32]: e = src(); tup = (e, 1); yield 1; yield tup[1]` (with `src() -> str`) raises `Internal error: resumable-frame local 'tup' in 'gen' still has unresolved type PendingStrType after resolve_all; a Pending* resolution sink did not sync current_ns` (`tpyc/sema/analyzer.py:75`, raised from `:1468`). Sema-level, so BOTH codegen paths fail identically. Annotating the local (`tup: tuple[str, int32] = (e, 1)`) compiles and runs, and the same body in a NON-generator function compiles -- only the frame-promotion path asserts. Same "a tuple element keeps its pending type" family as the crash entries below, reached through the frame-local sink instead of a spelled type. Fix shape: have the pending-str resolution sink sync `current_ns` for tuple ELEMENTS of a frame-promoted local, or resolve the tuple's elements before the frame assertion runs. Repro `/tmp/agents/thir-tail2-0822/r6/progs/r6a_frame_tuple.py`. Surfaced by the thir-tail2-0822 raw-vs-resolved mirror audit. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (crash, BOTH paths) A tuple carrying a pending-str element crashes codegen when the tuple sits one level inside a container or Optional decl.** `ts = [(e, 1)]` and `o = (e, 1) if c else None` (with `e` a pending-str local off a `str`-returning call) both raise `RuntimeError: PendingStrType should be resolved before codegen` on the AST path as well as the THIR one. The top-level flavor (`tup = (e, 1)`) is fine on both paths: the AST decl spells through `type_to_cpp`, whose tuple branch resolves each element, and THIR now mirrors that at its decl arm -- but only the DECL's own type is spelled that way, so a tuple one level down (a list element type, an Optional inner) reaches a bare `to_cpp()` with the pending element still in it. Distinct from the nested-LITERAL entries below (`list([[1, 2]])`, annotated dict-of-list-literals), which are about an expected type not reaching a nested literal; here the type is known and only its SPELLING skips resolution. Fix shape: resolve pending elements wherever a composite type is spelled, not only at the tuple-typed decl (the `_resolve_tuple_pending` docstring already states `to_cpp` does not resolve pending slots). Repros `/tmp/agents/thir-tail2-0822/r6/progs/r6b_incont.py` and `r6b_opt.py`. Surfaced by the thir-tail2-0822 raw-vs-resolved mirror audit. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (THIR-only crash, latent -- no corpus case reaches the shape) A tuple literal nesting a pending-str element crashes the THIR emit's own type spelling.** `tup = ((e, 2), 1)` (with `e` a pending-str local) emits fine on the AST path (`std::tuple<std::tuple<std::string, int32_t>, int32_t>`), while THIR raises `RuntimeError: PendingStrType should be resolved before codegen` from the container/tuple LITERAL render (`unwrap_qualifiers(e.result_type).to_cpp()`, `tpyc/thir/emit.py:1967`). The decl's own spelling is correct -- the crash is the literal expression spelling its own result type bare. Same class as the entry above, on the THIR side of the split: the AST is the oracle here, so the fix is a THIR change-set (spell the literal's result type through the resolving helper, as the decl arm does). A crash is neither a fallback nor a byte-diff, so the ratchet and the corpus byte-diff are both blind to it. Repro `/tmp/agents/thir-tail2-0822/r6/progs/r6_pendtuple_nested.py`. Surfaced fixing the decl-arm half on `thir-tail2-0822`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) `",".join([e])` with a pending-str LOCAL element is rejected as not conforming to `Iterable[str]`.** `e = src()` (with `src() -> str`) then `",".join([e])` errors `Type PendingList[str, 1]#0 does not conform to protocol Iterable[str] in argument 'items'`, while `",".join(["a", "z"])` and the annotated `xs: list[str] = [...]; ",".join(xs)` both compile. The pending-str ELEMENT keeps the enclosing list literal pending, and the pending list then fails protocol conformance at the arg slot. Adjacent to the pending-container-arg entries below (`d.get(k, [])`, the annotated dict-of-list-literals) but a different failure point: those are about an expected type never reaching a nested literal, this is a resolved-enough literal failing the conformance check. Loud reject-valid, trivial workaround (annotate the list, or the local). Fix shape: resolve the literal's str-family elements before the `Iterable[T]` conformance test at the arg slot. Repro `/tmp/agents/thir-tail2-0822/r6/progs/r6c_join.py`. Surfaced by the thir-tail2-0822 raw-vs-resolved mirror audit. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.


- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) A module-scope comprehension whose ITERABLE reads the same pointer-slot global its loop var shadows emits ill-formed C++.** `x = [10, 20, 30]` then `s = [x + 1 for x in x]` at top level: the comp scope registers the loop-var shadow BEFORE the iterable renders, so the iterable read emits the bare pointer (`auto& __obj_N = x;` on a `std::vector<int32_t>* x` slot) instead of the deref `(*x)`, and `__obj_N.begin()` fails the C++ build (g++: "request for member 'begin' in ... pointer type"). CPython evaluates the iterable in the ENCLOSING scope, so the correct render is the deref; the missing sized-reserve on the same emit is a second symptom of the shadow firing early. Loud (toolchain-caught), exotic shape. THIR keeps this shape on the AST path deliberately (`_comp_pointer_shadow` excludes iterable-referenced shadow names) -- do not widen that fence before this is fixed AST-side. Fix shape: render the iterable (and range bounds) before the comp-scope shadow registration in the AST comp emitters. Repro `/tmp/agents/thir-wave/smoke/f_self_iter.py`. Surfaced by the thir-tail-0821 iterables-comp lane's adversarial dualgen. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (latent render question -- no case covers the sites) A container-literal arg at a generic record method's `Iterable[T]` structural slot hoists `auto __tmp_N` where the AST passes the brace literal bare.** `Bag[str]().add_all(["a", "b", "a"])` against `def add_all(self, items: Iterable[T])`: the AST emits `b.add_all({"a", "b", "a"});`, THIR emits `auto __tmp_1 = std::array<std::string, 3>{...}; b.add_all(__tmp_1);`. The NON-generic sibling (`Iterable[str]` on a plain record) diverges the same way AND burns the temp counter, renumbering every later legitimate temp in the body (`__tmp_1` -> `__tmp_2`), so one wrong hoist cascades into whole-body diffs. Byte-diff-invisible until a corpus case witnesses the shape; pre-existing on master (both repros re-confirmed via `dualgen.py` 2026-08-22). Same unaudited-guess family as the TODO.md "Harden the UNAUDITED arg-temp guess" entry (top of TODO.md): `THIRArgTemp.would_defer` proxies the AST creator's site-specific slot formula, and this is a site where the proxy answers hoist while the AST inlines. Sibling of the method-position TypeParamRef entry below, which diverges the OPPOSITE way (AST hoists, THIR inlines). Repros `/tmp/agents/thir-tail-0821/impl-rd/smoke/f_litarg.py` (generic) and `f_litarg2.py` (non-generic + counter burn).

- **[LOW small] (latent render question -- no corpus case reaches the shape) A NARROWED `Own[list[str]] | None` param written to an OPTIONAL field derefs on the THIR path where the AST moves the whole optional.** `class Reader: names: list[str] | None` with `def __init__(self, fieldnames: Own[list[str]] | None = None)` and `if fieldnames is not None: self.names = fieldnames` emits `this->names = std::move(fieldnames);` on the AST path against `this->names = std::move((*fieldnames));` on the THIR path -- the param is a value-repr `std::optional<std::vector<std::string>>`, so the AST moves the OPTIONAL into the optional field while THIR moves the PAYLOAD. Both compile and both leave the field engaged, so the divergence is spelling-level at this shape; the missing fork is real, though -- with a NON-optional field (`names: list[str]`) the two paths AGREE on the deref, so THIR is carrying the non-optional slot's render into the optional slot instead of forking on the field's optionality. THIR arm: the merged reference field write's OPT_TAIL slot -> `_lower_tail_value` (`_lower_ref_field` in `tpyc/thir/lower/field_write.py`), whose narrowed-name read takes the generic `(*name)` in `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py`. Latent: the ctor body ROUTES (the reported fallback names a different body), and no corpus case has the shape, so the byte-diff and the ratchet are both blind. PRE-EXISTING -- re-confirmed at master `63fa95383` by running `dualgen.py` over a clean `git archive` tree of that commit, which diverges byte-identically. The AST is the oracle, so the fix is a THIR change-set (fork the field-write tail on the field slot's optionality), not an AST one. Repros `/tmp/agents/thir-tail-0821/sm/d2.py` (optional field, DIVERGENT) and `/tmp/agents/thir-tail-0821/verify/d2b.py` (non-optional field, IDENTICAL -- the contrast). Surfaced by adversarial dualgen on the thir-tail-0821 lane. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A dict LITERAL with a `T`-typed key inside a record generic over `[T: Hashable]` is rejected "not hashable" despite the bound.** `class Wrap[T: Hashable]: def one(self, x: T) -> int32: d = {x: 1}; ...` errors `Type 'T' cannot be used as a dict key (not hashable)`, while the annotated-empty-dict sibling (`d: dict[T, int32] = {}` then `d[x] = 1`) compiles and runs for `T=str`. The literal-site gate (`validate_hashable_container_elem`, `tpyc/sema/type_ops.py`) requires Hashable AND Equatable; the `T: Hashable` bound delegates only the Hashable half (`Hashable` declares just `__hash__`), so `equatable_ok` stays False and the (misleadingly worded) rejection fires -- and the annotation path disagrees by accepting the same key type. Whether the fix is bound-implies-key-ok or a demanded `Hashable & Equatable` bound, the two sites must agree and the message must name the missing half. Workaround: annotate an empty dict and insert. Repros `/tmp/agents/thir-tail-0821/apply/hashable_key.py` (rejects) and `hashable_key2.py` (passing sibling). **Same Hashable/Equatable split as the `Hashable` C++ concept entry further down** (membership needs `==`, which `Hashable` does not declare), reached from the opposite end: there the annotation path lets a hashable-but-not-equatable CONCRETE key through to a late C++ build error, here the literal-site gate over-rejects a `T: Hashable` BOUND. Different trigger path and opposite failure mode, so they stay separate entries -- but the "both sites must agree" fix above is what closes both; fix them together. Surfaced by the thir-tail-0821 review round. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (latent wrong render -- no witness at a body position) Both `@call_macro` arms lower the expansion TARGET-LESS, so it self-types from the expression instead of from its declared slot.** `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py:7497` (free call) and `:8790` (method call) call `_lower_expr(e.macro_expansion, lc, declared)` with no `target_type`, dropping the declared slot. At ordinary body positions this is invisible: a literal's target is reapplied after the fact by `_slot_literal_retype` (`:16263`), which repairs the common case. It is NOT invisible where no post-hoc retype runs -- routing the non-body constant positions surfaced it as `tpy.version.version_info` spelling `std::tuple<..., std::string, ...>` where the slot wants `std::string_view`. Fixed AT THE CONSTANT POSITIONS ONLY (unwrap the expansion, keep the slot, `tpyc/thir/constants.py`); the general arms are untouched. No corpus witness at a body position, and none expected while `_slot_literal_retype` keeps repairing them -- but the arms are wrong as written, so any future position that threads a non-literal target will hit it.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A `Ptr[readonly[T]]` source at a NON-readonly record slot emits an ill-formed bind at both the local-decl and the return position.** `p2: Point = cp` emits `Point& p2 = ::tpy::deref_check(cp);` and `def f(p: Ptr[readonly[Point]]) -> Point: return p` emits `Point& f(const Point* p) { return ::tpy::deref_check(p); }`; g++-14 reports `binding reference of type 'Point&' to 'const Point' discards qualifiers`. Root cause: const-ness lives on the POINTEE, and neither `is_const_union_source` nor its THIR mirror `_f1_const_rooted_source` (`tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py:6573`) looks through a `Ptr` to find it, so both paths independently derive `is_const=False`. AST-side; the THIR path currently FENCES the shape rather than mirroring it (`tpyc/thir/lower/checks.py`; the unit that pinned the reject went with the THIR unit suite), following the in-file precedent at `checks.py:1666-1671`. Fix the AST first; the fence is then convertible. No corpus witness. Repros `/tmp/agents/cell-coerce/b5_const_decl/main.py` and `b6_ro_ret_mut/main.py`. Surfaced by the boundary sweep of the `Ptr[T]` deref-coerce THIR cell. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++, loud) A polymorphic `match` inside a method whose readonly-ness is INFERRED casts away const: the emitted signature takes `const`, the `dynamic_cast` target does not.** The `auto& __match_subject_1 = this;` bind and the `dynamic_cast` of a `Pet**` this entry recorded are FIXED -- the subject now binds `(*this)`. What survives is BROADER than the `match self:` headline it was filed under: for any method sema infers `@readonly` for (no decorator), the emitted `std::string Animal::describe() const` pairs with `if (Dog* __mpoly_0 = dynamic_cast<Dog*>(&__match_subject_1))` off a `const Animal*`, and g++ reports `conversion casts away constness`. The SAME method with an EXPLICIT `@readonly` emits `dynamic_cast<const Dog*>` and compiles, which is what isolates the gap: `_poly_subject_const` (`tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py:7757`) decides from the subject expression's ReadonlyType / const-borrow-name facts and never consults the enclosing method's inferred `is_readonly`. It bites `match self:` and `match self.<field>:` alike (both verified as build failures), and the corpus witnesses (`tests/cases/match/poly_expr_*`) all spell `@readonly` explicitly, which is why nothing fails today. Loud and toolchain-caught. Repro: a `@dynamic` `Tag` protocol, `class Animal(Tag)` / `class Dog(Animal)`, then an UNDECORATED `def describe(self) -> str:` holding `match self: / case Dog(): return "dog" / case _: return "?"`. The record-ternary composition (`c = self if flag else other` then `match c:`) now compiles and prints correctly, so that half of the entry is closed. Fix shape: seed the poly-cast const from the receiver's EMITTED const-ness, not from the subject expression alone. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (silent CPython divergence, two positions) Work that a short circuit should skip is still evaluated in a comprehension with TWO OR MORE `if` filters and in a `match` OR-pattern guard.** Each hoists a temp for a conditionally-evaluated operand at the enclosing statement, so a ctor or call that CPython never reaches runs anyway. Exec-verified: `[x for x in xs if x > 100 if guard(Ctor(2))]` runs the ctor once per element with no element passing the first filter; `case Dog() | Cat() if guard(Ctor(9))` runs it against a non-matching subject (repros `/tmp/agents/shortcircuit/repro2.py`, `repro3.py`). **Neither is the conditional-region fix** that closed the `and`/`or`/ternary/chained-compare positions (`TempState.conditional_region`, `tpyc/codegen_cpp/context.py`): the comprehension one is a render restructure (the filter clauses are joined and their temps flushed together) and the match one looks like a misplaced temp flush in the guard path. The comprehension one was re-verified as still-divergent AFTER that fix landed (`repro2.py`, ctor still runs per element). The match one could NOT be re-verified: `repro3.py` as written is rejected by sema (`class pattern 'Dog' does not match subject type 'Animal'`) both before and after the fix, so the original "exec-verified" claim for that position rests on a repro that does not compile today -- re-establish a compiling repro before treating the match guard as confirmed. An adjacent agent also proposed `elif` / `while` / `assert` / single-filter comprehensions / non-OR match guards as already-correct -- NOT independently verified, so do not treat that as a closed list either. Surfaced while scoping the short-circuit arg-temp fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (silent CPython divergence; residue of the conditional-region fix) An `auto`-typed arg temp in a conditionally-evaluated operand is still evaluated UNCONDITIONALLY.** `TempState.conditional_region` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/context.py`) defers a conditional-operand temp by declaring it as an uninitialized `std::optional<T>` slot and banking `__tmp_N.emplace(init)` into the operand -- but `std::optional<auto>` is not a spelling, so `_slot_spellable` leaves any `auto`-typed temp eager. One site is a real divergence: `expressions.py:276`, the nullable-protocol-union arg path, which falls back to `create_typed("auto", gen)` when the analyzer has no type for the argument (`arg_expr_type is None`) and the argument is a genuine temporary -- so a ctor there still runs in a skipped branch. The two sibling `auto` sites (`expressions.py:1312`, `1325`) copy an LVALUE into an `Own[T]` slot; that copy runs no user code, so it is a wasted copy in a skipped branch (potentially of a large container) rather than a parity divergence. **Not witnessed live:** the `arg_expr_type is None` fallback is hard to reach and no repro was constructed -- confirm the shape is reachable before spending on it. Fix shape: give the site an explicit type so the slot can be spelled (the `Own[T]` str arm just above it already does exactly this, using `type_to_cpp(own.wrapped)` instead of `auto`), rather than teaching the region to handle `auto`. Surfaced while landing the conditional-region fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (silent CPython divergence; residue of the conditional-region fix) A NON-MOVABLE arg temp in a conditionally-evaluated operand is still evaluated UNCONDITIONALLY.** Sibling of the `auto`-typed residue above, different cause: `TempState._register` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/context.py`) defers by emplacing into a `std::optional<T>` slot, and `emplace(T(...))` requires `T` move-constructible where the eager `T t = T(...);` form compiles via guaranteed C++17 elision even with the move deleted. So a temp whose type is non-movable (`@nomove`, or a record transitively owning a `UninitArrayStorage` of a non-trivially-relocatable element without `__move__`) MUST stay eager or the program stops compiling -- the `movable` gate on `_register` does exactly that, and `tests/cases/operators/short_circuit_nomove_arg` pins it. The cost is that `flag and take(Pinned(7))` builds the `Pinned` even when `flag` is false, so a ctor with side effects diverges from CPython for this one type class. Verified live: without the gate, `emplace(Pinned(7))` is a hard g++ error (`no type named 'type' in 'struct std::enable_if<false, Pinned&>'`), so the fix without the gate would have been rejects-valid; with the gate the shape compiles and runs eagerly. **Also over-conservative in the safe direction:** `is_movable()` is False for any `@nomove` record, but codegen only emits the deleted C++ move when the record also has a `__del__` (`records.py` `nonmovable` branch, which early-returns on `del_method is None`) -- a `@nomove` record without `__del__` keeps an implicit move and could have deferred. Fix shape: emplace via an in-place factory whose `operator T()` returns a prvalue (direct-init through a conversion function is elided, so no move ctor is needed), which would close both this entry and let the gate be dropped -- a runtime-helper addition, so it needs a design pass, not a patch. `create_typed` also defaults `movable=False` (a C++ spelling alone cannot answer movability); measured as costing zero snapshot churn across the corpus, so no `create_typed` deferral is witnessed today, but a caller that knows its type moves can opt back in. Surfaced by /tpy-review (runtime-cpp-correctness) of the conditional-region fix. Needs `/tpy-add-feature` for the factory, or leave as-is.

- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A walrus target typed pointer-repr `Optional` has no lowering arm for a CALL source.** `if (x := maybe_get(i)) is not None:` for `def maybe_get(i: int32) -> Own[Item | None]` dies with `error: in function 'f': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (expr.walrus)` (verified with `uv run tpyc` on 2026-09-03; the earlier symptom, `x = maybe_get(i)` against an `Item* x` and a g++ `cannot convert 'std::optional<Item>' to 'Item*'`, is gone with the AST emitter). The `opt_ptr` arm (`tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py:6967`) delegates to `_walrus_opt_ptr_source`, which admits only a storage-Optional FIELD source, `None`, or an already-pointer NAME; a bare call rejects with detail `walrus.opt_ptr_src`. Closing it is not just adding the arm: the owning `std::optional<T>` rvalue must first materialize into stable storage before its address is taken, which is exactly the rebind-slot / resumable-ptr-slot machinery the sibling `TpyVarDecl` / `TpyAssign` pointer-rebind path already runs -- so a naive form fix would trade the compile error for a frame pointer into a destroyed temporary. Loud and reproducible in sync and resumable-frame bodies alike. Workaround: bind in a separate statement (the VarDecl path handles it). Everyday shape -- worth queueing. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) A borrow-tuple walrus bound from a tuple LITERAL over a `readonly` container spells a non-const element pointer -- ill-formed C++.** `(t := (i, nodes[i]))` for `nodes: readonly[list[Node]]` emits `t = std::tuple<int32_t, Node*>{i, &(nodes[...])}` where the address-of yields `const Node*`, and g++ reports `no matching function for call to 'std::tuple<int, Node*>::tuple(...)'` (verified directly, sync and resumable-frame bodies alike). The explicit tuple-type prefix comes from the walrus decl's borrow spelling, whose const-ness is read off `const_borrow_form_tuple_locals`, while the element render derives its own const from the SOURCE -- so a const-rooted literal element and the non-const tuple type disagree. Pre-existing and independent of the resumable-frame walrus fix, which reproduced it unchanged on both paths. Repros `/tmp/agents/walrus-fix/r3_consttuple.py` (frame) and `r3b_sync.py` (sync). - **[HIGH small] (silent wrong output) A `match` capture that reuses an already-bound REFERENCE name writes the subject THROUGH the name instead of rebinding it.** [`match-capture-reuses-alias-writes-through`] `x = b; match q: case Cell() as x: pass; x.n = 50` prints `50 2` where CPython prints `1 50`: the outer `x` is an `auto&`/`Cell&` alias of `b` and the capture emits `x = __match_subject_1;`, a copy-assign into `b`. Fix shape: a capture of an already-declared name counts as a reassignment of it (lvalue rebind), so the alias takes the pointer-local form the direct `x = q` rebind already gets.

- **[HIGH small, deferred: MIR] (silent wrong value; REGRESSION since v0.5.0 in the closure face) A return under a `finally` that rebinds the name moves the value at its "last use" while the `finally` still reads it through a closure.** [`finally-rebind-eager-move-alias-read`] `try: return t` + `finally: show(); t = Tok(2)` with a nested def `show` capturing `t` reads the moved-from object (`show 0 1` where CPython prints `show 1 1`); the alias face (`a = t` before the `try`, `print(len(a.xs))` in the finally) now copies and prints like CPython (re-measured 2026-09-29); the tuple return `return (t, 1)` is the same (verified 2026-09-23, probes `/tmp/agents/rvfin/fb_f_alias.py`, `fb_f_closure_read.py`).
