The *propagation*-matching half of this cluster (`error_return_matches` conflating two distinct same-short-name exceptions, the C++-build-error symptom) was fixed in `fix-error-return-identity` by comparing the full defining-module qnames. Keying the set by qname is **blocked on a re-export-canonicalization decision**: `StopIteration` is *defined* in `tpy._builtins._exceptions` but registered/looked-up as the public `builtins.StopIteration` (the `__next__` form at `methods.py` and the builtins-preference in `qualify_exception_name` both produce the public qname, while registering from the defining module would produce the private one), so naive qname-keying breaks `StopIteration` recognition (generators/iterators). **Fix shape:** decide whether the canonical identity of a re-exported builtin exception is its defining-module or its public (`builtins`) qname, make `qualify_exception_name` and the set-registration agree on that one form, then key `return_exception_names` (and `BUILTIN_RETURN_EXCEPTIONS`) by it; or replace the bare-name cache with a protocol-implementation check that consults the resolved record (the cache exists only to bridge the pre-`_exceptions`-compiled ordering). Audit finding B113 (residual half). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug` or `/tpy-add-feature` (the canonicalization decision). Since 2026-09-18 the same fact also lives per record as `RecordInfo.is_return_exception` (decided from the record's own protocols by qname at registration, which is what the C++ representation keys on); the name set is still what `raise` / `except` / `@error_return` validation consult, so the fix is now to route those lookups through the resolved record and delete the set (TODO.md "Return exceptions: follow-ups", item 3, "ONE CHANNEL FOR THE FACT").
- **[LOW] `os.stat` nanosecond timestamps overflow (signed UB) past year ~2262.** `tpy::stdlib::os::ts_ns` (`runtime/cpp/src/stdlib/os_impl.cpp`) computes `static_cast<int64_t>(tv_sec) * 1000000000LL + tv_nsec`; for `tv_sec` beyond ~9.2e9 (year 2262) the multiply overflows a signed `int64_t` -- UB the compiler may exploit. The float-seconds fields (`st_mtime` etc.) are unaffected. Benign in practice, but the multiply should saturate or use an unsigned intermediate. Surfaced by /tpy-review (runtime-cpp-correctness) of os stat. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `float`/`float32` arithmetic with `bool` is rejected (`3.0 + True`), though CPython treats `bool` as an `int`.** The float operators widen over the `AnyFixedInt` marker protocol (every fixed-width int extends it), but `bool` does not extend `AnyFixedInt`, so `float OP bool` finds no overload ("Invalid operand types"). Rejects-valid, not a miscompile; workaround is an explicit cast (`3.0 + int32(True)` or `3.0 + int(b)`). Fix shape: either add a `bool` (or a shared `AnyFixedInt`-including-`bool`) overload to the float/float32 arithmetic dunders, or treat `bool` as conforming where fixed-width ints do. Surfaced by /tpy-review (docs-sync) of the float-fixed-int-arith fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW] Subscript-assign / del on a class with `__setitem__`/`__delitem__` but no `__getitem__` is rejected at sema ("Cannot index type ... no `__getitem__`").** CPython allows a write-only / del-only mapping (`m[k] = v` / `del m[k]` need only `__setitem__`/`__delitem__`, not `__getitem__`), but TPy's subscript sema requires `__getitem__` even on the assign/del target path. Workaround: add a `__getitem__`. Surfaced fixing the write-subscript non-int-key dispatch (the inverse-test class needed a `__getitem__` it shouldn't have). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED medium, deferred: MIR] A `match` capture of an `A | B` (union) subject fails the C++ build -- two distinct sub-causes (spiked).** [`match-capture-union-subject`] The pointer-repr **Optional**-subject half was fixed in `fix-match-capture-indirect-subject` (the capture aliases the pointer directly); the union half remains and is **bigger than a codegen tweak**. (a) **Narrowed union**: `x: A | B = A(1); match x: case q:` -- the assignment narrows `x` to `A`, so the match analyzes as a *record-A* match (q typed `A*`), but `x`'s storage is the pointer-variant `std::variant<A*,B*>` -> `cannot convert std::variant<A*,B*>* to A*`. A narrowing-type-vs-storage-form mismatch. Reproducer `/tmp/agents/c3probe/mu.py`. (b) **Genuine union**: `def m(x: A | B): match x: case q:` -- `q` is hoisted in storage form (value-variant `std::variant<A,B>`) but the subject is borrow form (pointer-variant `std::variant<A*,B*>`) -> `no match for operator=`. This is the **borrow/storage-form duality for union captures** (the IR-gated class, IR_DESIGN OQ9): q must either be hoisted in borrow form (pointer-variant, aliasing the subject) or the bind must convert (`to_value_variant`). Reproducer `/tmp/agents/rev2/union_param.py`. The aliasing form for a union capture is a **design decision** (pointer-variant alias vs value-variant copy-out vs per-variant narrowing), so this is `/tpy-add-feature` (design) more than `/tpy-fix-bug`, and the form half is best sequenced with THIR. Workaround: narrow with `isinstance` per variant before mutating. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the audit-#11 work; root causes spiked.
- **[LOW small] A walrus aliasing a reference-type loop element assigns a `const T*` into a non-const `T*` local -- ill-formed C++, no TPy diagnostic.** `for x in items: if (y := x).v > 1:` over a `list[Node]` emits `const auto& x = *__beg_0;` next to `Node* y = nullptr;`, then `(y = &(x), *y)` -- g++ "invalid conversion from 'const Node*' to 'Node*'". It reproduces in a plain for loop as well as the comprehension form this entry was filed from (`result = [y for x in items if (y := x).v > 1]`), so the fault is the walrus BINDING, not the comprehension. The originally-filed symptom -- a borrow pointer pushed into the storage-form result container -- is GONE: the comprehension element read now derefs (`__result.push_back((*y));`, with the usual "copies Node into owned storage" warning). Site: the `expr.walrus_ptr_alias` arm of `_lower_expr` in `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py` sets `is_const = borrow_decls[e.target]` and prefixes `const` on the predecl from it; `borrow_decls` is sema's `function_stmt_borrow_decls` (assembled in `tpyc/sema/analyzer.py`), which leaves the target non-const even though the loop element binds `const auto&`. Toolchain-caught (hard C++ error), not silent. Workaround: none inside a comprehension; in a loop, read the field directly instead of binding it. Fix shape: make the walrus predecl inherit the const-ness of its borrow SOURCE (a read-only loop element), or bind the loop element non-const when a walrus aliases it. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] Generic constructor/function inference cannot bind a type parameter to a `readonly[T]` type.** When the only evidence points to a readonly binding -- an expected type of `Own[Rc[readonly[T]]]` and/or a `Ptr[readonly[T]]` argument against a `Ptr[T_param]` parameter -- inference produces no binding and raises `Cannot infer type arguments for '<Record>'`, even though `<Record>[readonly[T]]` is the obvious solution. Confirmed (DIAG) on the `@auto_readonly` const overload of `Rc.clone`: hint `Own[Rc[readonly[T]]]`, args `['Ptr[_RcCellBase]', 'Ptr[readonly[T]]']`, yet inference fails; the mutable overload (no readonly) infers fine. Root cause is the readonly-stripping in arg/seed handling (`_restore_readonly_arg` / `seed_subst_from_record_pattern` in `tpyc/sema/calls.py`) erasing readonly before the type param is bound, plus no path to bind a param *to* a readonly type. Worked around in interior-mutable fields by spelling the construction type explicitly (`Rc[auto_readonly[T]](...)`, transformed per-overload by `@auto_readonly`); if this inference gap is fixed, that explicit marker can be dropped in favor of plain `Rc(...)` inference. Surfaced building the interior-mutable / readonly-`Rc.clone` feature. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small, deferred: MIR] `collections.Counter.most_common` fails the C++ build for a REFERENCE-type key.** Its `sorted(pairs, key=lambda kv: -kv[1])` over a `list[tuple[T, int]]` is the stdlib witness of the key-lambda param-form entry further down: the lambda param is rendered `const std::tuple<val_or_ptr_t<T>, BigInt>&` (borrow form) while `builtin_sorted_key` calls it with the vector's storage element `std::tuple<T, BigInt>`. VERIFIED distinct from the tuple-literal slot selection and reproducible with a CONCRETE key type (`sorted(pairs, key=...)` over a `list[tuple[Item, int32]]` emits `[](const std::tuple<Item*, int32_t>& kv)`), so it is not a generics artifact. Latent for Counter itself because every current `Hashable` is a value type. Fix is the same one item 9 gates -- see the `key=` lambda entry below; kept here only so a search for `Counter.most_common` lands somewhere. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug` (IR-gated).
- **[LOW small] The `Hashable` C++ concept requires only `__hash__`, but membership (`::tpy::seq_contains` / `__contains__`) needs `==`.** A user type that satisfies TPy `Hashable` (defines `__hash__`) but not `Equatable` (no `__eq__`) compiles as a dict key / Counter key but fails the C++ build at the membership/contains site. Python's `Hashable` does not formally imply `__eq__` either, but a hashable-without-`__eq__` type is degenerate; the gap is that TPy accepts it as a key then fails late in C++ rather than rejecting at sema (dict key validation should require `Hashable` AND `Equatable`). Pre-existing protocol gap, exposed by `collections.Counter`'s `T: Hashable` `__contains__`. **Other end of the split recorded in the `[T: Hashable]` dict-LITERAL entry near the top of this file**: that literal-site gate (`validate_hashable_container_elem`) demands Hashable AND Equatable and so over-rejects a bounded `T`, while this annotation path demands neither and under-rejects a concrete key. Different trigger and opposite failure mode -- not duplicates -- but one consistent key-validation rule closes both; fix them together. Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A generator method that iterates `for k in self._data` AND subscripts `self._data[k]` with the loop var emits ill-formed C++.** The frame-hoisted loop var binds `k = &(*((*__for_it_0))++)` as mutable `T*`, but iterating a dict yields `const T*` -> g++ "invalid conversion from `const std::string*` to `std::string*`". A yield-only generator (`for k in self._data: yield k`) compiles fine; adding any `self._data[k]` subscript inside the generator triggers it (the loop var must be bound `const T*` in the frame). Blocks the natural `collections.Counter.elements()` (`for k in self._data: while j < self._data[k]: yield k`). No TPy diagnostic; C++ build error only. Workaround: build an eager `list[T]` in a non-generator method instead of a lazy generator. Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/gen_dict_sub.py`. Surfaced building `collections.Counter`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] Subscript-assignment through a FIELD-access target rejects a readonly-sourced key, while the same through a bare-name target works.** Inside a readonly method, `result._data[copy(k)] = self._data[k]` (where `k` iterates the readonly `self._data`, and `result` is a fresh local of a dict-wrapping class) fails sema with "Cannot pass readonly[T] as mutable T in dict key (expected T)"; the identical pattern with a bare `dict[T,int]` local target (`out[copy(k)] = self._data[k]`) compiles. So the subscript-assignment key check for a field-access target (`obj._data[key] = v`) does not unwrap/accept the key the way the bare-name-target path does (the readonly-dict read fix covered the READ subscript + bare-target paths, not the field-access assignment target). Blocks `collections.Counter`'s `+`/`-`/`&`/`|` operators (they build a fresh `result` Counter and write keys into `result._data`). No miscompile -- sema rejection. Workaround: route writes through a method whose receiver is mutable. Reproducers: `/tmp/agents/ctr_add.py` (fails) vs `/tmp/agents/iso27.py` (bare-target, works). Surfaced building `collections.Counter`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid, loud) An `and`/`or` whose result type is `bool` but with a RECORD operand is a hard compile error.** Three triggers, all refused: (a) two unrelated record types, `if dogs[0] or cats[0]:` -> `(stmt.if:if.cond_binop.||.record_f1_record_f1:truthy.shape)`; (b) a record `or` a non-record, `if a or 0:` -> `(stmt.if:if.cond_binop.||.record_f1_other_intliteraltype:truthy.literal)`. (c) two containers of which one is a literal, `if e or [5]:` with `e: list[int32]` -> `(stmt.if:if.cond_binop.||.container_container:truthy.shape)` (the value-context twin `x = e or [5]` lowers). This supersedes the older symptom (the bool-result path emitted the raw C++ `a || 0` and g++ answered "no match for 'operator||'"): the mis-render no longer has an emitter, so the shape is refused instead of miscompiled. Site: `_lower_truthy` in `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py` -- `raise ThirUnsupported("truthy.literal")` on a literal operand, `raise ThirUnsupported("truthy.shape")` on the residual-shape tail. Both rejects reach well past the record family this entry was filed for: `if a or 0:` with a plain `a: int32` is refused the same way (`scalar_other_intliteraltype:truthy.literal`), and a bare `if dogs[0]:` with no logical op is refused as `stmt.if:cond.subscript` -- everyday shapes, so the queueing case is stronger than the record-only headline suggests. The value-result path (same-type / `__bool__` records returning the operand) still routes. Fix shape: give the literal and record/subscript operands their truthiness renders in the bool-result path (the conversion the value-result path already applies), rather than leaving the tail as a reject. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] Sema's save/restore isolation deep-copies the whole per-function tracking state, so TYPE objects in it come back as CLONES after a nested def statement or a lambda trial.** `scope_tracker.nested_def_scope` and `SemanticContext.trial_scope` snapshot via `save_function_state` (a `deepcopy`) and restore the copy. What must survive that round trip as ITSELF is handled by `save`/`restore` and not by the call sites: `FunctionTrackingState.__deepcopy__` (`tpyc/sema/context.py`) carries the live handles over unchanged (`LIVE_HANDLE_FIELDS`: `current_scope`, `current_ns`, `own_ns`, `current_function`) and seeds its memo so every parse node and registry `FunctionInfo` the state reaches -- through a container or an attribute of a state object -- survives by identity. `TpyType` objects do not: the seed walk skips them (shared and possibly cyclic), so `narrowed_types`, `authoritative_types`, borrow tracker state and `write_history` hold clones afterwards -- any consumer keying on type identity (`is`, identity-keyed tables) across a nested-def statement or a trial can silently mismatch, and a parse node reachable ONLY through a type (`PendingGenericInstanceType.expr`) is cloned with it. Four faces of it were observed and closed on 2026-09-17 (a generic generator with a nested def silently took the VALUE yield slot; a frame-resident local's borrow yield was rejected; a local declared after a lambda trial never reached the frame layout, so the C++ build failed; and `super_init_call`'s `is` compare made a constructor's own `super().__init__()` look misplaced whenever a nested `def` followed it), which is why both the live-handle rule and the node seeding now live in `save`/`restore`; the residual is the still-cloned type objects. Fix shape: replace the blanket deepcopy with an explicit save/restore of the fields the isolated analysis actually mutates (or a shallow copy-on-write layer). Surfaced while making nested defs frame members. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] Mutation of a CAPTURED name via a call with mapped arguments inside a nested def is still lost -- only the direct-mark and self-receiver channels replay.** [`nested-def-call-edge-capture-lost`] The nested-def mutation-fact replay carries direct marks (field writes, structural mutations, not-known-readonly method calls) and self-rooted receiver call edges (`MutationCallEdge.receiver_idx`); edges that carry mutation through argument positions do not survive: a `MutationCallEdge` whose `param_map` indexes the nested def's own params is dropped (the indices don't translate to the enclosing function), and `helper(self)` / `helper(xs)` with a CAPTURED arg records no param entry at all (the `self -> -1` sentinel and the caller-index map are installed only for the enclosing function's own params, not for captures -- `_prescan_and_analyze_body` is method-body-gated). So `def fill(xs): def go(): helper(xs)` (or `helper(self)`) where `helper` mutates its param under-marks -> the enclosing param/method emits `const` and the C++ build fails at the mutation site (loud, no silent miscompile). Fix shape: capture-aware edges (a per-callee "captured name -> callee param idx" map on the nested def's FunctionInfo, resolved in the Phase-2 fixpoint). Surfaced implementing the nested-def self-access fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`. A generator expression inside a nested def reaches it with no callee at all: creating the frame is a call whose arguments are the captures, so a body that mutates a capture -- even directly, `sum(v for v in zs if xs.pop() > 0)` -- leaves the enclosing param `const` and fails the C++ build (`/tmp/agents/gxbody/p7.py` through a callee, `p8.py` direct). A generator expression in the nested def is the same route: `def f(xs: list[int32], big: bool): def inner(): for v in xs: t += sum(1 for _ in range(1) if big and grow(xs))` keeps `xs` const and fails the build (found 2026-09-23 while pinning the genexpr creation check in a nested def).
- **[LOW small] A nested-def PARAM (or staticmethod local) literally named `self` inside a record still renders through the receiver rule.** The codegen self-spells-this predicate (`self_renders_as_this` / `self_captures_this`) reads the ENCLOSING method's `current_func_params`, so a nested def declaring its own `self` param renders the body reference `(*this)` while the param binding is the shadowing local -- uncompilable C++ (the capture list correctly omits it). Staticmethod locals named `self` no longer capture `[this]` (the predicate requires `current_method_record_type`), but the body renderer shares the same blindness. Sema has the mirror twin: the mutation-fact replay's `replayable` set includes `"self"` unconditionally, so a nested def whose own param is named `self` inside a method replays that param's mutations onto the receiver (const-loss only, no semantic change). Degenerate shadowing shapes; loud C++ failure. Fix shape: track nested-def-scope param shadowing in the emission context (push/pop `current_func_params` per nested body). Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness) of the nested-def self-access fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A lambda INSIDE a nested def capturing `self` emits no capture for it -- loud C++ `'this' was not captured` error.** Inside the nested-def analysis the tracking state's `definitely_assigned` excludes `self`, so the inner lambda's capture filter (`free_names & definitely_assigned`) drops it: the emitted inner lambda has no `this` capture while its body renders `this->field`. Same blind spot family: `receiver_self_in_scope()` reads `current_function` (the nested def, `is_method` False), so the escape-mode skip and the Send by-ref pin would also miss the shape -- moot today since it never compiles. Reproducer `/tmp/agents/nested-self/lambda_in_nested.py`. Fix shape: include the receiver in the nested analysis's capturable set (and derive receiver context from the enclosing method, not `current_function`) when the enclosing method has one. Surfaced by the /tpy-ready retrospective of the nested-def self-access branch. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small, deferred: MIR] Borrow/consume facts other than mutation are not replayed out of nested-def analysis, and the nested def's own FunctionInfo carries no facts at all.** The nested-analysis restore discards `mark_param_returned` roots (a closure returning a borrow of `self`/captured storage), `mark_own_param_consumed`, and addr-escape names; only mutation marks and self-receiver edges replay. The nested `FunctionInfo` registered for call resolution is likewise built with no mutated/structural/return-borrow facts, so return-borrow dangle checks through closure calls are blind. Pre-existing blindness (facts were never carried), newly reachable now that self-capturing closures compile. Fix shape: stamp the nested FunctionInfo's Phase-1 facts from the nested tracking state before restore, and replay returned/consumed roots like mutation marks. Surfaced by /tpy-review (safety-model) of the nested-def self-access fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A `Callable`/`std::function` argument passed into an `async def`/generator is copied into the coro frame instead of moved.** `_classify_params` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/gen_async.py`) classifies a `Callable[[...], R]` param as `VALUE` (not `FN`), so `_factory_args_forwarded` forwards it by bare name (no `std::move`); the coro-frame ctor then copy-constructs the `std::function` from the factory local. `std::function` copy is well-defined but non-trivial (potential heap alloc), so e.g. `asyncio.start_server`'s `_accept_loop` copies its `cb` once per spawn instead of moving. Pre-existing (latent until a Callable param reached an async factory); not a safety issue. Fix: forward a last-use `Callable` factory arg with `std::move`. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the async-fn->Callable coercion branch. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[HIGH small] (silent use-after-free) An async-fn ref whose param is a borrow (`T`) coerced to a callable hint whose param is `Own[T]` is accepted by sema, and the coroutine reads a dead argument.** [`async-fn-borrow-param-own-hint`] `async def handle(c: Conn) -> None: await asyncio.sleep(0.0); print("handled " + str(c.id))` stored in a `_cb: Callable[[Own[Conn]], Own[Cancellable[None]]]` field and driven by `tasks.append(asyncio.create_task(self._cb(Conn(i))))` for `i` in `0..2`, then `for t in tasks: await t`, compiles and prints `handled -1` three times where CPython prints `handled 0`, `handled 1`, `handled 2` (re-measured 2026-09-29; it used to fail the C++ build). The function-ref match unwraps both `Ref` and `Own` on param types, so the borrow param is taken as compatible with `Own[Conn]`, and the handler's frame borrows the synthesized factory wrapper's local, which dies when the wrapper returns while the coroutine lives on. Fix: in the function-ref-to-callable match, require an `Own[T]` hint param to match an `Own[T]` (not borrow `T`) function param, with a clean sema diagnostic. Workaround: annotate the handler param `Own[T]`. Part of the async-fn->Callable coercion (`feat-async-fn-callable-coercion`). Surfaced by the `tplib/stream_server.py` in the `tpy-examples` repo handler. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A local assigned inside a `try` and moved after the `try` block is not recognized as last-use-movable -- a `@nocopy`/owned such local fails to move.** `try: conn, addr = await f() except OSError: break` then `Rc.new(conn)` after the try -> "@nocopy type 'socket' cannot be copied ... Only the original owner can be moved at its last use", even though `conn` is bound only on the non-exception path and read only after the try. The conservative "a value read on an exception path stays live across the whole try body" rule over-fires: it keeps a try-*assigned* local live across the try even when it is not read inside the try. Workaround: avoid the `try` (e.g. stop a loop via cancellation rather than catching the error), or move the binding+use entirely inside the try. Distinct from the await-tuple-unpack move (which works without the try). Surfaced building `asyncio.start_server` (catching listener-closed around `sock_accept`). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A generic (templated) `async def` awaited as a sub-coroutine loses its template args in the awaiter's frame slot -- C++ build error.** An `async def`/method that is generic OR takes an `Fn`/protocol-typed param (so its coro frame is a template, `__coro_g<F>`) and is `await`ed from another coro emits `std::optional<__coro_g> __sub_N;` in the awaiter frame (no `<F>`), then `__sub_N` is "not declared in this scope" at the poll site. The sub-coro frame-slot type omits the generic frame's template arguments. Reproducer: `async def spawn(factory: Fn[[int32], Own[Cancellable[None]]], n): asyncio.create_task(factory(n)); await asyncio.sleep(0)` then `await spawn(worker, 7)`. Distinct from the non-generic case, which monomorphizes fine. Blocks the `Fn`-template target of the async-fn-as-coroutine-factory coercion (the `Callable` type-erased target works). Toolchain-caught, not silent. Surfaced probing higher-order async for `start_server`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`. The GENERATOR side has the same hole: a `def` generator with an `Fn` param (a template through its deduced `F_<name>` slot) delegated to from another generator's `for` head is embedded as `tpy::frame_loop_slot<__gen_mapped>` with no template args, and the C++ build fails; reproduces on master 06dc4b905b. Seen reviewing the genexpr frames 2026-09-21.
- **[MED small] A concrete container passed where a GENERIC recursive-alias instance (`Tree[int32]`) is expected is accepted by sema but fails the C++ build -- no clean diagnostic.** `type Tree[T] = T | list[Tree[T]]; def depth(t: Tree[int32]): ...; xs = [1, 2, 3]; depth(xs)` -> g++ `invalid initialization of reference of type 'const Tree<int>&' from 'std::array<int, 3>'`. The std-container guard in `compatibility.py` `_check_compat` only catches a `UnionType`-with-wrapper element difference, not its generic sibling `RecursiveAliasInstanceType`, so `_check_union_member_type_args` accepts the element-wise coercion and codegen can't emit it. The non-generic case is rejected cleanly (a concrete container into a `UnionType` wrapper hits a diagnostic that names the workarounds); the generic sibling falls through to the raw C++ error instead. Fix shape: extend the guard's element check to fire for `RecursiveAliasInstanceType` too (and ideally cover the cross-container `Array`->`list`-member route, which the same-name guard misses). Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/deepconv/genalias.py`. Surfaced surveying recursive-union argument forms. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] Mutating a recursive-union param's nested container through a `match` binding fails the C++ build (param wrongly inferred `const`) -- CPython mutates and propagates.** `type V = int32 | list[V]; def mutates(x: V): match x: case list() as items: items.append(1)` emits `void mutates(const V& x)` -- mutation tracking does not follow the `case list() as items` binding back to the param, so const inference marks `x` non-mutating; the match binding `items` is then `const`, and `items.append(1)` is a g++ error (`passing const ... discards qualifiers`). CPython mutates the caller's list in place (`reads(a)` 2 -> `mutates(a)` -> `reads(a)` 3). Toolchain-caught, not silent. Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/deepconv/mutprobe.py`. Fix shape: mutation tracking must propagate a structural mutation of a match-arm capture alias back to the matched param (the alias is a borrow of the subject). Surfaced probing recursive-union param mutation. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A list literal does not coerce to an `Iterable[T]` (generic protocol) parameter: `f(["a", "b"])` where the param is `Iterable[T]` fails the C++ build.** `c.add_all(["a", "b"])` where `add_all(self, items: Iterable[T])` errors `no matching function ... add_all(<brace-enclosed initializer list>)`. The literal isn't materialized into a concrete `list[T]` (then matched against `Iterable[T]`) at the call boundary. Workaround: bind to a local first (`xs: list[str] = [...]; c.add_all(xs)`). Sibling of the literal-into-`Optional[list]` gap below (collection-literal contextual coercion not firing for a wrapper/protocol target). Surfaced building `collections.Counter`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A collection literal does not coerce to an `Optional` collection param: `f(["a", "b"])` where the param is `list[str] | None` fails the C++ build.** `csv.DictReader(fp, ["name", "age"])` (param `fieldnames: Own[list[str]] | None = None`) emits a brace-init `{...}` that g++ can't convert to `std::optional<std::vector<std::string>>` ("no known conversion from <brace-enclosed initializer list>"). A plain `list[str]` param takes the literal fine (`DictWriter(out, ["name","age"])` works) -- only the `| None` wrapper breaks it. Workaround: bind the literal to a local first (`fn: list[str] = [...]; DictReader(fp, fn)`). Root: the list-literal materialization targets the bare element type, not the `optional<vector>` storage, so the brace-init is ambiguous. Likely the same family as the dict/set-literal contextual-coercion gap (a plain concrete target hits the peer-unify branch); here the target is `Optional[list]`. Fix: route a collection literal whose expected type is `Optional[C]` through the same materialize-into-`C` path, then lift to the optional. Surfaced building `csv.DictReader`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] An `async def` returning a tuple built from named owned (`@nocopy`/`Own`) locals COPIES the elements instead of moving them -- C++ build error.** `async def f() -> tuple[Own[A], Own[B]]: ...; a = A(...); b = B(...); return (a, b)` emits, in the coro frame, `std::tuple<A, B>{(*a), (*b)}` from the `std::optional<A>`/`std::optional<B>` frame slots (lvalues) with no `std::move`, so g++ fails `use of deleted function A(const A&)` for a `@nocopy` element. The async-return tuple-literal path does not apply last-use move to its frame-slot element locals. Workaround (used in `asyncio.open_connection`): build the tuple from fresh rvalues inline (`return (A(...), B(...))`), which C++ move-constructs. Sync-function tuple returns and the single-element / rvalue cases work; only the async-return tuple of multiple *named* owned locals is broken. Same move-out-of-named-owned-local family as the named-source whole-tuple unpack entry below, different site (async return tuple construction). Toolchain-caught, not silent. Surfaced building the asyncio streams layer (`StreamReader`/`StreamWriter` returned from `open_connection`). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `KeyError` from a missing dict key carries the message `"KeyError"` instead of the key value -- `str(e)` is `"KeyError"`, CPython's is `"'absent'"`.** A missing-key read (`d["absent"]`) raises a `KeyError` whose *type* is correct (so `except KeyError` works), but `tpy::__getitem__` for `ordered_map` (`runtime/cpp/include/tpy/dunder.hpp` ~167) calls `raise_key_error("KeyError")` with a fixed string rather than the formatted key. CPython reprs the key (`KeyError: 'absent'`). One-sided: catching works, message-comparing diverges. Same shape as the documented `str(KeyError(k))` gap noted for the builtins dict surface. Fix: format the key into the message (gated on the key type being printable/repr-able). Pre-existing; surfaced by /tpy-review (cpython-parity) of the const-container subscript-read fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (perf) A `with ... as` target whose `__enter__` returns `StrView` gets owning frame storage but its read still carries BORROW form, so a `yield` of it copies an already-owned string.** `with_owning_str_targets` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/gen_async.py:3291`, feeding `FrameLayoutPlan` via `_frame_layout` at `:1183`) gives the target an owning `std::string` frame field, but the yield sink `_wrap_view_owned_sink` (`tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py:478`, called from `tpyc/thir/lower/resumable.py`) keys on the lowered value's Form fact, which still says BORROW for that read -- so `yield label` emits `return std::string(label);`, an owned->owned copy. Pinned by `tests/cases/generators/gen_yield_view_from_frame::with_view_target`, so a fix shows up as a snapshot delta. An `__enter__ -> str` target is NOT affected: view deduction promotes it and the read is storage form. The sibling instance -- a `str`/`bytes` PARAM copied into owned frame storage on the way in (`is_owned_in_coro_frame`) -- is already correct, pinned bare by `owned_param_stays_bare` in the same case. This one is really a SYMPTOM of the entry below (the target should not have been promoted to owning storage at all), so fixing that removes it. Fix shape: derive the read's Form fact from `FrameLayoutPlan`, the declared single source of truth for the frame-field form, since the instance is exactly "this field is owning". Note the plan's domain must be WIDENED first -- `_frame_layout` classifies `func.generator_locals` only, and params are classified separately (`_CoroParamKind`), so this is not a drop-in lookup. Pure perf (an owned string copied twice), no wrong output. Surfaced by the /tpy-merge-master check once `FrameLayoutPlan` landed.
- **[LOW small, deferred: MIR] (perf) A `with ... as` target whose `__enter__` returns a VIEW is promoted to owning frame storage on the strength of its type CATEGORY, not its provenance.** The with-prescan (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/gen_async.py` ~2993) adds the target to `with_owning_str_targets` whenever `is_str_category(resolved_enter_t)`, and that category spans `str`, `String`, `StrView` and `FStr`. The rationale in the comment there is specifically the `__enter__ -> str` case, where the C++ signature returns `std::string` BY VALUE and a `string_view` field really would alias a temporary dying at the assignment's semicolon -- owning is required for that one. For `__enter__ -> StrView` the C++ return is already a `std::string_view`, so nothing owns, and whether a view field dangles depends on what it views: `with h as label:` where the frame holds `Holder& h` and `__enter__` returns a view of `self.label` is lifetime-stable, so the copy at `label = (*__with_ctx_0).__enter__();` buys nothing. That lifetime-stability argument holds only for a BORROWED manager, and only because the promotion covers the shape at all: an OWNED (rvalue) manager whose view target skips the promotion has nothing keeping the viewed object alive, which is why the manager is now frame-homed whenever the target's field points into it (`_with_field_points_into_manager`) -- so removing this promotion is safe for the owned case too, but only alongside that homing. Costs one owned-string copy per `__enter__`. It is also the CAUSE of the redundant yield-sink copy in the entry above: the field is owning while the read predicate still calls it a view, so the wrap fires on an already-owned string -- with a correctly-viewed field the wrap would be doing real work instead. Pinned as-is by `generators/gen_yield_view_from_frame::with_view_target`, so a fix surfaces as a snapshot delta. Fix shape: split the promotion by the enter type's C++ ownership -- keep it for the owning returns (`str` / `String`), and route a view return through the source-lifetime question `frame_unsafe_source` already answers for deduced view locals (`tpyc/sema/local_deduction.py`). Same shape-vs-provenance call, and this is the last view-family frame-storage decision still keyed on shape alone. Surfaced by user review of the yield-sink branch's with-target snapshot.
- **[LOW small] `json.dumps((1, 2, 3))` (a tuple) is rejected** -- `tuple` is not a `JsonValue` member, so a tuple argument fails the union match. CPython serializes tuples as JSON arrays. Divergence: idiomatic `json.dumps((a, b))` works in CPython. Resolving it means either adding tuple handling to `JsonValue` / `json.dumps` (tuples are heterogeneous value types -- not a clean union member) or a dedicated tuple->array coercion in the json layer. Surfaced surveying json.dumps input forms. Likely `/tpy-add-feature`.
- **[LOW small] `csv.writer(..., doublequote=False)` silently emits malformed CSV for a field containing the quotechar.** With `doublequote=False` and no escapechar, a field that needs quoting and contains the quotechar is wrapped in quotes without escaping the inner quote (`lib/tpy/csv.py` `_format_row`), producing unparseable output; CPython raises `csv.Error("need to escape, but no escapechar set")`. Only on the non-default `doublequote=False` path. Fix needs a small surface decision first: TPy `csv` has no `csv.Error` type -- either add one (matching CPython's hierarchy) or raise `ValueError`. Surfaced by /tpy-review (cpython-parity) of csv v1. Needs `/tpy-add-feature` for the error-surface call, then a localized fix.
- **[LOW small] Module-qualified construction of a generic class fails: `mod.GenericClass(...)` reports "Module has no function 'GenericClass'".** `csv.DictReader(fp)` (a generic `class DictReader[W]` accessed via the module attribute) is rejected, while `from csv import DictReader; DictReader(fp)` resolves and deduces `W` correctly. Module-attribute access resolves functions and non-generic classes but not generic-class construction. Workaround: direct import. Surfaced building `csv.DictReader`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`. The website docs audit (2026-09-28) met the same error on `collections.Counter([...])`, `asyncio.Queue()` and `asyncio.Future()`; probes `/tmp/agents/rel06/audit/mq_csv.py`, `mq_counter.py`, `mq_asyncio.py`, `mq_future.py` (control `mq_ctrl.py`).
- **[LOW small] `sorted(d.items(), key=...)` (and other element-type inference) on a readonly dict fails: `items()` yields `readonly[value]` for a value-typed V.** `d.items()` on a `readonly[dict[K, int]]` is typed `dict_items[K, readonly[int]]`, so iterating yields `tuple[K, readonly[int]]`; passing it to `sorted(..., key=lambda kv: -kv[1])` makes overload/type-param inference conflict (`tuple[K, readonly[int]]` vs the lambda's `tuple[K, int]`). `readonly[int]` is pointless (a value V read from a dict view is a copy), but it is materialized eagerly by `@auto_readonly` on `items()`/`values()`. The other readonly-dict reads (`.get`, `in`, for-iteration, `d[k]` with a readonly key, readonly *reference*-value reads) now work; only `.items()`/`.values()` projecting readonly onto a VALUE element is unfixed. Workaround: build the pairs list manually (`for k in d: pairs.append((k, d[k]))`) then sort that. **Fix shape:** the collapse must be POSITION-AWARE -- `readonly[value-type]` collapses to the value type only in a value position (tuple/dict-view element), NOT under `Ptr`/`Span`/`SpanIter`/`Ref` where it is the const-pointee/element (a broad `substitute_type_params` collapse breaks `Ptr[readonly[T]]` / ReadOnlyPtr -- verified). Cleanest is making `auto_readonly` value-aware at substitution (resolve `AutoReadonlyType[V]` to bare V when V is value, `readonly[V]` when reference) rather than the eager `apply_auto_readonly`. Surfaced building `collections.Counter`'s `most_common`; deferred from the readonly-dict read-access fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A yield of a CONDITIONAL rejects unless both arms are frame-resident locals.** [`yield-ternary-source-non-local-arms`] `yield a if c else b` compiles and lends when `a` / `b` are locals of the generator (the shape docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md documents), but rejects at the resumable yield sink (`res.yield_type`) when they are PARAMETERS of the same generator, and one rung earlier (`expr.ifexpr`) when they are `self` FIELDS -- although each arm on its own is a lending yield source at that slot, and CPython yields the selected object either way. Probe `/tmp/agents/genyield_impl/ternary.py`, verified 2026-09-17; it is the yield sink's ladder, not the conditional: the same arms bound to a local first (`s = a if c else b; yield s`) work. The provenance rule that picks a generic generator's slot already recurses into both arms (`is_dangling_return`, `tpyc/sema/compatibility.py`), so only the lowering arm is missing. In a GENERIC body the local-arm spelling rejects too, one rung earlier again (`res.alias_bind` on the `s = a if c else b` bind of two subscript locals, measured 2026-09-17 while filling the position matrix of `tests/cases/iterators/gen_generic_yield_borrow`), so no conditional yield source is expressible there. Sibling of BUGS.md#subscript-elem-record, which is the same shape of gap one expression form over. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++ on valid code, toolchain-caught; everyday shape) A `for` over a literal of record PARAMETERS inside a generator or `async def` spells the frame's source slot as `std::array<T&, N>`.** [`frame-for-literal-of-params-reference-array`] `def gen(a: Cell, b: Cell) -> Iterator[int32]: for x in [a, b]: x.v += 10; yield x.v` (and the non-suspending twin whose body binds a frame local) emits `::tpy::frame_loop_slot<std::array<Cell&, 2>> __for_src_0;` and `__for_src_0.emplace(std::array<Cell&, 2>{a, b});` -- *forming pointer to reference type* at the `frame_slot` constraint. The frame prescan spells the slot from the literal's resolved type, whose element type still carries the parameter's reference; the plain-function route strips it (`_owned_literal_type`, `tpyc/thir/lower/statements.py`, `tests/cases/iterators/for_literal_ref_elements`), so the same literal in a plain function compiles and mutates the parameters. The frame OWNS the source it iterates, so the owned spelling is the right one here too. Fix shape: apply the owned-element spelling where the frame prescan names the `__for_src_N` slot type (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/gen_generators.py`), one spelling for both routes. Same family as the entry below and `comprehension-elem-borrow-call-array`. Surfaced 2026-09-22 merging the frame for-source rule into THIR batch 7 (identical on master alone; probe `/tmp/agents/batch7/final/merge_probe.py`). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (ill-formed C++ on valid code) An `Array`-optimized local built from GENERIC reference values spells `std::array<T&, N>`.** [`generic-array-literal-of-references`] `def plain[T](a: T, b: T) -> int32: box = [a, b]; return len(box)` emits `std::array<::tpy::val_or_ref_t<T>, 2> box = {::tpy::param_to_storage<T>(a), ::tpy::param_to_storage<T>(b)};`, and at a reference instantiation `val_or_ref_t<T>` IS `Point&` -- an array of references, which the standard forbids (*forming pointer to reference type*, *too many initializers*). Inside a generator the same literal additionally fails the `frame_slot` constraint check. A value instantiation compiles, so the rejection depends on the type argument, not on the source. The array-literal local borrowed the ELEMENT spelling from the generic PARAMETER form (`val_or_ref_t`, `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/type_traits.hpp`), which is a parameter's borrow form and not a storage form -- the sibling `val_or_ptr_t` exists for exactly this reason on the tuple side. Fix shape: an owning-slot element type for a generic array local (the same question `Own[T]` storage answers), or refusing the Array optimization for an open `T` so the literal falls back to the `list` path. Probes `/tmp/agents/yield_round1/arrayref.py` (generator) and `arrayref2.py` (plain function), measured 2026-09-17; pre-existing, found while filling the yield-source position matrix of `tests/cases/iterators/gen_generic_yield_borrow` (the local container section uses a `list[T]` + `append` instead because of it). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (SILENT CPython divergence, no warning) `itertools.cycle` lends its elements on the FIRST pass only; every later pass yields copies.** [`itertools-cycle-later-passes-copy`] `for n in cycle(f): n.v += 10` over `f = [Node(1), Node(2)]`, stopped after four steps, leaves `f` at `11 12` where CPython reads `21 22` (probe `/tmp/agents/yr_parity/p5_itertools.py`, verified 2026-09-17). `cycle` is TPy source (`lib/tpy/itertools.py`): its first loop yields the argument's element -- a lend -- but also does `saved.append(x)`, which COPIES the element into the generator's own list, and the replay loop then lends out of `saved`. So the mutation of pass 1 lands on the source and the mutation of pass 2 lands on the copy, which is why the divergence is a doubling rather than a total loss. Nothing warns, because the copy is the documented generic owning-slot contract at the append. `islice` / `takewhile` / `dropwhile` / `filterfalse` / `repeat` have no such buffer and match CPython. A TPy-source combinator that copies where CPython aliases (the C++ ones lend since 2026-09-22), and what it needs to close is an element buffer that holds BORROWS of the argument's elements rather than copies, which is the representation question TODO.md "Builtin combinators in TPy source" is about. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small, deferred: MIR] (SILENT CPython divergence, no warning) ONE ephemeral yield source demotes every other yield in the same generic generator.** [`generic-yield-mixed-source-demotes-frame`] `def mix[T](items: list[T], extra: Iterator[T]) -> Iterator[T]` that yields `items`' loop var and then `extra`'s prints `mixed 1 2 5` where CPython reads `101 102 105` (probe `/tmp/agents/yr_parity/p8_mix.py`, verified 2026-09-17); the same body without the `extra` loop mutates the source correctly. The slot is ONE type for the whole frame, so the per-generator verdict conjoins every yield source and a single unrooted one takes the value slot for all of them -- stated conservatism of the rule (`docs/ITERATOR_DESIGN.md`), not an oversight, but the result is still a silent copy at the yields that would have lent. Closing it needs a per-yield slot, i.e. a frame that can hand out a borrow at one yield and a value at another (today's `next_iter_mixin` element type forbids that), or the ephemeral source itself lending -- which is what BUGS.md#mono-iterator-relay-yield-rejects is about on the concrete side. Pinned read-only as the third inverse section of `tests/cases/iterators/gen_generic_yield_borrow`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small, deferred: MIR] (silent) A generic generator that yields a CALLABLE's result copies the element even when the callable lends it.** [`generic-yield-fn-result-copies`] `def mapped[T, U](fn: Fn[[T], U], it: Iterable[T]) -> Iterator[U]: for x in it: yield fn(x)` consumed as `for p in mapped(lambda p: p, pts): p.x += 100` leaves `pts` at `1 2` where CPython reads `101 102` (probe `/tmp/agents/genyield_impl/fnborrow.py`, verified 2026-09-17). The per-generator provenance verdict that picks the open-`T` yield slot (`is_dangling_return` read closed-world, `tpyc/sema/compatibility.py`) can prove a CALL lends only when the resolved signature says its return borrows from an operand; an erased `Fn` return carries no ownership at all, so the generator falls to the VALUE slot and copies the element out. A NAMED callee is unaffected -- sema infers its `U` as `Ref[Point]` and the call site substitutes `val_or_ref<Point>`, so the same generator lends (`named 101 102` in that same probe, and `iterators/gen_ref_compose` relays through one). The copy is the reason the LAMBDA `fn` section of `tests/cases/iterators/gen_generic_yield_borrow` reads instead of mutates; its `named-fn` neighbour mutates, since a named callee lends. Closing it needs the callable's declared return to carry its ownership: see `docs/CALLABLE_CONTRACT_DESIGN.md` and TODO.md "`Fn` return ownership visible at the definition site". Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`. The everyday face is `map` with a LAMBDA: `for c in map(lambda z: z, cells): c.v += 100` leaves `cells` unchanged (TPy `[11, 12]`, CPython `[111, 112]`) because the lambda's inferred return carries no borrow fact and `map`'s declared element `U` is spelled as the owned `Cell`, so the step copies -- where the named twin `map(same, cells)` with `def same(c: Cell) -> Cell` lends and mutates correctly. Silent; the one combinator spelling that still copies since the element-form unit of 2026-09-22 (the others lend off their source). The NESTED-DEF face: `def pick(r: Rec) -> Inner: return r.inner` defined inside the caller, then `map(lambda r: pick(r), rs)` renders `[&pick](Rec& r) -> Inner { return pick(r); }` -- a call through the nested def's closure value carries no borrow fact, so the lambda's result is a by-value `Inner` and a write through the element misses `rs` (TPy `[2, 1]`, CPython `[102, 101]`; same on `1ea64345ea`; probe `/tmp/agents/safety-lt2/xm/m2.py`).
- **[MED small, deferred: MIR] (SILENT CPython divergence, no warning) A generic generator that re-yields the element of an INNER generic producer hands out a copy, so mutation through the consumer's loop var never reaches the source.** [`generic-relay-inner-producer-copies`] `def eachl[T](items: list[T]) -> Iterator[T]: for it in items: yield it` and `def lend_twice[T](items: list[T]) -> Iterator[T]: for a in eachl(items): yield a`, then `for p in lend_twice(pts): p.x += 100` -- TPy prints `1 2`, CPython `101 102` (probe `/tmp/agents/relay_generic_producer.py`; identical on master 2cb3c41d3f). The loop var `a` borrows the inner frame's step slot, which the next step overwrites, so the relay takes the VALUE yield slot -- the same conservatism `tests/cases/iterators/gen_generic_yield_borrow` pins as its "inverse 2" for an `Iterator[T]` PARAMETER source, applied here to an inner producer the relay owns. Either the element must be lent from where the inner producer lends it (its own source list, which outlives both frames), or the copy needs the copy diagnostic and an escape hatch like every other owned-storage sink. Related: `generic-yield-mixed-source-demotes-frame`, `mono-iterator-relay-yield-rejects`. Found by the merge check of the generator-frame perf branch 2026-09-18. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small, deferred: MIR] (silent copy, conservative) A generic generator whose lending callee is analyzed in a LATER module falls to the value yield slot, so it copies where its same-module twin lends.** [`generic-yield-cross-module-callee-value-slot`] `_settle_deferred_generic_yields` (`tpyc/sema/analyzer.py`) runs at the END of one module's `analyze_bodies`, over a list that the same pass cleared at its start, so a verdict can only read `return_borrows_from` of callees whose bodies that module already analyzed. Within a module that is exactly what makes the verdict order-independent; across modules it holds only in one direction. Modules are analyzed in topological order (`tpyc/compiler.py`), so an imported callee is always analyzed first -- the only way a lending callee's body can be analyzed AFTER the generic generator that yields its result is an import CYCLE, whose members are analyzed as a group. For a cycle peer the fact is still `None` at settle time, the rooting half answers conservatively, and the frame gets the value slot `T` instead of `::tpy::yield_slot_t<T>`: the consumer sees a copy and cannot mutate the element, where the byte-identical single-module spelling aliases (and CPython aliases). Conservative, so not unsafe -- the divergence is a silent CPython parity gap, not a dangle. Sibling ordering hole through the same fact, on the unsafe side: BUGS.md#cycle-peer-borrow-fact-read-as-stub. **Fix shape:** settle the deferred verdicts once per cycle GROUP (the compiler knows the SCC) or at the workspace-wide finalize, which is the same widening the sibling needs. Not reproduced end-to-end; read off the settle site and the module ordering 2026-09-17.
- **[LOW small, deferred: MIR] (missing sema diagnostic, loud THIR backstop) A generator that yields the result of a NESTED def call escapes the yield-rooting check, so an unsound borrow yield reaches codegen and is refused there under an internal construct name.** [`nested-def-callee-yield-root-unchecked`] `def g_mk(n: int32) -> Iterator[Node]` whose body defines `def mk(a: int32) -> Own[Node]: return Node(a)` and then does `yield mk(n)` passes sema: the free-call arm of `is_dangling_return` (`tpyc/sema/compatibility.py`) gates its "a function returning `Own[T]` makes a temporary" test on `self.ctx.registry.get_function(expr.func_name)`, and a nested def is absent from the module registry, so with no recorded borrow sources the open-world reading the yield-root drain uses (`assume_unknown_calls_safe=True`) falls through to "safe". THIR then refuses the body -- *this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (res.yield_type)*, reported on the generator def line -- while the module-level twin (the same `mk` hoisted out of the body) gets the rule it broke: *Cannot yield local or temporary as reference ... Declare the generator `Iterator[Own[Node]]` to yield by value*, on the yield line. No miscompile, since the program is refused either way, but under an internal name and at the wrong line. Probes `/tmp/agents/fix_curfn/neg_provider.py` vs `neg_toplevel.py`, verified 2026-09-17; unaffected by the live-handle preservation in `save_function_state` (reproduces identically on both sides of it). Fix shape: resolve a nested-def callee where it lives (the enclosing body binding, `func.nested_def_nodes`) instead of gating the arm on the module registry. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] The for-loop result slot in a resumable frame is spelled from the ELEMENT type, so a non-value element makes it `std::expected<T&, StopIteration>` -- ill-formed C++, since a reference cannot live in `std::expected`. Two arms of `_analyze_for_strategy` do this.** (a) The `er_elem` arm: `class BagIter: @error_return(StopIteration) def __next__(self) -> Point` iterated inside a two-yield generator emits `std::expected<Point&, ::tpy::StopIteration> __for_r_0`, and libstdc++ rejects it (`non-static data member ... in a union may not have reference type` / `forming pointer to reference type`). Repro `/tmp/agents/prereq/ernext.py`. (b) The `typing.Iterator` arm for a NAMED source: same slot, same error; the temporary-source path already avoids it by spelling `decltype(std::declval<__gen_X&>().__next__())` from the stored struct rather than from the element. Arm (b) is mostly shadowed by the over-broad ephemeral-borrow rejection (a yield touching the loop var is rejected at sema first), so its reachable window is a body that mutates the element but never yields anything derived from it; arm (a) has no such shield. Loud (toolchain-caught), rejects-valid. Same borrow-form-leaked-into-an-owning-slot family as the since-fixed coro-frame `str`/view local defect, different site: there the owning slot was the yield result, here it is the `__next__` result field. Note the `er_elem` arm is also missing the borrow-form loop-var classification, but that is moot until the slot is spellable. Fix shape, covering both arms: derive the result slot from the SOURCE (its `__next__` return type, as the temporary path already does) instead of from the element type, so the borrow lands in the loop var where the storage-form classification can hold it. Was filed as two entries -- one per arm, with different prescriptions -- until the merge-master check spotted they are one defect. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A `dict`/`set` literal with a coercible-but-not-equal element type rejects-valid instead of applying the runtime-checked `BigInt -> fixed-width int` coercion.** `d: dict[str, int32] = {"k": make_big()}` / `s: set[int32] = {make_big()}` (where `make_big() -> int`) is rejected at sema with `Type mismatch in variable 'd': expected int32, got int`, even though the same `int` value coerces cleanly at scalar (`x: int32 = make_big()`) and now list/tuple-element positions (the runtime-checked `to_fixed_check`). Root: the dict/set literal analyzers' per-element contextual-coercion branch only fires when the expected element type is a union/optional/Any/recursive-wrapper/covariant-generic shape; a plain concrete target (`int32`) falls to the `else` peer-unify branch, so the literal's type becomes `dict[str, BigInt]` / `set[BigInt]`, which the strict container-assignment element check then rejects. Distinct from the list/tuple gap that this sibling fix closed -- those *silently miscompiled* (ill-formed C++); dict/set instead *reject-valid* with a clean error, so it is lower severity. Fix shape: widen the contextual branch to any known concrete target and route plain-target elements through the same materialize-narrowing-coercion path `_analyze_array_literal` now uses (`_materialize_narrowing_element_coercion`), verifying the strict element check still rejects user-record slicing. Surfaced fixing the list/tuple aggregate-element coercion (`tests/cases/int/int_to_fixed_in_aggregate`). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED medium] A protocol whose method is typed with a *same-module* recursive type alias fails the C++ build -- the protocol's concept / `@dynamic` base + `Adapter`/`RefAdapter` are emitted before the recursive-alias wrapper struct is declared.** `type Tree[T] = T | list[Tree[T]]` plus `class Counter(Protocol): def count(self, t: Tree[int]) -> int32: ...` (or the `@dynamic` form) in one module emits, in the header, a virtual `count(Tree<BigInt>&)` / a `Counter` concept referencing `Tree<...>` *before* the same-module `template<...> struct Tree` (or its forward decl) appears -- g++ reports `'Tree' has not been declared` (structural: `concept 'Counter' not in namespace scope`; `@dynamic`: `RefAdapter` pure-virtual `count` not overridden due to the broken signature). Affects both structural and `@dynamic` protocols, generic recursive alias confirmed (non-generic recursive union likely same root, unverified). **Works cross-module**: importing the alias (`from treelib import Tree`) brings the wrapper in complete via the included header, so the ordering is satisfied -- this is the workaround. Toolchain-caught (C++ build error), not silent. Fix shape: in `codegen_cpp/generator.py` emit ordering, the recursive-union wrapper forward-decl/definition for a *local* alias must precede protocol (concept / `@dynamic` base / adapter) emission, mirroring the guarantee the imported-header path already provides. Surfaced by /tpy-ready coverage-hardening probes for generic recursive aliases (the `@dynamic`-protocol-method coverage gap). Covered cross-module by `tests/cases/protocols/dyn_recursive_alias_method`; the same-module case is the gap. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (parity) `open(dir, "r")` on a directory succeeds silently and `read()` returns `""` where CPython raises `IsADirectoryError` immediately.** `std::ifstream::open` does not fail for a directory in read mode (Linux `open(2)` with `O_RDONLY` succeeds on a directory; the failure only surfaces at `read(2)` as EISDIR, which iostreams swallow into failbit/empty), so `TextFile`/`BinaryFile`'s `is_open()` gate passes and the EISDIR arm of the errno-mapped open path is unreachable for read mode -- probe: `open("/tmp", "r").read()` prints `""` in TPy, raises `[Errno 21] Is a directory: '/tmp'` in CPython. Write-mode open on a directory DOES correctly raise `IsADirectoryError` (EISDIR at `open(2)` time). Silent divergence, and it defeats the read-mode half of the `IsADirectoryError` mapping the CPython-exact-OSError feature wired up; also blocks writing an EISDIR-through-`open()` test until fixed. Fix shape: after a successful read-mode open, `stat` the path (or attempt a zero-byte read and check EISDIR) and raise `IsADirectoryError` like CPython's `io.open` does at fd-wrap time. Pre-existing (the `is_open()` gate predates the errno mapping); surfaced by /tpy-review (cpython-parity) of the oserror-exact branch. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `TextFile`/`BinaryFile` reads do not surface a genuine I/O error (badbit) -- a read that fails on a device error returns "" / b"" instead of raising `OSError`.** `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/file.hpp`: the full-read path (`read()` / `read(size<0)`) drains via `ss << fs_.rdbuf()` / `istreambuf_iterator` and never checks `fs_.bad()`; the sized-read path (`read(size>=0)`) now preserves badbit across its short-read `clear()` but still doesn't *raise* on it -- a subsequent read just returns empty. CPython raises `OSError` on a real read error. Latent: badbit on a regular file is a hardware/FS fault, near-unreachable in tests; EOF (the common short-read cause) is correctly handled as empty. Fix shape: after each read, if `fs_.bad()` (not merely `eof`/`fail`), `raise_os_error(...)` -- consistently across both the full-read and sized-read paths. Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness) of the io `read(size)` change.
- **[HIGH medium, postponed: evaluation-order policy] Subexpressions evaluate in the C++ COMPILER'S order, diverging from CPython's guaranteed left-to-right -- confirmed for positional call/constructor/method arguments, both operands of a binary operator, and f-string interpolations.** [`subexpression-right-to-left-eval`] Measured against CPython with a counter function `nxt()`: `three(nxt(), nxt(), nxt())` prints `3 2 1` (CPython `1 2 3`), `print(nxt() - nxt())` prints `1` (CPython `-1`), `f"{nxt()} {nxt()}"` prints `7 6` (CPython `6 7`) -- probe `/tmp/agents/dsr/r29_evalorder.py`. Brace-initialized list/tuple literals and `print(a, b)` ARE sequenced with respect to EACH OTHER (the standard sequences a braced-init-list and a `<<` chain), while a literal that MOVES its elements -- a `@nocopy` or movable-local element, or an `Own`-returning call at a container-element slot (admitted 2026-09-15) -- renders through the `::tpy::make_vector` / `make_ordered_map` / `make_ordered_set` helpers, whose operands are call arguments like any other's (`tests/cases/list/container_elem_from_call` pins that render and cites this entry); but a print argument's own OUTPUT still interleaves wrongly: `print("x:", f())` where `f` prints emits `std::cout << "x:" << f()`, and `<<` operands evaluate left-to-right, so the prefix reaches the stream before `f()` runs -- TPy prints `x: ` then f's output then `7`, CPython evaluates every argument first and prints f's output then `x: 7`. Likewise when a print argument RAISES, the text before it has already been written: `print("result:", f())` with `f` raising prints `result: ` and then the handler's output, where CPython evaluates every argument first and prints nothing of that call. Any print whose arguments write to stdout (or stderr on the same terminal) diverges, with no call-order bug in sight; the fix shape is the same sequencing -- materialize every side-effecting argument into temps before the first `<<`. Silent wherever the subexpressions are pure, wrong wherever they are not, and `f() - g()` needs no call syntax to trigger. Found downstream in a path tracer, where `V3(random() * 2.0 - 1.0, random() * 2.0 - 1.0, random() * 2.0 - 1.0)` drew from the random stream backwards: the result was a correctly rendered but DIFFERENT image, so nothing short of a byte comparison against CPython caught it. Raised MED -> HIGH on that evidence: the original entry was scoped to the single binary op, and the shape that actually bites -- an ordinary multi-argument call -- is both more common and equally silent. The three sub-entries below record the shapes as originally measured. **Original binary-operand measurement:** `a() + b()` (each appending to a shared list) runs `b()` then `a()` -- TPy emits the C++ expression `a() + b()` and g++ evaluates function-call arguments right-to-left (C++ leaves the order unspecified), so any observable side effect in the operands is sequenced backwards. The *result value* is correct (operator is applied to the right values); only the side-effect *order* diverges. Reproducer: `order=[]; def a(): order.append("a"); return "A"` + same for `b`; `a()+b()` gives `order==['b','a']` (CPython `['a','b']`). Notably the 3+-operand chain `a()+b()+c()` is correct (`['a','b','c']`) -- it routes through a left-to-right fold -- so the bug is specific to the single binary op. Applies to any binary operator (`+`/`-`/`*`/comparisons/etc.) whose two operands both carry side effects, not just str concat. No diagnostic; silent. Affects `<`/`==` operand order, `x[f()] = g()`-style too (unaudited). Fix shape: sequence binary-op operands left-to-right at emit (materialize the left operand into a temp before evaluating the right when either operand is non-trivial). Sequence the operands: capture the left one's VALUE before evaluating the right when either can run user code -- a reference alias is not enough, it re-reads after the write. The membership / chained-comparison sibling of this is filed above and was implemented then reverted; the two should land together so the rule is not half-applied, and the cost (a copy per affected expression) priced once for both. Probe `/tmp/agents/chain-dup/reorder.py`. Surfaced authoring the io `read(size)` tests (`fp.read(4) + "|" + fp.read()`). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`. **Same class, hoisted-arg shape:** an arg materialized as a named temp STATEMENT before the call (a ref-param rvalue -- container/record literal or call result -- to a free function, or any reference-type rvalue to a generator/coro method) evaluates before sibling inline args, so a multi-arg call mixing a hoisted arg with side-effecting inline args sequences wrong vs CPython's left-to-right (probe: `take(side("a"), [side("x"), side("y")], side("b"))` -> `x y b a`, CPython `a x y b`). Newly reachable via the resumable-method rvalue args that previously failed the C++ build. The fix shape generalizes: hoist ALL side-effecting args left-to-right once any arg hoists. A comprehension argument joins the hoisted shape at a CONSTRUCTOR's container slot since 2026-09-11 (`Flat(f(), [g(x) for x in h()])` runs `h`, `g`, then `f`; the free-call twin always did) -- `cases/calls/ctor_comprehension_arg` cites this entry rather than pinning the order. **Value-typed generic slots joined the scope on 2026-09-08:** an rvalue at a generic `T` parameter used to hoist a named temp, which incidentally SERIALIZED it ahead of its sibling arguments; the temp is now taken at the instantiation, so `f(side("A"), side("B"))` at a value-typed `T` renders both inline and g++ runs B then A. Not a new class and not a reason to re-add the hoist -- the monomorphic twin always had this order, so hoisting only at the generic slot would make the generic and its twin differ (the `generic-equals-monomorphic-twin` pitfall) while leaving the twin wrong; the fix is the sequencing below, which covers both. **POSTPONED 2026-09-16 -- do not fix any site of this class until the policy is decided.** The order is not "backwards", it is the C++ compiler's: g++ evaluates call arguments right-to-left and clang left-to-right in practice, and the standard guarantees neither, so a program that observes it is also toolchain-dependent (no case may pin the order in `output.txt`; pin the render). Whether TPy guarantees Python's order everywhere (a temporary per observable operand at every multi-operand site -- the sequenced stmt-expr build that was built for the moving container literal in bundle 2 and reverted for exactly this reason), only outside hot-path annotated sections, or nowhere, is one language decision (TODO.md "Evaluation-order policy"), and per-site fixes before it are inconsistent by construction. Known sites, one list: positional call / constructor / method arguments; both operands of a two-operand binary operator (everyday instance: CPython's `c.compress(x) + c.flush()` over a `zlib.compressobj` runs `flush()` first, so `compress()` then raises on the finished stream -- `tests/cases/stdlib/zlib_basic` spells it as two statements) (the 3+-operand chain folds left to right by accident); f-string interpolations; a hoisted argument beside inline side-effecting ones (since 2026-10-01 also at a field write of a container literal whose element hoists a temp, and at a demoted constructor member-init whose source hoists one -- `cases/records/field_admission`, class `Placed`); value-typed generic slots; the moving container literal (list, set, and dict, where Python also runs each key before its own value); the dict comprehension key/value pair (`dict-comp-key-value-order`, same class). One site currently REJECTS instead of diverging: `print` with a computed `sep=`/`end=` beside a call-valued positional argument (`_expr_evaluation_inert`, `tpyc/thir/lower/checks.py`) -- relax it to the same declaration, or keep it, when the policy lands. A stdlib face turns the divergence into a panic (website docs audit, 2026-09-28): `co = zlib.compressobj(); blob = co.compress(b"abcabcabc") + co.flush()` renders `::tpy::bytes_concat(co.compress(...), co.flush())`, `flush()` runs first, and the program dies with `uncaught tpystd::zlib::error: Error -2 while compressing data: inconsistent stream state` (CPython prints the round-tripped bytes); probe `/tmp/agents/rel06/audit/zlib_order.py`.
- **[MED, deferred: MIR] A generator holding an `Optional[T]` local across iterations and yielding a tuple of (the narrowed previous value, the current loop var) miscompiles -- the previous-value tuple element silently reads the current loop var.** `def pairwise[T](it): prev: Optional[T] = None; for x in it: (if prev is not None: yield (prev, x)); prev = copy(x)` over `[1,2,3,4]` yields `(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)` instead of `(1,2),(2,3),(3,4)` -- the `prev` element of the yielded tuple reads `x`, not the stored `prev`. Reproduces in a plain `for a, b in pairwise(...)` loop (not a comprehension artifact), so the fault is in the generator's tuple-yield of a frame-held `Optional[T]` element alongside the loop var, not the consumer. No diagnostic; silent wrong output. The single-element `Optional[T]`-across-yield path (e.g. just `yield prev`) is untested here; the miscompile is observed for the tuple-of-(prev, x) shape. **Blocks `itertools.pairwise`** (and any windowed generator that carries a previous value). Workaround: none clean (the natural formulation miscompiles). Surfaced probing itertools v2 feasibility. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A generator with a generic `Optional[T]` accumulator written across the loop fails the C++ build (`__slot_1 is not captured` / `std::optional<int>::optional(int*&)`).** `def accumulate[T](it, func): acc: Optional[T] = None; for x in it: (acc = copy(x) if acc is None else func(acc, x)); yield acc` -> g++ errors at the resumable-frame body: the `Optional[T]` accumulator frame slot is mis-emitted (a captured-temp `__slot_1` referenced out of scope, and an `optional<int>` constructed from `int*`). The narrowed `acc` (Optional -> T) assigned back into the Optional slot across the resumable frame is the trigger. No TPy diagnostic; C++ build error only. **Blocks `itertools.accumulate`** (the generic running-fold shape). Workaround: none in the generic generator form. Surfaced probing itertools v2 feasibility. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A function/method that returns a recursive-union alias referenced *qualified* (`json.JsonValue`) fails to type-check (`expected JsonValue, got JsonValue`); the *unqualified* import (`from json import JsonValue`) compiles.** `import json; def p(s: str) -> json.JsonValue: return json.loads(s)` (and the `Own[json.JsonValue]` form, and the method form) is rejected -- the qualified alias resolves to a recursive-union form that does not match `json.loads`'s own return form, even though both print as `JsonValue`. `from json import loads, JsonValue` + `-> Own[JsonValue]` works. Almost certainly the recursive-union borrow/storage-form duality (OQ9): the cross-module qualified-alias reference produces a different form than the defining module's. Toolchain... actually a *sema* error, not silent. Workaround: import the alias by name (used by `tplib.requests.Response.json`). Reproducers `/tmp/agents/req/{m2,g1}.py`. Surfaced building `tplib.requests`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED] `isinstance`-narrowing a recursive-union element *extracted* from a container fails the C++ build unless the element is first bound to an explicitly-annotated local.** `d = json.loads(s); if isinstance(d, dict): v = d["k"]; if isinstance(v, int): ...` -> g++ `no matching function for call to holds_alternative<tpy::BigInt>(JsonValue&)` -- the extracted element is a *borrow* form (`JsonValue&`) on which `holds_alternative` is not callable. Binding `v: JsonValue = d["k"]` first (forcing a storage-form copy) makes the narrow compile and run. Shallow narrowing of the `loads` root (`isinstance(d, dict)`) is unaffected. Borrow/storage-form duality (OQ9) at the element-access boundary. Toolchain-caught, not silent. Workaround: explicit `: JsonValue` local (documented in `tplib.requests` -- affects every consumer of `Response.json()`). Reproducers `/tmp/agents/req/{g2,h2}.py`. Surfaced building `tplib.requests`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] For-iterating a narrowed `Optional[list]` accessed through an *attribute* emits a double-deref and fails the C++ build.** `if args.header is not None: for h in args.header: ...` (where `args.header: list[str] | None`, e.g. an argparse `action="append"` result) emits `auto& __obj_0 = (*(*args.header));` -- g++ `no match for operator* (operand type is std::vector<...>)`. The narrowing of the attribute does not carry to the for-loop's iterable lowering, which then derefs an already-deref'd value. *Subscripting* the same narrowed attribute works (`args.tag[0]` in `tests/cases/argparse/list_and_const_actions`), so the gap is specific to for-iteration of an Optional-list *attribute*. Binding to a local first (`hl = args.header; if hl is not None: for h in hl: ...`) narrows correctly and compiles -- used in `programs/curl/curl.py` in the `tpy-examples` repo. Toolchain-caught, not silent. Sibling of the narrowed-Optional-dict key-iter entry above. Surfaced building the curl example on `tplib.requests`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] An `@overload`-ed generator METHOD is rejected at the stub: `Protocol type 'Iterator' cannot be used as a return type`.** `class C: @overload def rep[T](self, obj: T) -> Iterator[T]: ...` + a second stub + a `yield`-bodied implementation errors at the first stub's `def` line. Root: the `...`-bodied stub has `is_generator=False` (no `yield` in its body), and the method-registration return-type validation (`tpyc/sema/registration.py:1258`) rejects an `Iterator[T]` return unless `method.is_generator` -- whereas the free-function overload path (`register_overload_group`) does no protocol-return check on stubs at all, so it is lenient. Distinct from the free-function overloaded-generator crash (now fixed: the impl's `generator_yield_type` is set via `_set_generator_yield_type`); the method analog fails earlier and never reaches that path. The free-function form is the common one (itertools uses free functions), so this is lower priority. Fix shape: in the method return-type validation, treat an `Iterator[T]`-returning `@overload` stub whose group has a generator implementation as a generator (or relax the protocol-return check for overload stubs, mirroring the free-function path), then set the impl method's `generator_yield_type` (same `_set_generator_yield_type` helper). Surfaced by /tpy-fix-bug of the free-function overloaded generator. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] An annotated dict/list literal whose VALUES are container literals is rejected: `Type mismatch in variable 'g': expected list[int32], got PendingList[int32, 2]#0`.** `g: dict[str, list[int32]] = {"a": [1, 2], "b": [3]}` fails, and so does the list flavor `m: list[list[int32]] = [[1], [2, 3]]`. The annotation's element type never reaches the NESTED literal, so each inner literal stays a `PendingListType` and the outer coercion compares it against the resolved `list[int32]` slot (`_analyze_var_decl` -> `compat.coerce_expr`, `tpyc/sema/statements.py:4196`). The named-local workaround compiles (`row: list[int32] = [1, 2]; g = {"a": row}`). This is the sibling BUGS entry below already names as "the annotated dict-literal-of-list-literals case" -- it had no entry of its own. Loud reject-valid, no miscompile. Fix shape: thread the annotated container's element/value type into nested container literals during literal resolution, the same expected-type-into-nested-literal hole as the `d.get(k, [])` default. Repro `/tmp/agents/d2dbg/x/main.py`. Surfaced writing the value-position container-element exec case. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] `d.get(k, [])` (empty-list / collection-literal default) fails to compile: the literal default arg never resolves its element type.** `d: dict[str, list[int32]]; d.get("k", [])` -> `No matching overload for 'get' with argument types (str, PendingList[???, 0])` -- the `[]` stays a `PendingListType` (no element-type context flows from the `default: V` param to the literal), so overload resolution can't match `get(key, default: V)`. The named-local workaround (`fb: list[int32] = []; d.get(k, fb)`) compiles. Same expected-type-into-nested-literal hole as the annotated dict-literal-of-list-literals case (audit cluster 14 family); the `default` param's `V` should hint the literal. Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/getb/absent_rvalue.py`. Blocks the rvalue-default path of the dict.get(k,default) aliasing work (Stage B). Surfaced reproducing that work.
- **[LOW small] The F1 borrow-local const rule may emit `const T*` for a mutable borrow when a `@readonly` `@native` record method returns a reference type.** Now that native `-> V` reference returns alias (the native-record exclusion was removed), the readonly-method ref-return arm of `_f1_is_const` (`tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py:7772`, the `isinstance(stmt.init, TpyMethodCall)` branch keyed on `fi.is_readonly and call_returns_cpp_ref(...)`) fires and renders the bound local `const T*`; if such a method intentionally exposes a mutable `T&` and the caller wants a mutable `T*`, the borrow is silently over-constrained. No current stdlib case (the affected methods -- e.g. uninit `load` -- pick the non-const C++ overload on a non-const receiver, and `const T*` from a mutable `T&` is a safe narrowing). Latent trap for future native bindings; confirmed by reading the surviving arm, not by a reproducer. Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness).
- **[LOW small] `@cpp_template` accessor methods on `@native` containers (`list`/`Span`/`Array`/`varargs.unchecked_get`) now alias for reference-type element instantiations, untested.** The native-record exclusion removal generalized aliasing to all native `-> V` reference returns, including `@cpp_template` `operator[]`-style accessors; the `unchecked_get` family is exercised only for value-type elements, so the reference-element aliasing path (`list[SomeRecord].unchecked_get(i)` bound and mutated through) has no regression test. Behavior is believed correct (operator[] returns `T&`); the gap is coverage. Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness).
- **[LOW small] Free `@native` functions returning a bare reference type `-> V` value-copy the result where a `V&`-returning C++ function should alias.** `call_returns_cpp_ref` (`tpyc/value_category.py`) bails out for `is_native_import` (free native functions) before the `-> V` vs `-> Own[V]` return-shape check that now governs both user methods and `@native` *record* methods (the native-record exclusion was removed). So a free `@native` func whose hand-written C++ returns `V&` into an argument has its result copied at the call site, not aliased -- the same asymmetry the record-method fix closed, one layer up. Latent: no in-tree free native function currently returns a bare reference `-> V` (they return values, `Own`, `Optional`, or views). Fix: drop the remaining `fi.is_native_import and not fi.is_method` guard in `call_returns_cpp_ref` (the method half is already handled) so free functions also reach the return-shape check, after auditing free native bindings the way the record-method bindings were audited (confirm each bare-`-> V` free function actually returns `V&`, retype by-value ones to `-> Own[V]`). Surfaced removing the native-record return-convention exclusion.
