- **[MED medium, deferred: MIR] Two-arg `dict.get(k, default)` returns a copy of the stored value where CPython returns the stored object -- warned, not yet aliased.** [`dict-get-default-copies-not-aliases`] The dict-accessor aliasing work (audit cluster 7) made `items()`/`values()`/`setdefault()` borrow, but two-arg `get` stayed by-value: its result conditionally borrows EITHER the map slot (hit) OR the default argument (miss), and an rvalue default needs a materialization slot whose lifetime is unresolved for loops (per-iteration freshness vs slot reuse) and resumable frames (suspension-crossing borrows). Loud since the same work: a call-site warning fires for reference-type values, silenced by wrapping in `copy()`; value-type results are parity-clean. Fix shape: `V& dict_get_default(m&, key, V& def)` + const overload (value-type V keeps the by-value helper, dispatched by codegen), an emit-site slot for rvalue defaults with defined loop/suspension semantics, and `return_borrows_from={-1, default}` so borrow tracking roots at both sources; typing the return as a bare `-> V` (not `Own[V]`) then makes the result alias with no extra mechanism (the precedent: setdefault is a plain `-> V` native method that aliases because native `-> V` reference returns are treated as `T&`), and the `@copy_returns_warn` decorator is dropped from the overload at the same time (the warning becomes unnecessary once the result aliases). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A pending dict/set LOCAL passed to a param with a wider value/element type is rejected instead of widening (`{"a": 1}` local into `dict[str, int64]` param -> "expected int64, got int32").** Symmetric everywhere (free functions, methods, ctors) -- `mark_container_param_context`'s dict/set arms only call `_widen_inferred_type`, which records the widening for the literal's storage but the arg-check still compares the pre-widening pending type against the param and errors. The LIST arm handles this (`coerced_element_type` makes `xs = [3]; take(xs)` into `list[int64]` compile), so the gap is dict/set parity with the list behavior. Loud reject-valid, trivial workaround (annotate the local). Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/setbug/dictwiden.py`. Surfaced authoring the pending-arg-marks tests. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small]** Async finally-with-await (CFG-based finally) is silently skipped when the coroutine frame is dropped mid-suspension WITHOUT cancellation (a frame abandoned outside the executor's cancel-drain path). The frame destructor runs helper-based finallies and `with.__exit__`s, but a finally body that itself suspends cannot run in a destructor. The generator sibling (yield-in-finally) gets a compile-time warning; the async shape does not, because the normal executor path runs such cleanup via cancellation (CancelledError at the suspension) and a blanket warning would flag every legitimate `finally: await ...`. Fix shape: warn only for frames that can escape executor-managed lifetime, or drain-to-completion in the owning slot before drop. CPython runs the finally at GC close.
- **[LOW small]** An `except BaseException:` (or `except GeneratorExit:`) handler around a `yield` does not observe the close when the generator is abandoned: CPython throws GeneratorExit INTO the frame, so such a handler catches it and its body runs; TPy's frame destructor runs only pending finally helpers and `with.__exit__`s (it cannot resume arbitrary handler code inside a destructor), so the handler body is skipped silently. Same can't-resume-in-a-destructor family as the warned yield-in-finally skip, but no diagnostic fires for the handler shape. Fix shape: extend the yield-in-finally warning to yields lexically inside an except-BaseException/GeneratorExit-guarded try, or accept and document. Surfaced by the GeneratorExit-on-close design pass.
- **[HIGH small] (silent divergence: a `finally` skipped)** `break`/`continue` crossing a CFG-based finally (finally body contains a suspension) silently skips that finally body: `CFGBuilder._build_break/_build_continue` emit a plain Fall to the loop's break/continue BB without routing through `finally_entry_bb` (returns are parked via the pending-return slot; break/continue have no analogous path). Same hole for break inside an except handler of such a try (`ExceptRegion.parent_finally_entry_bb`). Repro in the 2026-06-10 audit (B62): async `for` + `try/finally`-with-await + `break` drops `cleanup 1`; the generator shape shares the emitter. Fix shape: park a pending-jump target the way pending returns are parked. Helper-based finallies are unaffected. Re-verified 2026-09-25 on d4827a6abb and on `frame-borrow-order`: `for i in range(2): try: if i == 0: continue; print("body", i) finally: await asyncio.sleep(0); print("fin", i)` in an `async def` never prints `fin 0` (probe `/tmp/agents/fbo-n/p/acont.py`); `_build_continue` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/resumable_cfg.py`, ~1369) falls straight to the loop head while the finally's entry block is allocated separately (~1733). Raised to HIGH: silent, and a `continue` in a `try` is everyday code.
- **[HIGH small] (silent divergence: a `finally` skipped) In a generator or coroutine, an exception leaving an `except` handler resumed after a suspension skips its try's `finally` when that `finally` itself suspends.** [`frame-handler-skips-suspending-finally`] `try: (try: raise ValueError / except ValueError: yield 1; raise KeyError / finally: print("cfg finally"); yield 2; raise IndexError) / except IndexError: print("caught I") / finally: print("outer finally")` -- CPython prints `1`, `cfg finally`, `2`, `caught I`, `outer finally`; TPy prints `1`, `outer finally` and panics on the uncaught `KeyError` (probe `/tmp/agents/fbo-unwind/p/q11.py`, verified on master 1ea64345ea and unchanged by the unwind-levels fix, 2026-09-27). The resumed case sits in an `ExceptRegion` whose parent finally is CFG-based (`parent_finally_entry_bb`, no helper), so no unwind level captures the exception into the try's captured-exc slot and jumps to the finally entry the way the TryRegion catch-all does. Fix shape: an ExceptRegion with a CFG parent finally opens a level whose catch parks `std::current_exception()` and transitions to the finally entry. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] An explicitly-annotated `Array[T, N]` comprehension rejected by the stack-build gates fails with a misleading generic type mismatch.** `xs: Array[int32, 2000] = [i for i in range(2000)]` (over the `_COMP_ARRAY_MAX_SIZE` cap) and `xs: Array[int32, 4] = [g(i) for i in range(4)]` with `@error_return` `g` inside try/except both error with "expected Array[...], got list[...]" -- the gates in `_try_comp_array_size` (`tpyc/sema/expressions.py`) suppress the PendingListType machinery entirely, so the explicit-annotation resolution rule never runs; both shapes compiled at the pre-builder base via the old loop build. Loud rejection, not a miscompile, but it rejects previously-valid code with a diagnostic that doesn't name the cause. Fix shape needs a design call: either honor the annotation with a non-lambda build for gated shapes (the loop-fill reintroduces the default-ctor side-effect divergence the builder fixed, so only sound where construction is side-effect-free) or emit a targeted error ("cannot stack-build: element calls @error_return / size exceeds cap") at the annotation-mismatch site. Surfaced by the /tpy-ready retrospective challenger.
- **[LOW small] Reading an `@error_return` property outside try/except is not rejected; the same call spelled as a method is.** The unhandled-error_return check (`tpyc/sema/calls.py:4706`) fires for direct and method calls but not for the getter hidden behind a property read: with `@property @error_return(E) def val(...)`, a bare `g.scaled(1)` outside try/except errors with "must be handled with try/except" while the adjacent `g.val` compiles and the unwrap panics at runtime on error instead. Missing safety diagnostic, not a miscompile (codegen's panic fallback is sound). Fix, RESTATED 2026-09-18: there is no `property_getter_call` any more -- a property read IS a resolved `TpyMethodCall` from sema on, so the getter reaches `analyze_call`'s unhandled check by the same route a spelled method does. What still exempts it is that the read's analysis returns before that check runs (it resolves through the record's property table, not through the call analyser), so the check has to be asked once where the read resolves, keyed on the getter's `error_return_type` like any other callee's. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the index-sequence builder (the gate-test regeneration flagged only the method line).
- **[LOW small] Repeating a mutable reference-type element has no "copies" diagnostic, asymmetric with the bulk-copy warning.** `[obj] * N` evaluates the element once and copies it into every slot where CPython aliases the same object N times -- mutating `xs[0]` updates all CPython views but only one TPy copy. The divergence is declared in `docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md` (list repetition) but emits no compile-time signal, while the sibling bulk-copy path (`list(b)` over reference elements) warns "copies X elements" with `copy_iter()` as the acknowledgment spelling (`tpyc/sema/calls.py`). Pre-existing for the vector repeat path; the Array repeat path now shares it. Fix shape (design-gated: new warning + acknowledgment spelling need sign-off): warn on repeating a mutable reference-type element, silenced by an explicit per-slot construction or an acknowledgment spelling consistent with `copy_iter`. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the repeat-pair fix.
- **[LOW small] A comprehension whose element is a reference-typed field access (`[obj.ref_field for obj in src]`) fails the C++ build with "forming pointer to reference type".** `[b.inner for b in bs]` where `Box.inner: Inner` (a reference-type field) and `bs: list[Box]` emits a `std::vector<Inner>` build that g++ rejects (`forming pointer to reference type 'Inner&'` inside `allocator`/`construct_at`). Pre-existing and independent of the source's ownership -- reproduces identically over a borrowed `list` source and an `Own[T]`-yielding generator. The comprehension element binds the field access as `Inner&` and the storage-form result vector mis-forms a pointer to it. Loud build error, not a miscompile. Workaround: bind the field to a local first (`[copy(b.inner) for b in bs]` or an explicit loop). Surfaced building a derived-sink test case for the list/set comprehension-element move fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small, diagnostics] Growing an inferred fixed-`Array` sublist via the outer subscript surfaces a raw g++ error, not a TPy diagnostic.** `rows = [[i, i + 1] for i in range(3)]; rows[0].append(99)` -- the inner literal `[i, i+1]` is constant-size and unmutated, so it resolves to `std::array<int32_t, 2>` (the stack-Array optimization), and `rows[0].append(...)` then fails the C++ build with `'std::array<int, 2>' has no member named 'push_back'`. Mutation *through the outer subscript* is not tracked back to the inner literal, so the inner is never promoted to `list`. Loud failure, not a miscompile; the workaround is an explicit `rows: list[list[int]] = [...]` (forces `vector<vector<...>>`, append works -- covered by `tests/cases/list/comp_nested_vector_inner`). A leaky-C++-error class (raw g++ message instead of a TPy diagnostic). The uniform outer/middle levels of a deep-nested literal (e.g. `[[[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[5, 6], [7, 8]]]`) are another way to reach it: those levels stay fixed `Array`, so `xs.append(...)` / `xs[0].append(...)` on them hits the same raw g++ error. Fix shape: either detect element-mutation through a container subscript and promote the inner pending list to `list`, or emit a TPy diagnostic at the `.append` site pointing at the `list[list[T]]` annotation. The fix's regression test (a now-rejected-with-clean-message `error_` case, or a happy case once promotion lands) goes in with the fix. Surfaced while finishing the nested-list-literal work. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small, diagnostics] Pending container type names leak into type-mismatch / unresolved-type diagnostics** (`PendingList[int32, 2]#0`, `PendingDict[...]#1`). User-facing errors expose the internal deferred-resolution representation instead of a resolved display name (`list[int]`, etc.); the `error_append_incompatible_nested` and `error_jagged_incompatible_elem` cases show both sides of a mismatch as raw `PendingList[...]`. Worse, the mixed-types error's *suggested fix* embeds the same repr -- `Use a type annotation like list[PendingList[int32, 2]#0 | PendingList[str, 3]#1]` -- which is unwritable (a user can't type `#0`), so the suggestion is useless until the names resolve. Pre-existing, cross-cutting all pending-type errors. Fix shape: a `PendingList`/`PendingDict`/`PendingSet` -> resolved-display-name helper (defer to the inferred element type) applied at the diagnostic-formatting boundary, *including the suggested-annotation string* (which then reads `list[list[int] | list[str]]`). Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness) of the pending-container-compat fix; suggestion face flagged reviewing the jagged-nested-list diagnostics. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small, postponed: evaluation-order policy] A dict comprehension evaluates the key and value in unspecified order (CPython evaluates the key first), observable only with ordering-dependent side effects.** [`dict-comp-key-value-order`] `{f(): g() for _ in it}` emits `__result.insert_or_assign(f(), g())` -- C++ leaves the two argument evaluations unsequenced, so `g()` may run before `f()`, whereas CPython's bytecode evaluates the key expression before the value. Pure/side-effect-free key/value (the overwhelming common case) are unaffected; only a key and value with a mutual ordering dependence (e.g. both mutate a shared counter) diverge. The owned-value-move path already sequences the key into a local before the value move (`{ auto __k = key; insert_or_assign(std::move(__k), std::move(value)); }`), so it is key-before-value correct; only the non-owned/non-moving path stays unsequenced. **Fix shape:** sequence the key into a local for the non-owned path too (or whenever either side may have side effects). Pre-existing; surfaced by /tpy-review (cpython-parity) of the dict comprehension owned-element move. Same class as `subexpression-right-to-left-eval` and postponed with it (2026-09-16).
- **[MED small] Annotated assignment to an attribute (`self.vals: list[int32] = [5]` in `__init__`) is rejected with `error: Invalid assignment target`.** CPython accepts annotated attribute targets (PEP 526); this is the idiomatic way to declare-and-init instance fields in `__init__`, so plain Python sources hit it immediately. The unannotated form (`self.vals = [5]`) plus a class-level annotation works, so the workaround is trivial, but the diagnostic does not say that. **Fix shape:** either accept the annotated form (treat the annotation as the field declaration, mirroring the class-level path) or reject with a targeted message pointing at the class-level-annotation convention. Surfaced writing repros for audit item #5. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] The "copies X into owned storage" warning renders unresolved internal type names for list-literal locals.** When the copied variable is an unannotated list literal, the warning prints the pre-resolution placeholder -- `copies PendingList[IntLiteral(1), 3]#1 into owned storage` -- because the coercion-path warning fires during body analysis, before container-literal resolution picks the final `list[T]`/`Array[T, N]` type. Cosmetic only, but the leaked `PendingList`/`IntLiteral`/`#N` internals are baked into two `auto_move` test snapshots (`borrowed_by_generator`, `value_result_keeps_move`-adjacent shapes), which will regenerate when this is fixed. **Fix shape:** defer the warning's type rendering (store the literal id, render at diagnostic-flush after resolution) or print the variable name instead of the type for pending literals. Surfaced adding the auto-move borrow-gate tests. The field-write spelling leaks the same name (`copies PendingList[IntLiteral(1), 2]#75 into field; use copy()`, 45 cells of the reference-sink sweep 2026-09-22, whose table normalises the `#N` counter because it changes with the other cells sharing the compilation).
- **[MED small] A full-Optional match capture read after narrowing inside a GENERATOR/async frame does not deref: C++ build error.** `def gen(v: int32 | None) -> Iterator[int32]: match v: case x: yield 1; ... else: yield x` (suspending match; `x` is a `std::optional<int>` frame field; the `yield x` sits under an `if x is None: ... else:` narrowing) emits `return x;` without the `*` deref -- `could not convert std::optional<int> to std::expected<int, StopIteration>`. The sync sibling derefs correctly through the same narrowing, so the gap is the resumable frame-field read path not consulting the Optional narrowing facts for value-repr fields bound by match captures. Loud (toolchain-caught), not silent. Surfaced verifying the binds-full-optional capture semantics on the resumable sibling (audit cluster #3 fix).
- **[LOW small] An `as`-binding on an or-pattern arm that includes `None` is rejected on an Optional subject.** `case (None | 5) as v:` on `int32 | None` errors at `stmt.match`. Semantically unsettled, which is why it is the half left open: on the `None` alternative CPython binds `v = None`, which the inner-typed binding the tier draws cannot represent -- it needs the binds-full-optional treatment that plain captures got, or a clean sema rejection. Groups WITHOUT a `None` alternative (`case 1 | 2 as x:`) lower since 2026-09-14 (case `tests/cases/match/or_group_as_binding`). Filed while unifying the match guard lowering (audit cluster #4).
- **[MED small] (rejects valid code, loud) An `as`-binding on an or-pattern arm of a UNION-subject match is a hard compile error.** `case (Cat() | Dog()) as a:` on `Cat | Dog` errors `in function 'describe': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.match)`: `_union_arm_ok` declines the arm and `_lower_match_union` raises (`tpyc/thir/lower/match.py:2938`). The older symptom was a DROPPED binding -- usually an undeclared-identifier C++ error, but SILENT when the name was pre-declared by another arm or the branch-decl hoist, leaving a stale value where CPython binds the matched object -- and the emitter that dropped it is gone, so the shape is refused up front instead. Worth queueing: CPython accepts it and the type sema gives the binding is usable. The record and Optional tiers' `as`-name half closed on 2026-09-14; this one did NOT go with them because there the group's alternatives are the subject's own type, so sema's "the `as` binds the full subject" typing is correct, while on a union it is over-wide. That is the sema-side twin BUGS.md#or-pattern-as-binding-no-join, and it asks for the set to land as one unit: the lowering side alone is small (`_union_arm_ok`'s or-branch declines any bound arm; the binding path below already spells `from_case_var=False` for `member is None`, and `_emit_match_switch_union` already emits whole bindings), but the typing decision is not. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid code, loud) PER-ALTERNATIVE captures on a RECORD-subject or-pattern are a hard compile error.** `case Point(x=a, y=0) | Point(x=0, y=a):` on a concrete record subject errors `in function 'on_axis': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.match)`: sema binds the names fine, then `_record_arm_ok` declines the arm (a sub-pattern that is neither a wildcard nor a literal) and `_lower_match_record` raises. The name binds a DIFFERENT field per alternative, so the fix is the per-alternative block the union tier already builds for the same shape (`match.union_or_bind`), not one shared block. The `as`-NAME half of this entry closed on 2026-09-14 -- an or-group binds the whole subject, which is one thing however many alternatives there are (case `tests/cases/match/or_group_as_binding`). CPython accepts both spellings. Sibling of the union-subject entry in this group. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) An exhaustive or-pattern arm with field sub-captures on a UNION subject is rejected when the arm body does not terminate.** [`or-arm-subcapture-nonterminating`] `match a:` over `Cat | Dog` with the single arm `case Cat(tags=ts) | Dog(tags=ts): ts.append("x")` errors `in function 'f': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.match)`. Four one-token variations all lower: ending the arm with `return`; adding a `case _: pass` arm; dropping the sub-captures (`case Cat() | Dog(): pass`); or naming one member only (`case Cat(tags=ts):`, non-exhaustive). So the trigger is the conjunction -- an or-group covering the whole union, binding names, whose body falls out of the arm -- not or-patterns or sub-captures on their own, and `tests/cases/match/or_nested_union` carries the same shape with a `return` and passes. CPython accepts it. Distinct from the or-pattern-bindings group directly above: those reject the BINDINGS, this one binds them fine and rejects on the fall-through. Surfaced writing the or-pattern section of `tests/cases/match/match_capture_mutation_credited`, which carries the `case _: pass` workaround. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A capture name REUSED by a nested match whose subject is `T | None` is rejected at `stmt.match`.** [`nested-optional-capture-name-reuse`] `match h:` over a `Counter` param with `case q:`, containing `match g:` over `Counter | None` with `case None: pass` / `case q: q.n += 9`, errors `in function 'reseated_optional2': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.match)`. Binding the inner arm to a DIFFERENT name lowers and runs, and so does the same nested pair when both subjects are records, so the trigger is the name reuse across a record tier and an Optional tier -- one hoisted slot that the two binds want in different forms. CPython accepts it (`match` is not its own scope, so the inner bind just rebinds the local). Sibling of the or-pattern/hoist group; distinct from the generator narrowed-subject entry above, which needs a resumable frame. Pre-existing: identical on master. Reproducers `/tmp/agents/probe_optional_reseat2.py` (rejects) and `/tmp/agents/probe_opt_distinct.py` (same shape, distinct names, lowers). Surfaced by /tpy-review of the capture-attribution branch. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (uncompilable C++, toolchain-caught) A mutating METHOD CALL on a capture re-seated between `self.<field>` and a param credits only self, so the param keeps its const borrow.** [`multi-root-receiver-drops-param`] `def touch(self, other: Bag)` whose body matches `self.mine` and then `other`, binding `q` in both arms and calling `q.bump()`, emits `void touch(const Bag& other)` and then `q->bump()` against a `const Counter*` -- g++ reports `passing 'const Counter' as 'this' argument discards qualifiers`. The receiver's self-rooted loan sets `receiver_idx` on the call edge and the self-call deferral then suppresses the direct mark, so the receiver's OTHER roots get no attribution at all. A field WRITE through the same re-seated capture (`q.n += 4`) credits both and is covered by `tests/cases/match/match_capture_mutation_credited`'s `self_and_param_reseat` section; only the method-call receiver is affected, and only when one of its roots is self. Fixing it needs a way to say "the callee's self-mutation reaches caller param N", which `MutationCallEdge` cannot express today: `receiver_idx` names ONE caller param the receiver is, and a receiver with several roots needs a SET of them, so it is a design question, not a lowering arm. Reproducer `/tmp/agents/probe_selfmulti.py`; the single-root twin `/tmp/agents/probe_methodrecv.py` builds and runs. Surfaced writing the multi-root section for the capture-attribution branch. Needs `/tpy-add-feature` for the edge shape, then the fix.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A BARE capture arm on a `@dynamic`-protocol subject is rejected when the arm body does not terminate.** [`poly-bare-capture-nonterminating`] `def poke(p: Pet): match p: case seen: seen.bump()` errors `in function 'poke': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.match)`. The same arm ending in `return seen.bump()` lowers, and so does a class pattern (`case Dog() as seen: seen.bump()`) with the identical body -- so the trigger is the irrefutable capture arm falling out of the match, not the capture or the poly tier alone. Very likely the same fall-through gap as the union entry directly above; check them together. CPython accepts it. Surfaced writing the poly section of `tests/cases/match/match_capture_mutation_credited`, which uses the class-pattern spelling instead. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud) A module-level `match` on a RECORD subject is not lowered.** [`module-level-record-match`] `top = C(0)` followed by `match top: case C(): print("c")` errors `at module level: this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.match)`; the identical statement inside a function lowers and runs, and a module-level match on a SCALAR subject (`match x: case 1: ... case _: ...`) lowers too, so it is the record tier at module scope specifically, not module-level `match` as such. A capture in the arm is not required to trigger it. Module-level statements are their own body with their own variable model (pointer slots), which is the likely cause. Valid Python, and the natural spelling for a small script. Surfaced writing the module-level-position section of `tests/cases/match/match_capture_mutation_credited`, which falls back to a local subject inside a function. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid code) Sema types an `as` over an or-group as the FULL subject and requires or-pattern alternatives to bind IDENTICAL types, so an `as` on a multi-class or-pattern of a union subject cannot be written at all.** [`or-pattern-as-binding-no-join`] Two halves of one rule. First, `case (Dog() | Cat()) as y:` on `Dog | Cat | Bird` binds `y` as `Bird | Cat | Dog` rather than `Dog | Cat` -- every non-class `as` inner falls to `bindings[name] = subject_type` in `tpyc/sema/match.py`, so `y.n` is rejected even when every alternative has the field. Second, `_analyze_or_pattern` raises `variable 'y' has type 'Dog' in first alternative but 'Cat' in another` whenever alternatives disagree, so the per-alternative spelling `case (Dog() as y) | (Cat() as y):` and the nested `case ((Dog() | Cat()) as y) | (Bird() as y):` (pinned as-is by `tests/cases/match/error_or_nested_as_binds_wide`) are refused outright. CPython binds `y` to the matched object in every one of these. TPy has a well-formed type for it: the JOIN of the alternatives' binding types (a union, the subject's own type in the widest case), which is what the borrow-form variant already carries. Fix shape: an `as` over an or-group binds the union of its alternatives' resolved types, and `_analyze_or_pattern` joins per-name types across alternatives instead of demanding equality (the name-set check stays strict). Sema-side twin of the dropped-emit trio directly above (Optional / union / record); land them as ONE unit, since fixing the typing alone flips those loud C++ errors into silent stale-value reads for pre-declared names. The June audit recorded the typing half with this fix direction and it never reached this file. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid code) `case A() | None:` on a nullable union subject is rejected, though `case None:` alone dispatches on the same variant index the or-group would need.** [`or-pattern-none-alt-union`] `match v:` over `A | B | None` with `case A() | None:` errors `unsupported alternative in an or-pattern over a union subject; every alternative must name a union member class -- give 'None' or a literal its own 'case' arm` from `_check_union_or_alternatives` in `tpyc/sema/match.py:1562` (pinned as-is by `tests/cases/match/error_or_union_none_alt`). The rejection's stated reason -- that `None` names no member class so there is no label to emit -- is wrong for `None`: both union tiers already emit a `None` arm as a numeric `case <idx>:` off `_union_member_index(members, NoneType())` (`tpyc/thir/lower/match.py:3026` and `:3139`, scanning the member order `_union_index_members` builds at `:201`), so stacking that label under the class labels of the same group is the whole fix for the None alternative, with the as-binding (BUGS.md#or-pattern-as-binding-no-join) being the only interaction to think about. A LITERAL alternative on a union carrying a value member (`case A() | 5:` on `A | int32`) is the genuinely unimplemented half: it needs the value member's index plus an `==` on the payload, i.e. the guarded tier's shape. Split the diagnostic accordingly -- accept `None`, and report a literal as not-yet-implemented rather than as a rule. CPython matches both. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid code, loud) A guarded-union arm with BOTH a field condition and a field capture the guard reads is a hard compile error.** `case Dog(legs=4, name=n) if n == "rex":` on `Dog | Cat` errors `in function 'describe': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.match)`: the union tier adds the pattern's captures to `lc.forbidden_reads` while lowering the guard whenever the arm carries field conditions (`tpyc/thir/lower/match.py:3193`), and the guard's read of `n` then raises at `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py:4958`. Without a field condition the guard may read the capture. The older symptom was ill-formed C++ -- the composed `if (__case_1.legs == 4 && (n == "rex"))` preceded the `auto& n = __case_1.name;` declaration -- so it was loud either way; it is now caught in the front end instead of by the toolchain. CPython evaluates the guard after all pattern bindings, so the correct emit is bindings-then-nested-guard (`if (conds) { bindings; if (guard) ... }`), which is also the shape the record tier already uses. Worth queueing -- a field literal plus a named capture in one pattern is an everyday `match`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED, deferred: MIR] Reading / narrowing the UNION ELEMENT of a borrow-form tuple fails the C++ build.** `def f(pair: tuple[Dog | Cat, int32]): e = pair[0]; if isinstance(e, Dog): return e.bark` -- binding the union element to a local emits `std::variant<Cat*, Dog*> e = ::tpy::to_ptr_variant(std::get<0>(pair))`, wrong twice: in a borrow-form tuple the element is ALREADY a (const) pointer variant `variant<const Cat*, const Dog*>`, so `to_ptr_variant` (which expects a storage variant) is the wrong helper, and the local `e` is typed with mutable pointees that don't match the const source. The tuple-element read reuses the union-FIELD read path (storage -> pointer lift) instead of recognizing the borrow-tuple element is pointer-form already. No TPy diagnostic; C++ build error only. The boundary conversion (passing a `tuple[A|B,...]`, reading non-union elements, param->param passthrough) now works -- only extracting/narrowing the union element itself is broken. **Fix shape:** a union element read from a borrow-form tuple is already pointer-form -- bind the local to the element's const pointer-variant directly (no `to_ptr_variant` lift), and type the local to match (const pointees). Distinct mechanism from the boundary borrow-conversion (subscript read + `ptr_variant_locals` tracking + narrowing). Surfaced by /tpy-fix-bug of the union-tuple-element boundary fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED, deferred: MIR] The storage / local / field directions of a union tuple element are not wired (only the param/return/passthrough boundary works).** `TupleType._element_is_pointer_repr` (`tpyc/typesys.py`) deliberately EXCLUDES `UnionType`, so `has_pointer_repr_element()` is False for a union-only / union+value tuple -- the storage<->borrow wrap sites (`tuple_to_storage` / `tuple_to_pointer`) never fire for it, and a union-element tuple bound to a local from a storage source, stored in a record field / container, or moved as `Own[tuple[...]]` is not converted between the value-variant storage form and the pointer-variant borrow form. The boundary case works through a different path (`UnionType.to_cpp_return` for the param/return signature + `borrow_value_elem` for the rvalue call-arg, neither gated on `has_pointer_repr_element`). Also unwired: `readonly[tuple[A|B,...]]` params and nullable union elements (`tuple[A|B|None,...]`) beyond the boundary. No TPy diagnostic; C++ build error (or silent miss) only. **Fix shape:** the missing half is the gate -- extend `_element_is_pointer_repr` (and the per-element tuple storage/borrow converters in `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/format.hpp`) to route union elements through `to_ptr_variant`/`to_const_ptr_variant`/`to_value_variant`, with a const-aware (copy, not move) borrow->storage path since a union tuple element is always a const borrow. Related to the union-element extraction entry above and the recursive-wrapper-element exclusion below. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the union-tuple-element boundary fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug` (or `/tpy-add-feature`).
- **[LOW] An inherited async construct is rejected when the coro-struct owner's type args are not concretely bound (not yet supported).** Two triggers, same root cause: (a) a MULTI-LEVEL chain -- `class C(B[int32])` where `B[U](A[U])` and `A[T]` defines `async def fetch(self) -> T`; (b) a GENERIC subclass of a generic base instantiated concretely -- `class Child[U](Box[U])` then `Child[int32](...)`. In both, `await c.fetch()` (or inherited `async with` / `async for`) is rejected with a clear diagnostic ("multi-level generic inheritance chain is not yet supported") rather than miscompiled. Root cause: `RecordInfo.mro_ancestors` (`compute_mro_ancestors`, `tpyc/typesys.py`) records each base with the *defining* class's own type params, not the receiver's instantiation -- `C.mro_ancestors` holds `A[U]`, and `Child.mro_ancestors` holds `Box[U]` (U unbound) -- so the coro-struct owner carries an unbound `TypeParamRef`, which codegen cannot spell. Async-only: coro-struct naming is the one path that reads ancestor type args off `mro_ancestors` directly; sync method resolution / field access substitute via the *receiver's* own `type_args` and are unaffected (a sync inherited method on `Child[U](Box[U])` instantiated concretely works correctly). The direct single-level case (`IntBox(Box[int32])` -- a *non-generic* subclass) also works. **Fix shape:** thread the receiver's instantiation args (and each intermediate level's args) into the `mro_ancestors` binding so ancestor type params resolve to concrete args, then drop the codegen guard in `gen_async.py::_sub_struct_qualname`. Surfaced by /tpy-fix-bug of the single-level generic-base inherited-async fix.
- **[LOW small] `with` / `async with` / `async for` walk the MRO for their dunders, but subscript (`__getitem__` / `__setitem__`) lookup does not.** A subclass that inherits `__getitem__` / `__setitem__` from a base (without overriding) silently fails the subscript operator -- the slice-lookup sites in `tpyc/sema/expressions.py` (`record.methods.get("__getitem__")` / `"__setitem__"`, ~lines 3479/3520) are own-only, unlike the MRO-aware `get_method_overloads_with_parents` now used for the with/async-with/async-for manager/iterator dunders. Pre-existing (present on master); same inherited-dunder gap, different operator. **Fix shape:** route the subscript dunder lookups through `get_method_overloads_with_parents` too. Surfaced by /tpy-review (architecture-fit) of the inherited-async fix.
- **[LOW small] A generic record's type-parameter bound is not enforced at a bare annotation that does not construct.** `x: Box[Rc[int32]]` where `class Box[T: Send]` is accepted with no error even though `Rc[int32]` violates the `T: Send` bound -- `tpyc/sema/type_ops.py::validate_record_type_args` (reached from variable-annotation validation) checks arity / kind / forward-refs but never consults `record_info.type_param_bounds` via `satisfies_bound`. Construction sites DO enforce it (`_analyze_record_constructor` in `calls.py`, and the generic-factory call path), so a record obtainable only via a constructor/factory (e.g. `Channel` via `channel[T: Send]()`) is covered in practice; the gap is bare annotations with no construction. Affects every bounded generic record, not just Send/Sync markers (protocol/subtype bounds too); no diagnostic. Surfaced designing `Channel[T]` Send enforcement (Phase 4); applies directly to the channel's `Sender`/`Receiver`/`_ChanState` records (which now carry the `T: Send` bound) -- e.g. `rx: Receiver[SharedCache]` as a bare annotation is not rejected, only `channel[SharedCache](...)` at construction is. **Fix shape:** have `validate_record_type_args` validate substituted type args against the record's `type_param_bounds` via `satisfies_bound`, mirroring the construction-site check. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] The `Iterable[Own[T]]` copy-warning suppression is position-agnostic, silently dropping a legitimate warning for multi-arg containers.** The conformance check (`tpyc/sema/compatibility.py`, `actual_provides_own`) suppresses the "copies T elements; use copy_iter()" warning whenever the actual type carries `Own` in ANY type-arg slot. For an actual whose `Own` sits on a non-iterated arg -- e.g. `dict[K, Own[V]]` passed where `Iterable[Own[K]]` is expected (a dict iterates its keys `K`) -- the copy warning for reference-typed `K` is suppressed even though `K` is not owned. Not unsound (the copy still materializes correctly); a missed diagnostic only. Mirrors the pre-existing position-agnosticism of the expected-side strip. **Fix shape:** make the suppression position-aware -- fire only when the actual's `Own`-position signature aligns with the expected's iterated-element slot, not any slot. Surfaced by /tpy-review (safety-model) of the Own/Iterable symmetric-strip fix.
- **[MED small] An overloaded *method* rejects a `Protocol | Concrete` union implementation param that the same shape on a *free function* accepts.** `class Agg: @overload def add(self, xs: Iterable[Own[int32]]) -> int32 / @overload def add(self, xs: int32) -> int32 / def add(self, xs: Iterable[Own[int32]] | int32) -> int32` errors at the impl signature with `Cannot mix protocol types ('Iterable[Own[int32]]') with concrete types in a union` (`tpyc/sema/type_ops.py:405-414`), but the byte-identical free function (`def total(xs: Iterable[Own[int32]] | int32)`) compiles and runs (exercised by `tests/cases/iterators/own_iter_overloaded_iterable`). The union here is an overload-*dispatch* union (covers the two stubs, narrowed by `isinstance` in the impl body), never materialized as a value-variant, so the protocol+concrete-union restriction should not apply -- the free-function overload path exempts it, the method path does not. Net effect: the entire overloaded-protocol-stub pattern is unavailable on methods (compounds the separate "overloaded generic methods are not supported" gap; see TODO method-parity item). Rejection of valid code; clear diagnostic, no miscompile. **Fix shape:** exempt overload-implementation param types from the protocol+concrete-union check on the method path, mirroring the free-function path. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A `readonly[list[T]]` (and likely other `readonly[container]`) parameter of an `async def` / generator fails the C++ build.** `async def peek(items: readonly[list[Box]]) -> int32: await asyncio.sleep(0); return items[0].n` -> g++ `no matching function for call to 'std::optional<__coro_peek>::emplace(std::array<Box, 1>&)'` at a spurious `__sub_0.emplace((*items))`. The plain (non-`readonly`) `list[Box]` param compiles and runs; only the `readonly[...]` wrap breaks it. The readonly container param is lowered to a borrow (`(*items)`) and the resumable-frame arg handling mis-emplaces it. No TPy diagnostic; C++ build error only. Workaround: drop `readonly` on the container param. Pre-existing and independent of the borrow-alias-across-suspension fix (the same program without any local alias fails identically). The sibling `readonly[tuple[Record,...]]` coro-param bug is fixed (root: readonly was being stripped from a borrow-form tuple param); the `list` case is a distinct mechanism -- the borrow `(*items)` mis-emplace, not a field-type spelling -- so it remains. Surfaced exercising the const-alias path of the tuple-unpack-across-await fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] The scalar `Own[T]` non-last-use arg check uses `is_type_nocopy`, which misses `__del__` records (copy is C++-deleted but the type isn't `@nocopy`-declared).** `_check_own_param_arg` (`tpyc/sema/calls.py`) gates its clean use-after-move error on `_is_nocopy_type` -> `is_type_nocopy`; a record with a `__del__` (deleted copy ctor) but no `@nocopy` decorator slips through to the warn+auto-copy path, which then emits a copy g++ rejects. The owned-*tuple* arg check added alongside (same file) uses the correct superset `is_type_non_copyable` ("will C++ reject the copy"), so the two diverge on `__del__` types. Pre-existing scalar gap, exposed by the predicate comparison during /tpy-review of the owned-tuple-arg fix. **Fix shape:** switch the scalar `_check_own_param_arg` nocopy gate to `is_type_non_copyable` (align with the tuple path). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] An owned value-variant union local (`Own[A | B]`) moved onward into an `Own[A | B]` param fails the C++ build: the move emits `std::move` on the borrow `variant<A*, B*>` form, which can't bind to the value-variant `variant<A, B>&&` param.** Reproducer: `def make() -> Own[A | B]: return A(1)` then `v = make(); w = consume(v)` where `consume(v: Own[A | B]) -> Own[A | B]`. g++: `invalid initialization of reference of type 'std::variant<A, B>&&' from ... 'std::variant<A*, B*>'`. The owned union local is materialized in borrow (pointer-variant) form, but transferring ownership into an `Own[union]` sink needs the value-variant storage form -- the storage-form<->borrow-form conversion (the `to_ptr_variant` / value-variant family, sibling of the value-variant-union-return entry below) is not applied on the move. Affects BOTH single-assign (`v = make()`) and whole-tuple unpack (`v, _ = pair()`): the rvalue movability path marks `Own[A | B]` movable in both, then the move hits the form mismatch. The optional analog (`Own[P | None]`, pointer-repr) compiles -- only the value-variant union errors. Toolchain-caught, not silent; no TPy diagnostic. Pre-existing -- independent of the owned-tuple-unpack feature, which only made unpack reach the same movable-rvalue path single-assign already used. Surfaced by /tpy-review (safety-model) of owned-tuple-unpack, confirmed pre-existing via /tpy-fix-bug reproduce (single-assign fails identically). **Fix shape:** materialize the value-variant form when moving an owned pointer-variant-union local into an `Own[union]` sink (mirror the storage-form conversion the field/container-init path uses). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (silent CPython divergence) An argument-position await hoists the awaited call AHEAD of its sibling arguments, and a narrowed-field sibling keeps its pre-suspension elision.** `use(self.opt.v, await f())`: CPython evaluates `self.opt.v` before running `f()`; the suspension lifter rewrites to `__await_lift_N = await f(); use(self.opt.v, __await_lift_N)`, so the sibling read executes post-resume (evaluation-order divergence) -- and since sema analyzed it in source order (before the await's fact kill), a narrowed-field elision on it is baked in and stale at the post-resume execution point. Not reachable through the yield / frame-write unwrap sinks (statement-level sources only). Fix shape: hoist pre-await sibling operands into temps alongside the await lift, restoring CPython evaluation order and aligning sema's analysis order with execution order. Surfaced by the suspension-fact-kill readiness retrospective (second-opinion pass).
- **[LOW] `await asyncio.sleep(0)` does not yield to other scheduled tasks before re-waking the awaiter.** A zero-second sleep builds a `SleepFuture` timer that resolves immediately rather than performing a cooperative yield, so `create_task(f()); await asyncio.sleep(0)` reads the awaiter's view of any state `f()` mutates as still-stale (`f()` has not run yet), whereas CPython runs the spawned task up to its first suspension during the `sleep(0)`. Concretely `ran` stays `False` under TPy where CPython sees `True`. No diagnostic; silent scheduling divergence. Workaround: use a non-zero sleep (`sleep(0.01)`), or join the task explicitly (`await gather(...)`). Surfaced choosing the regression shape for the async-global-mutation fix.
- **[MED small] A structural-protocol method whose name is a C++ keyword (`double`, `new`, `delete`, `operator`, ...) emits an unmangled name in the generated concept, breaking the C++ build.** The struct method is correctly mangled (`int32_t double_() const;`) but the concept constraint emits the raw Python name: `concept Doubler = requires(T& t) { { t.double() } -> std::convertible_to<int32_t>; };` -> g++ `error: expected unqualified-id before 'double'`, and the bounded generic call (`run<N>(...)`) then fails its constraint. The concept-constraint emitter does not apply the C++-keyword mangling the struct-method emitter already applies; the two name renderings must agree. Reachable whenever a structural protocol used as a generic bound declares a method named after a C++ keyword. No TPy-level diagnostic -- the user sees only C++ errors. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug` (mirror the struct-method keyword mangle at the concept-constraint emit site). Surfaced by /tpy-fuzzy-test (protocols) during 0.3.0 smoke testing.
- **[LOW] Resumable match-arm binding has no frame-storage redirect for forwarded proto-param aliases (latent, unreachable today).** Forwarded proto-param aliases (`xs = it`, see the proto-param-alias feature) route name READS through `lc.forwarded_map` (`tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py:4901`) to the backing param. The match-arm field-write path does not: `_lower_field_subpatterns` (`tpyc/thir/lower/match.py:1650`) gates the pointer-hoist capture on `inner.name not in lc.frame_local_types`, and a comment at the site (`:1644`) records that `frame_local_types` is a STRICT SUBSET of what counts as a frame field -- it misses params, `__self` and forwarded proto-param aliases -- so a forwarded local used as a match-capture *target* would emit a write to a non-existent field. Unreachable today, doubly: the resumable match gate rejects every record-field capture before this runs, and a forwarded local is a static-protocol-typed alias, which cannot be a match-capture target anyway. Guarded by that comment. Fix when (if) it becomes reachable: replace the `frame_local_types` conjunct with a real frame-field membership test, and reject writes to a forwarded alias, which has no storage of its own. Surfaced by /tpy-review (safety-model) of the proto-param-alias feature.
- **[MED small] `print()` of a `Ptr[T]` field emits the raw pointer value (`0` for null) instead of `None` / a Python-style repr.** `n.nxt = None; print(n.nxt)` outputs `0` rather than `None`; a non-null `Ptr[T]` would print a nondeterministic address. Inconsistent with `Optional[T]` fields, which print `None` correctly. `x is None` narrowing on the Ptr is unaffected (only the print/`__str__`/`__repr__` representation is wrong). Incorrect output, no diagnostic. Fix: route `Ptr[T]` through the Optional-style printer (null -> `None`; non-null -> the pointee's repr, or at least a stable non-address form). Surfaced by /tpy-fuzzy-test (classes-ownership) during 0.3.0 smoke testing.
- **[LOW small]** The Python-clamp logic in `varargs<T>::slice` (`runtime/cpp/include/tpy/varargs.hpp`, both the value and non-value specializations) does the negative-index adjustment `i += size_` / `j += size_` in `int32_t`; a near-`INT32_MIN` bound combined with a large `size_` overflows (signed UB). Impractical (a vararg never holds INT32_MAX elements) and pre-existing in spirit -- it mirrors the non-value `slice` and the `BasicSlice` clamp; the value-type `slice` added with the `varargs[T]` body-view type copy-pasted the same pattern. Fix: widen to `std::ptrdiff_t` before the adjustment (as the generic `list_slice` in `container_ops.hpp` already does). Surfaced by /tpy-review (runtime-cpp) of the varargs body-view type.
- **[MED small, deferred: MIR]** A non-value value coerced into a recursive-union-wrapper *tuple element of a local* is refused under an internal code-generation name (`return.wrapper_ref_tuple_source`) instead of the clean dangle diagnostic. `def f(n: int32) -> tuple[Tree[int32], int32]: pair = (n, 0); return pair` (or `pair: tuple[Tree[int32], int32] = (n, 0)`) used to emit a `std::tuple<int,int>` -> `std::tuple<Tree<int32_t>&, int>` coercion that g++ rejected; it now stops at the located internal reject (re-measured 2026-09-29). Loud, NOT a silent dangle. The literal form `return (n, 0)` is correctly rejected with the clean wrapper-element dangle diagnostic; only the tuple-*local* form hits the internal reject. Same return-time-tuple-coercion family as the wrapper-as-tuple-element storage/borrow conversion gaps. This is one symptom of the literal/deferred-path divergence in the fresh-member fact derivation: the literal path's per-element loop catches a value coerced into a wrapper element (via the pre-coercion source type), the name-based deferred flag does not -- the eventual single-dataflow-fact fix should unify both rather than patch the coerce case in isolation. Surfaced building repros during /tpy-fix-bug of the bare-name wrapper-tuple-dangle.
- **[LOW small] A *durable* recursive-union-wrapper member of a bound-local tuple still copies (or fails to build) instead of sharing.** The tuple borrow-pointer unification deliberately kept recursive-union wrappers on their nominal `X&` borrow form (excluded from `_element_is_pointer_repr`), so `def f(t: Tree[int32]) -> tuple[Tree[int32], int32]: pair = (t, 0); return pair` remains the wrapper analogue of the (now-fixed) durable non-wrapper case: the bound local does not alias the wrapper member. The *fresh* wrapper member IS rejected (the fresh check and `_tuple_elem_still_borrow` are wrapper-aware); closing the durable sibling means extending the `T*` borrow form (and its construct/access/convert paths) to wrapper elements. Surfaced merging the wrapper-fresh-dangle fix over the durable-member rejection; scoped out of the unification branch.
- **[LOW small] Mutating through a tuple local that aliases an EXPLICITLY-readonly param's element fails the C++ build with no TPy diagnostic.** `def f(items: readonly[list[tuple[int32, Box]]]): t = items[0]; t[1].val = 99` -- the aliasing binding is `auto&&` over const storage, and the write trips a C++ const error ("assignment of member ... in read-only object") instead of the sema "cannot mutate readonly" rejection the direct form gets. The const-INFERRED variant of this entry was fixed by the storage-provenance work (tuple aliases now register element borrows; write-through marks the source param mutated, so it stays non-const -- `tests/cases/tuple/tuple_storage_local_alias`); the residual is only the explicit `readonly[...]` annotation, where the right outcome is a sema rejection of the write through the alias. Toolchain-caught, not silent. Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/tuple-soundness/probes/readonly_alias_mut.py`. Surfaced probing the /tpy-review borrow-local reassignment fix; narrowed by the storage-provenance fixes.
- **[LOW small, deferred: MIR] An RVALUE generic tuple element (call result of type `T` in a tuple literal with a `val_or_ptr_t<T>` slot) is not routed through the borrow helpers.** `(i, fn(x))` under a generic `tuple[int32, T]` target falls to the plain value path; at a non-value instantiation the `T` value cannot convert to the `T*` slot (C++ error, no TPy diagnostic). Lvalue generic elements go through `to_val_or_ptr` and work. Same dangling-rvalue family as the concrete rvalue-into-borrow-slot entry below; the concrete case routes through `tuple_value_to_borrow`, the generic case needs the same temp-materializing treatment. Filed during the val_or_ptr generic-tuple work.
- **[LOW small] A reassigned tuple local that mixes an owning-call binding with a storage alias inside a GENERATOR/ASYNC body is not yet handled.** [`frame-tuple-reassigned-owning-alias`] The sync owning/alias mix (`if c: t = make_pair() else: t = h.pair`, straight-line rebind, branch-mixed) is fixed on `tuple-rvalue-slot`: the local stays borrow form (`std::tuple<..., T*>`), an owning-call RHS materializes into a hoisted `std::optional<std::tuple<..., T>>` slot lifted via `tuple_to_pointer`, the owning fact is flow-correct (FlowFacts snapshot + UNION merge), and `_reject_owning_alias_rebind` is deleted. A *non-reassigned* owning tuple local in a resumable body is also fixed (storage `tpy::frame_slot<std::tuple<..., T>>` field). The residual is the REASSIGNED owning+alias mix in a resumable body: it needs BOTH a `frame_slot<std::tuple<..., T>>` slot field (for the owning RHS) AND a borrow `std::tuple<..., T*>` field (for the alias), whereas a frame local currently gets one field. The ELEMENT-alias shape above is no longer silent or toolchain-caught: the per-element ownership join (`owning_generator_tuple_locals`) sees one init hand the element over and another only borrow it, and rejects at the second binding ("bound both to a tuple holding a fresh object and to one borrowing an existing object ... Bind the two forms to separate names"; `tests/cases/tuple/error_frame_tuple_call_borrow_conflict`). The WHOLE-tuple alias variant is not covered by that: `t = make_pair(); u = t; t = make_pair()` in a generator still raw-rejects at `u = t` with `in function 'gen': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (res.btuple_source)` -- an internal lowering tag in a user-facing message, with no hint at the shape or the fix (that message shape is the general `BUGS.md#reject-tag-reaches-the-user`). Verified 2026-09-10. A REASSIGNED all-owning local (`t = make_pair(); yield ...; t = make_pair()`) is fixed by that same join -- each init emplaces fresh storage into the one slot. Surfaced implementing the owning/alias-mix umbrella; the broad case is resolved, this resumable-reassigned sub-case is scoped out.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, toolchain-caught) Unpacking an OWNING tuple frame local fails the C++ build -- the unpack binds the frame-slot wrapper instead of the tuple.** [`frame-tuple-unpack-slot`] `a, b = t` on a generator/async local whose tuple is owned by the frame (`t = (A(1), A(2))`, or `t = make_pair()` at `Own[tuple[A, A]]`) emits `auto& __tup_1 = t;` -- `t` is the `tpy::frame_slot<std::tuple<A, A>>` FIELD, not the tuple -- and the following `std::get<0>(__tup_1)` fails with `no matching function for call to 'get<0>(tpy::frame_slot<std::tuple<...> >&)'`. Every other read of the same local in the same body dereferences correctly: a `yield t[0].v` one line down spells `std::get<0>((*t))`, so the unpack path is the only reader that misses the `frame_slot` deref. Toolchain-caught, not silent. Pre-existing for the non-reassigned owning form (a literal or a single owning call); newly REACHABLE for the reassigned owning-call form, which used to stop at the `res.btuple_source` reject before the per-element ownership verdict admitted it. Reproducers: the two shapes above, each `a, b = t` between the init and a `yield t[0].v`, verified 2026-09-10. Fix shape: route the unpack's tuple binding through the same frame-slot deref every other read uses, rather than binding the field by reference. Same owning-frame-slot family as the tuple paragraph of BUGS.md#resumable-alias-identity. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, toolchain-caught) A `readonly` reference element of an OWNING tuple frame local renders `val_or_ref<const T>` in the slot, so every member access on it fails the C++ build.** [`frame-tuple-readonly-elem`] `t: tuple[readonly[A], int32]` bound in a generator to either an owning call (`Own[tuple[readonly[A], int32]]`) or a tuple literal takes the owning `frame_slot<std::tuple<tpy::val_or_ref<const A>, int>>` field, and `t[0].v` emits `std::get<0>((*t)).v`, which g++ rejects: `'tpy::val_or_ref<const A>' has no member named 'v'`. The element access is missing the `unwrap_ref` the borrow-form tuple paths apply; the owning slot should not be spelling a `val_or_ref` element at all, since it owns the storage. Both init forms fail identically, in the same body. Toolchain-caught, not silent; pre-existing (the readonly element never took a different path). Reproducer: `def make_ro() -> Own[tuple[readonly[A], int32]]: return (A(7), 3)` then `def gen(): t = make_ro(); yield t[0].v`, and the literal twin `t2: tuple[readonly[A], int32] = (A(1), 2)`; verified 2026-09-10. Fix shape: drop the `val_or_ref` wrapper from an OWNED element's storage spelling (readonly is a const on the owned `A`, not a borrow), rather than adding an unwrap at each access. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A multi-source borrow-form tuple local with differing source const-ness, written through, fails the C++ build (independent of `Optional`).** `def alias2(h: Holder, h2: Holder): t: tuple[int32, Box] = h.pair; t = h2.pair; t[1].val = 99` -- the write-through marks only `h2` mutated (the `t->h.pair` binding is overwritten before any write), so `h` stays const; `_compute_borrow_tuple_const`'s OR-over-all-sources then marks the local const, emitting `std::tuple<int32, const Box*> t` and g++ rejects the write (`passing 'const ...' as 'this' discards qualifiers`) through the live `h2` alias. Toolchain-caught, not silent. The const verdict should track per-reaching-binding (which source is live at the write), not OR across all sources. Surfaced implementing the Optional-of-borrow-tuple shape (the const inference is shared); reproduces on the bare `tuple[...]` form with no `Optional`. (Same const family: `gen_async.py` save/restores `borrow_form_tuple_locals` / `optional_borrow_tuple_locals` around a nested coro body but NOT the matching `const_*` sets, so an outer sync function's const-element election for a (nullable) borrow tuple local is trashed if a nested `async def` precedes those locals in source order -- edge-gated, no current reproducer.) (The spurious *copy warning* and the *type-record split* that used to accompany the `Own`-annotated form of this shape were fixed by the reassigned per-element-`Own` collapse unification; the `Own`-annotated decl now errors at the redundant-`Own` rejection before reaching this const build error, so only the bare-`tuple[...]` form below remains a live const-OR reproducer.)
- **[MED small] A single-element unannotated list literal of a BORROWED SCALAR infers a fixed `Array` of C++ references and fails the C++ build.** `xs = [borrow(b)]` (a call returning a borrow of a reference type) emits `std::array<Box&, 1>`, which is ill-formed -- `std::array` cannot hold references. An explicit `list[...]` annotation works around it. Same root as the tuple-element half, which IS fixed: an inferred container element type now takes the owned storage form, so a tuple element no longer keeps the `Ref`/`Own` markers that rendered as `std::tuple<..., T&>`. The scalar element type is not put through that transform, so a bare `Ref[T]` element survives and renders `T&`. Toolchain-caught, not silent. Fix shape: strip the borrow marker from an inferred container element type generally, not only inside a tuple. Repro `/tmp/agents/mixstep1/residual.py` (`singleton_array`). Surfaced building tests for the tuple-member copy warning. The everyday face is a record PARAMETER as the element: `def g(p: P) -> None: ps = [p]; print(ps[0].n)` emits `std::array<P&, 1> ps = {p};` and g++ fails with *forming pointer to reference type*; `[p, p]` emits `std::array<P&, 2>` the same way (probe `/tmp/agents/ge/file/k_arr.py`, 2026-09-28). The `for x in [a, b]` loop source over parameters strips the reference in a plain function (`BUGS.md#frame-for-literal-of-params-reference-array` is its frame twin), so the local-binding sink is the one left. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A generic `ValueType` class with an `Array[T, N]` field over its OWN int type param `N` is rejected as a non-value field.** `class Buf[N: int](ValueType): _d: Array[int32, N]` errors `ValueType class 'Buf': field '_d' has non-value type 'Array[int32, N]'`, even though `std::array<int32_t, N>` is a perfectly valid value-type member (the same field with a concrete size, `Array[int32, 3]`, is accepted). The value-type field validator does not recognize `Array[value, N]` as a value type when the size `N` is an unresolved (type-param) extent -- it should treat `Array[T, N]` as a value type whenever the element `T` is, independent of whether `N` is concrete. Blocks the natural fixed-capacity generic-buffer pattern (a generic `ValueType` wrapping a compile-time-sized array). Loud reject-valid, not a miscompile. Reproducer: `class Buf[N: int](ValueType): _d: Array[int32, N]`. Surfaced during `/tpy-fix-bug` of the generic-base inherited-ctor fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A fresh tuple LITERAL as a dict-literal VALUE with a reference member is rejected with a spurious `Own[...]` type mismatch.** `d: dict[int32, tuple[int32, P]] = {0: (1, c)}` -> `error: Type mismatch in variable 'd': expected tuple[int32, P], got tuple[int32, Own[P]]`. The tuple-literal value's reference member is analyzed as `Own[P]` (owned storage form) but the dict-value coercion does not collapse the per-element `Own` to match the annotated `tuple[int32, P]` slot (the list-literal element path does collapse it -- `[(1, c)]` builds). Pre-existing; loud, not silent. Also note the raised error aborts the module analysis, masking any earlier warnings. Workaround: build the dict with `d[0] = (1, c)` assignment, or a whole-tuple lvalue value. Sibling of the storage-vs-borrow tuple-member family. Surfaced building tests for the fresh-tuple-literal-member copy warning. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (silent hidden copy; one wrong remedy) A returned owned element that is dead after the return COPIES instead of moving.** [`returned-owned-element-copies-not-moves`] `t = mk(); return t[1]` into `Own[C]` renders `return C(std::get<1>(t));`, a copy with no diagnostic, although `t` dies at the return (probe `/tmp/agents/rv1cg/sret2.py`). The tuple spellings copy too, but warn: `return (len(g.xs), g)` renders `{::tpy::__len__(g.xs), g}` and `return (t[1], t[0])` copies both members, each warning "copies C into owned storage (tuple element N); use copy()" -- truthful, but `copy()` is the wrong remedy, since nothing needs the source afterwards (probes `/tmp/agents/rv1sm/p19.py`, `/tmp/agents/rv1cg/ret6.py`). The last-use move keys on a bare NAME read, so a subscript of a dying owning tuple, or a name read again by a sibling member of the same result, never moves. Fix shape: at a return, move a member whose root dies with the return unless another member of the same result aliases that root; the warning then fires only where a copy remains.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud, wrong message) A subscript store into a list of tuples with a REFERENCE element is refused as a read-only target.** [`list-setitem-ref-tuple-false-readonly`] `xs[0] = (9, P(5))` on `xs: list[tuple[int32, P]]` (and `list[tuple[P, P]]`, and a nested `list[tuple[int32, tuple[int32, P]]]`) fails sema with "Cannot assign to elements of list[tuple[int32, P]] (read-only)", where CPython stores the tuple (verified 2026-09-22). A value-element tuple list (`list[tuple[int32, int32]]`) and `list[P]` store fine. The `MutableSequence[elem_type]` conformance check in `_analyze_assign` (`tpyc/sema/statements.py`) fails because `list.__setitem__` takes `value: Own[T]` and an `Own` of a tuple with a reference element normalizes per element, so the protocol's `__setitem__` does not match; the message then blames mutability. Fix shape: compare the setitem value slot with the per-element `Own` normalization on both sides, and keep the read-only message for a real read-only receiver (`Span[readonly[T]]`).
- **[LOW small] An `Array[T, N]` element in a tuple literal fails the C++ build.** `xs: list[tuple[int32, Array[P, 2]]] = [(1, Array[P, 2](c, c))]` emits a braced init g++ rejects (`array must be initialized with a brace-enclosed initializer`, then no matching `std::tuple` ctor). Toolchain-caught, not silent. The `std::array` member needs its own brace layer inside the tuple init. Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/nesttup/probe7.py`. Surfaced during /tpy-fix-bug of the nested-tuple-member depth limit (probing whether a value-typed `Array` hides a reference member the way a nested tuple does -- it never gets that far).
- **[MED small] An `@error_return` function returning a borrowed `T | None` emits ill-formed C++ -- compile failure, not silent.** `@error_return(E) def maybe(self, ok: bool) -> list[int32] | None: return self.items` lowers the return ABI to `std::expected<::tpy::val_or_ref<std::optional<std::vector<int32_t>>>, E>` (the `val_or_ref` wraps the whole Optional), but the body emits `return &(this->items);` (a `vector*`) for the borrow leg and `return nullptr;` for the None leg -- neither converts. The ABI wrap (`_resolve_return_type`, `tpyc/codegen_cpp/functions.py`) and the return-site emit disagree about where the nullability lives; the borrowed-Optional-return shape needs its own design (a `val_or_ref`-of-inner + null state, or a plain pointer payload). Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/er_alias/opt_ret.py`. Surfaced during /tpy-fix-bug of the @error_return borrow-alias fix.
- **[LOW small] Statement-level unwrap of a tuple-of-borrows payload fails the C++ build.** `kv = next(it)` over a `dict[K, Rec].items()` iterator inside `try` assigns the unwrapped payload tuple to the borrow-form local `std::tuple<K, Rec*>` with no element conversion (post-proxy-iterator shape: g++ rejects the tuple `operator=` on const-assignability of the element slots). Sibling of the storage-vs-borrow tuple conversion family; the fix is a per-element `tuple_to_pointer`-style conversion at the unwrap site, plus a function-scope materialization slot for any owned elements. Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/cluster7/next_items_try.py`. Surfaced during /tpy-fix-bug of the @error_return result-into-storage move; error shape updated by the dict-accessor aliasing work.
- **[LOW small] A list-literal `return` from an `@error_return` function with an `Own[list[T]]` return type emits a braced-init that cannot convert to the `std::expected`.** [`error-return-list-literal-return`] `@error_return(E) def make(n: int32) -> Own[list[int32]]: ... return [n, n + 1]` emits `return {n, ...};` -- ill-formed for `std::expected<std::vector<int32_t>, E>` (two user conversions). Binding the literal to a local and returning the local works (and now moves). Fix: wrap the literal in an explicit `std::vector<T>{...}` (or construct in place) when the enclosing function is `@error_return`. Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/er_move/owned_list2.py`. Also a tuple-local element: `return [t]` at `-> Own[list[tuple[P, P]]]` emits `return {::tpy::tuple_to_storage<..>(t)};` and fails the same way (`/tmp/agents/b2fix/s2.py`, 2026-09-24). Surfaced during /tpy-fix-bug of the @error_return result-into-storage move.
- **[MED, deferred: MIR] Silent capture-by-value divergence on in-place MUTATION of an escaping-closure capture (the reassignment half now warns).** [`escaping-capture-mutation-snapshot`] An escaping (`Callable`) closure captures a local by value, so the closure holds a snapshot taken at creation; CPython late-binds (captures the variable) and observes later changes. The *reassignment* half (`k = 10; f = hold(lambda: k); k = 20; print(f())` -> `10` in TPy vs `20` in CPython, and counters/aug-assign) now emits a compile-time warning (`_warn_stale_value_captures` in `tpyc/sema/analyzer.py`, covering escaping lambdas and nested defs). The remaining gap is **in-place mutation** of a captured container/record: `xs = [1, 2]; g = hold(lambda: xs[0]); xs[0] = 99; print(g())` prints `1` in TPy vs `99` in CPython with no warning -- the divergence is silent. Mechanism: codegen emits a by-value capture (`[xs]`, not `[&xs]`) because a by-reference capture into an escaping closure would dangle (`docs/CLOSURES_CALLABLE_DESIGN.md` capture table); TPy's no-cell zero-cost model has no shared cell, so the snapshot severs the alias. **Not fixable to match CPython** in the zero-cost model; the remedy is to extend the existing warning to the mutation case. **Blocked on** the mutation-after-capture fact, which is not tracked today (`closure_written_names` collects only `nonlocal`/`global` rebinds, not in-place field/element writes from nested-def bodies) -- see the `closure_written_names` "Closures mutating captures without `nonlocal`" entry in this section. Workaround: bind a fresh non-mutated snapshot (`snap = copy(xs)`) for the closure to capture. (Non-escaping `Fn` closures capture by reference and do NOT diverge -- escaping-`Callable` only.) **All three closure positions behave alike**: a sync body, the single-yield generator peephole (whose wrapper lambda captures the param `[&xs]` and the inner closure copies out of it), and a resumable frame (whose member reads into a by-value init-capture, `[xs = xs]`) each copy the container at the escaping slot. Pinned by the `copied` section of `tests/cases/nested_def/frame_lambda_snapshot` (a `no_cpython` case -- the divergence is the point), whose non-escaping `Fn` twin in `tests/cases/nested_def/lambda_in_gen_method` aliases and agrees with CPython. A **`Callable` FIELD** reached through an ordinary method parameter is the same face and is equally silent: `b.set(lambda: xs[0])` storing into `Box.cb: Callable[[], int32]`, then `xs[0] = 99`, prints `1` under TPy and `99` under CPython with no diagnostic (`/tmp/agents/fn_doc_probes/p_hold.py`, measured 2026-09-15 on 0.6.0.dev0).
- **[MED small] (rejects valid code, raw toolchain spew) A lambda nested inside another lambda never captures transitively, so a name only the INNER one reads is missing from the outer's capture list and the C++ build fails.** [`nested-lambda-no-transitive-capture`] `apply(lambda x: apply(lambda y: y + n, x), 1)` over a local or param `n` emits `apply([](int32_t x) -> int32_t { return apply([n](int32_t y) ... ; }, 1)` -- the outer capture list is empty, so g++ reports `error: 'n' is not captured`. Inside a resumable frame the same source is the frame face of it, `error: 'this' was not captured for this lambda function` followed by `invalid use of non-static data member '__gen_outer_only::n'`, because the inner entry is the frame member's init-capture (`[n = n]`) and the outer supplies nothing to read it from. Root cause is one fact, not two: `TpyLambda.children()` returns `[]` (a lambda is its own scope), so `collect_name_refs` in `_analyze_lambda_with_fn_hint` (`tpyc/sema/expressions.py`) never sees a free name that occurs only under a nested lambda, and `captured_names` is computed per lambda with no transitive closure. PRE-EXISTING and position-independent -- the plain sync free function fails identically, so this is not a property of the frame capture rule. Fix shape: union each nested lambda's own `captured_names` into the enclosing lambda's, minus the enclosing lambda's params; that also has to decide the enclosing entry's MODE (an inner by-value capture read out of an outer by-reference one composes, the reverse does not) and feed the escape/stale-capture analyses the widened set, which is why it is not a capture-list one-liner. Repro `/tmp/agents/fr14b/nested_lambda.py` (frame) and `nested_lambda_sync.py` (sync). Found by the fix round on the frame lambda capture rule 2026-09-10. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED] Loop-variable capture into an escaping closure diverges silently from CPython, with no warning.** `for k in range(n): funcs.append(hold(lambda: k))` then calling the collected closures gives `0,1,...,n-1` in TPy but `n-1,n-1,...` in CPython. Each TPy closure snapshots the loop var by value at the iteration it is created; CPython shares one cell, so every closure sees the final value (the classic Python loop-capture gotcha). TPy's result is arguably the more intuitive one, but it is still a divergence and there is no diagnostic. The `_warn_stale_value_captures` reassignment warning deliberately does NOT cover this: the rebinding is the loop back-edge (the loop var is re-bound at the closure's own statement, not a later one), and a fix needs loop-back awareness plus a decision on the reversed-divergence direction (warn even though TPy is "more correct"?). Workaround: bind a per-iteration fresh local is no help (same edge); capture into a per-iteration default arg or restructure. Reachable today via `hold(lambda: k)` (the `hold` Callable context lets the lambda infer its type inside the loop). The resumable FRAME position behaves the same and is equally unwarned: a lambda over a loop variable the frame stores as a member reads it into a by-value init-capture, so each closure keeps its own iteration's value. Measured (`/tmp/agents/fr14b/loopvar2.py`, three closures collected then called): TPy prints `0 1 2` in a sync body and `0` / `3` across a two-yield generator's two pulls, CPython `2 2 2` and `2` / `4`. The single-yield peephole was probed too and does not discriminate -- only the last closure survives there, and its snapshot equals CPython's final cell value -- so it is untested rather than known-divergent. Surfaced by /tpy-review (cpython-parity) of the escaping-capture warning.
- **[LOW small] (rejects valid code, loud) A tuple-unpack discard of a float, bytes, bool or None LITERAL is unlowered.** [`tuple-unpack-literal-discard-unlowered`] `c, _ = (n, 1.5)` errors `this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.expr_stmt:expr_stmt.float_literal)`; `b"x"`, `True` and `None` in the `_` slot reject the same way (`expr_stmt.bytes_literal` / `bool_literal` / `none_literal`). A `str` literal in that slot compiles and emits no statement at all. The parser's `_maybe_desugar_tuple_literal_unpack` (`tpyc/parse/parser.py`) turns a `_` slot into `TpyExprStmt(elt_expr)`, and the expression-statement lowering (`tpyc/thir/lower/statements.py`) has a void-cast row for an int literal, a name and the operator forms (`k, _ = (2, 0)` renders `(void)(0);`, `a, _ = (n + 1, n)` renders `(void)(n);`) but none for these four. Fix shape: one literal row in that arm rather than a row per literal kind. All five literal kinds probed 2026-09-21. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[LOW small] (rejects valid code, loud) A container conversion as a bare statement is unlowered while its bound form compiles.** [`container-conversion-bare-statement-unlowered`] `list(xs)` / `set(xs)` in statement position errors `this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (expr.call)`; `v = list(xs)` compiles, and CPython accepts both. The discarded record constructors and scalar conversions (`Tick(k)`, `str(s)`, `int32(k)`) lower, so the gap is the container-conversion arm's DISCARD use, not the statement arm. Nobody writes this for effect, which is why it is LOW; it matters only as the one type-call family a discarded statement still rejects. The RENDER half of the same discarded-statement gap is `BUGS.md#discarded-value-bare-statement-family`. Found by the cpython-parity review of the discarded-constructor fix, 2026-09-21. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED medium] (one SILENT miscompile, the rest loud) A discarded value whose callee is NOT a type still renders as a bare C++ statement, and one of those renders is a declaration.** [`discarded-value-bare-statement-family`] The expression-statement lowering casts a discarded CONSTRUCTION to void (a `THIRCtorCall`, or a `THIRCall` whose arm recorded a type callee), because `T(name);` in statement position declares `name`. The fact it keys on -- "the callee is a type" -- is narrower than the fact the render needs -- "a non-void value is discarded". Measured 2026-09-21: `copy(xs)` as a statement renders `std::array<int32_t, 3>(xs);`, and `copy(s)` renders `std::string_view(s);` for a view-typed `s` or `std::string(s);` for a `str` parameter -- a FUNCTION callee whose `@cpp_template` is a functional cast, so in a nested block it declares an uninitialized shadow of the argument and later reads of the name see garbage (silent; CPython prints the real values). The loud members fail only under the suite's strict `-Werror` set and build under the default `tpy` flags: `StrView(sv)` renders `sv;`, `round(k)` renders `(k);`, `chr(k)` renders `static_cast<char>(k);`, `ord("a")` folds to `97;`, `abs(k)` renders `::std::abs(k);` (verified to build and run under default flags on gcc and clang), and clang rejects `::std::min(k, 3);` as a discarded nodiscard result. The type-callee arms that lower to a `THIRCall` without the flag (the viewfam / span / native-iter instantiation arms, `call.instantiation_template`, `ctor.ptr_null`) belong to the same gap. This is a REDESIGN of the verdict, not another arm: the rule has already had two shapes (an AST-spelling predicate, then a per-arm flag), so the next change starts from a verdict matrix of discarded-expression kind by render mechanism built on master. Two candidate rules, both changing existing snapshots: cast whenever the lowered node's `result_type` is non-void (the fact is already on every node; reverses the bare-call render `tests/cases/list/discarded_container_result` pins, touching a few hundred cases by a rough name-keyed estimate), or cast a constructor node plus any non-void `cpp_template` render (on the order of ten snapshots; leaves `abs` and the folded literal as residue). Nobody writes a discarded `copy()` for effect, which is why a silent member rates MED. The REJECT half of the same gap is `BUGS.md#container-conversion-bare-statement-unlowered`. Found by the closing review of the discarded-constructor fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

- **[MED small] (rejects valid code, loud) A NESTED-class constructor drops the `std::move` on an `Own[T]` argument that every other constructor spelling emits.** [`nested-ctor-own-arg-not-moved`] With `class Outer: class Inner: def __init__(self, c: Own[C])`, `x = Outer.Inner(c)` renders `Outer::Inner(c)` against `explicit Inner(C&& c)`, a hard C++ error; the bare (`Inner(c)`), module-qualified and `@inline`-expanded spellings all render `std::move(c)`. Value position and statement position alike, so it is the nested-constructor arm's argument lowering (`tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py`, the `is_nested_constructor` arm, whose own comment says "args render plainly"), not a discard bug. Always a compile error, never a silent copy. Reproduced twice in review, 2026-09-21. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects-valid, loud)** A *mutable* recursive-union wrapper param that is variant-narrowed and then WRITTEN through the narrowed alternative is a hard compile error. `type JsonValue = int32 | dict[str, JsonValue]` with `def g(v: JsonValue) -> None: if isinstance(v, dict): v["k"] = 1` fails with `error: in function 'g': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.assign:setitem.const_narrowed_recv)`.
